With that he began to put on his armor. And then, Menelaus, your life would have come to its end at the hands of Hector, far the stronger man, had not the Greek leaders sprung up and held you back. Agamemnon himself, lord of men, caught his brother by the right hand and said: "This is madness, Menelaus. You don't need such folly. Hold back, hard as it is, and don't long to fight a man stronger than you — Hector, son of Priam, whom others dread as well. Even Achilles, far the better man, shrinks from meeting him in the fighting where men win glory. Go, sit down among your own people, and the Greeks will send out another champion against him. Fearless as Hector is, and greedy for battle, I think he will be glad enough to rest his knees, if he comes out of this fight alive, out of the brunt of it."

So the warrior spoke, and with sound words he turned his brother's heart; and Menelaus obeyed, and his attendants gladly took the armor from his shoulders. Then Nestor rose and spoke among them: "Now grief has truly fallen on the land of Greece. How the old horseman Peleus would groan to hear it — that fine speaker and counselor of the Myrmidons, who loved, when I was in his house, to ask me about the breeding and the line of all the Greeks. If he heard that they all cower now before Hector, he would lift his hands again and again to the immortal gods and pray that the life leave his body and go down to the house of Hades. By father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo — if only I were young again, as I was when the men of Pylos and the Arcadians fought by the rushing river Celadon, under the walls of Pheia, around the streams of the Iardanus. Their champion was the godlike Ereuthalion, with the armor of King Areithous on his shoulders — Areithous whom everyone, men and women alike, called the Mace-man, because he fought with neither bow nor spear but broke the enemy's ranks with an iron club. Lycurgus killed him, not by fair strength but by cunning, trapping him in a narrow pass where the club was no use to him; for Lycurgus got in first and ran him through the middle with a spear, and the man fell on his back to the ground. Then Lycurgus stripped the armor that Ares had given him and wore it himself in battle ever after; but when he grew old at home, he gave it to his faithful attendant Ereuthalion to wear. And Ereuthalion, in that armor, challenged the best of us. They all hung back, shaking with fear; not one would face him. But my proud heart drove me to take him on, hot as I was — and I was the youngest of them all. So I fought him, and Athena gave me the victory. He was the biggest, strongest man I ever killed, and he covered a great stretch of ground, sprawling there. If only I were young again, with that strength still in me — then Hector, son of Priam, would soon find his match. But you who are the best of the whole army, not one of you has the stomach to face Hector."

So the old man shamed them, and nine men sprang to their feet. First of all rose Agamemnon, lord of men, and after him brave Diomedes, son of Tydeus; then the two named Ajax, clothed in furious courage; and after them Idomeneus and his comrade-in-arms Meriones; then Eurypylus, son of Euaemon, and Thoas, son of Andraemon, and Odysseus too. All of these were ready to fight Hector. Then Nestor, the horseman of Gerene, spoke again: "Cast lots, all of you, to see who is chosen. The man who wins it will do good service to the Greeks, and to his own heart too, if he comes out of this fight alive."

So he spoke, and each man marked his lot and threw it into the helmet of Agamemnon, son of Atreus. And the soldiers lifted their hands in prayer to the gods, and one of them would say, looking up at the wide sky: "Father Zeus, let the lot fall to Ajax, or to the son of Tydeus, or to the king of rich Mycenae himself."

So they prayed, and Nestor, the horseman of Gerene, shook the helmet, and out leapt the very lot they wanted — the lot of Ajax. The herald carried it through the crowd and showed it to all the chiefs of the Greeks, going left to right, but none of them owned it. Only when he came at last to the man who had marked it and dropped it in did brave Ajax hold out his hand, and the herald stopped and laid it in his palm. Ajax looked at the mark, knew it, and was glad. He threw it to the ground at his feet and said: "My friends — the lot is mine, and my heart is glad, for I think I will beat glorious Hector. Come now, while I put on my armor, pray to lord Zeus, the son of Cronus — quietly among yourselves, so the Trojans won't hear, or aloud if you like, for we are afraid of no one. No man will drive me off against my will, by force or by skill, for I was not born and raised on Salamis to be a fool in war."

So he spoke, and they prayed to lord Zeus, the son of Cronus, and one of them would say, looking up at the wide sky: "Father Zeus, who rule from Ida, most glorious, most great — grant the victory to Ajax and let him win bright glory. But if you love Hector too and care for him, then give the two of them equal strength and equal fame."

So they prayed, and Ajax armed himself in gleaming bronze. When the armor was all on his body, he strode out like monstrous Ares, who goes among men when the son of Cronus sets them fighting in heart-eating strife. So huge Ajax sprang forward, the bulwark of the Greeks, with a grim smile on his face, taking long strides and shaking his long spear. The Greeks rejoiced to look at him, but a hard trembling came over the limbs of the Trojans, every man, and the heart of Hector himself beat fast in his chest. But there was no drawing back for him now, no slipping away into the ranks behind, for he was the one who had given the challenge. Ajax came on, holding his shield before him like a wall — bronze, with seven folds of ox-hide, the work of Tychius, far the best leather-worker in Hyle, who had made it from the hides of seven well-fed bulls and laid an eighth layer of bronze over them. Holding this shield before his chest, Ajax, son of Telamon, came close up to Hector and spoke his threat: "Hector, now you'll learn, man to man, what kind of champions the Greeks still have, even apart from Achilles, the lion-hearted breaker of men. He lies by the curved ships now, nursing his anger at Agamemnon, shepherd of the people — but there are plenty of us able to face you. Begin the fight."

And great Hector of the gleaming helmet answered him: "Ajax, son of Telamon, sprung from Zeus, leader of armies — don't try me like some weak boy, or a woman who knows nothing of war. I know war and the killing of men. I know how to swing my ox-hide shield to the right and to the left — that, I think, is the art of standing one's ground. I know how to charge into the rush of chariots and horses; I know, in the close fight, how to step the dance of murderous Ares. But I won't strike a man like you on the sly, watching for a chance. I'll hit you in the open, if I can."

He spoke, drew back his long spear, and hurled it. It struck the dread sevenfold shield of Ajax on the outermost layer, the eighth, which was bronze, and tore through six of the folds, but the seventh hide stopped it. Then Ajax, sprung from Zeus, hurled in his turn and struck the round shield of the son of Priam. The heavy spear drove through the gleaming shield and pressed on into the finely-worked breastplate; it ripped the tunic against his flank, but Hector swerved aside and escaped death. Then both of them pulled the long spears free and fell on each other like ravening lions, or wild boars whose strength is not easily worn down. The son of Priam struck the center of Ajax's shield, but the bronze did not break, and the point of his spear was bent back. Then Ajax sprang in and pierced Hector's shield; the spear punched straight through and checked him in his charge, and it grazed his neck, and the dark blood welled up. But even so Hector of the gleaming helmet did not stop fighting. He gave ground and seized in his broad hand a stone lying on the plain, black and jagged and huge, and hurled it and hit the great seven-layered shield of Ajax on the boss in its middle, so that the bronze rang loud. But Ajax caught up a far bigger stone, whirled it around, and let it fly with all his strength behind it. This boulder, big as a millstone, smashed Hector's shield inward and knocked his knees out from under him; he was thrown flat on his back, pinned beneath the shield — but Apollo lifted him up at once. And now the two of them would have closed and slashed each other with their swords, had not the heralds, the messengers of gods and men, come between them — one from the Trojans, one from the Greeks, Talthybius and Idaeus, both wise men. They held their staves out between the fighters, and the good herald Idaeus spoke: "Stop now, dear sons. Fight no more. Zeus who gathers the clouds loves you both, and you are both spearmen — that much we all know. But night is coming on, and it is good to give way to the night."
Ajax, son of Telamon, answered: "Idaeus, tell Hector to say so himself — for he was the one who called our best men out to fight. Let him speak first, and whatever he says, I'll agree to it."

Then great Hector of the gleaming helmet said: "Ajax, since a god gave you size and strength and good sense, and you are the best of the Greeks with a spear, let us break off the fight and the killing for today. Another day we'll fight again, until the gods decide between us and give the victory to one of us. Night is coming on, and it is good to give way to the night. Go now and gladden the hearts of the Greeks beside your ships, and most of all your own people and your kinsmen; and I will go through the great city of King Priam and gladden the Trojans and the Trojan women in their long robes, who will be praying for me in the temples. But come — let us trade gifts with each other, so that men may say, Greeks and Trojans both: 'They fought each other in heart-eating strife, and then they parted, joined in friendship.'"

So speaking, he gave Ajax a sword studded with silver, with its scabbard and its well-cut belt; and Ajax gave him a war-belt bright with purple. So the two of them parted, the one going to the army of the Greeks, the other to the throng of the Trojans, who rejoiced to see him coming back to them alive and whole, safe from the fury and the unbeatable hands of Ajax; and they brought him into the city, hardly daring to believe he was saved. On the other side, the Greeks led Ajax, glad of his victory, to noble Agamemnon.

When they had come to the huts of the son of Atreus, Agamemnon, lord of men, sacrificed an ox for them, a male of five years, to the almighty son of Cronus. They flayed it and made it ready, cut it all into joints, sliced the meat with care, ran it on the spits, roasted it through, and drew it off. When the work was done and the feast was ready, they ate, and no man's hunger went unsatisfied at the shared meal; and Agamemnon, the warrior son of Atreus, gave Ajax the long cuts of the chine to honor him. And when they had put away their desire for food and drink, the old man Nestor, whose counsel had always proved the best, was first to weave his thoughts before them; and with good will he spoke:

"Son of Atreus, and you other leaders of the Greeks — many of the long-haired Greeks are dead now, their dark blood spilled by Ares along the lovely streams of the Scamander, and their souls have gone down to the house of Hades. So when morning comes you should hold the fighting back. We will gather our dead and bring them in on wagons drawn by oxen and mules, and burn them a little way from the ships, so that each of us may carry home the bones of his fallen comrades to their children, when we sail back to our own land. And around the pyre let us heap one single mound, raised from the plain for all in common. Close by it let us build a high wall, a shelter for ourselves and for our ships, and set well-fitted gates in it so that there is a road through for our chariots. And just outside it let us dig a deep trench all the way around, to hold off their horses and their men, so the proud Trojans can never break in upon us."

So he spoke, and all the leaders shouted their approval. Meanwhile the Trojans held an assembly up on the height of Troy, by the gates of Priam's palace, an angry, turbulent assembly. And wise Antenor was the first to speak: "Hear me, Trojans and Dardanians and allies, while I say what is in my heart. Come — let us give Argive Helen and all her wealth back to the sons of Atreus, and let them take her away. We are fighting now as men who have broken their sworn truce, and I see no good coming of it for us, unless we do as I say."

So he spoke, and sat down. Then Paris, the husband of lovely-haired Helen, rose among them and answered with winged words: "Antenor, what you say does not please me. You can think of a better word than this if you choose. But if you have really said it in earnest, then the gods themselves have destroyed your wits. I will speak out plainly among the horse-taming Trojans: I say it straight — I will not give up the woman. But the wealth I brought home with her from Argos, all of that I am willing to give back, and to add still more of my own."

So he spoke and sat down, and Priam rose among them, of the line of Dardanus, who matched the gods in counsel; and with good will he spoke before them: "Hear me, Trojans and Dardanians and allies, while I say what is in my heart. Take your supper now through the city as you always have, and remember to keep the watch, every man awake. At first light let Idaeus go down to the hollow ships and tell Agamemnon and Menelaus, the sons of Atreus, the offer of Paris, through whom this quarrel began. And let him put this wise word to them as well: ask whether they will hold off from the bitter fighting until we have burned our dead. Afterward we will fight again, until the gods decide between us and hand the victory to one side or the other."

So he spoke, and they heard him and obeyed. They took their supper through the army in their companies, and at first light Idaeus went down to the ships. He found the Greeks, the men of Ares, in assembly by the stern of Agamemnon's ship, and the loud-voiced herald stood in their midst and spoke: "Son of Atreus, and you other leaders of the Greeks — Priam and the other noble Trojans have sent me to tell you, in hope you will find it acceptable, the offer of Paris, through whom this quarrel began. All the treasure that Paris carried in his hollow ships to Troy — would that he had died first — he is willing to give back, and to add still more of his own; but the wedded wife of glorious Menelaus he says he will not give up, though the Trojans urge him to it. And they told me to ask this too: whether you will hold off from the bitter fighting until we have burned our dead. Afterward we will fight again, until the gods decide between us and hand the victory to one side or the other."

So he spoke, and they all sat silent. At last Diomedes of the great war cry spoke out: "Let no one take anything now from Paris — not the treasure, and not Helen either. Even a fool can see it: the noose of destruction is already around the Trojans' necks."

So he spoke, and all the sons of the Greeks shouted their approval, marveling at the words of Diomedes, breaker of horses. Then lord Agamemnon said to Idaeus: "Idaeus, you have heard for yourself the answer of the Greeks; it is theirs, and it is mine as well. But as for the dead — I do not begrudge you the burning of them. When men are dead there is no holding back the swift mercy of fire. Let Zeus be witness to it, the loud-thundering husband of Hera."

So he spoke, and held up his scepter to all the gods, and Idaeus went back to holy Troy. The Trojans and Dardanians were sitting gathered in assembly, all of them waiting for him to return; and when he came he stood in their midst and gave them the message. Then they set quickly to their double task — some to gather the dead, others to bring in wood. And on their side the Greeks too hurried out from their benched ships, some to gather the dead, others to bring in wood.

The sun was just striking the fields, rising fresh into the sky out of the deep, slow-flowing stream of Ocean, when the two armies met on the plain. It was hard to know each man for who he had been; but they washed the clotted blood from the corpses, and weeping hot tears, lifted them onto the wagons. Priam had forbidden the Trojans to wail aloud, so they piled their dead on the pyre in silence, grieving in their hearts, and when they had burned them they went back to holy Troy. And in the same way the Greeks piled their dead on the pyre in silence, grieving in their hearts, and when they had burned them they went back to the hollow ships.

In the twilight, while it was still not day, chosen men of the Greeks gathered around the pyre and heaped a single mound, raised from the plain for all in common. Close beside it they built a high wall, a shelter for themselves and for their ships, and set strong gates in it so that there was a road through for the chariots. And just outside it they dug a deep, wide trench, and planted sharp stakes along it.

So the long-haired Greeks labored; and the gods, sitting beside Zeus the lord of lightning, looked on in wonder at the great work of the bronze-armored Greeks. But Poseidon, who shakes the earth, spoke among them: "Father Zeus — is there any mortal left on the wide earth who will tell the gods his mind, and trust them, after this? Don't you see? The long-haired Greeks have built a wall around their ships and run a trench around it, and they offered no fine sacrifice to the gods. The fame of this wall will spread as far as the dawn itself spreads its light — and men will forget the wall that Phoebus Apollo and I toiled to raise for the hero Laomedon."

Deeply troubled, Zeus who gathers the clouds answered him: "What a thing to say, you who shake the wide earth. Some other god, weaker than you, might be afraid of this scheme of theirs; but your fame spreads as far as the dawn itself spreads its light. Take heart. Once the long-haired Greeks have gone home in their ships to their own land, then break this wall down, every stone of it, and sweep it into the sea, and cover the long beach again with sand. So the great wall of the Greeks will be wiped away."

So they spoke to each other; and as the sun went down the work of the Greeks was finished, and they slaughtered oxen by their huts and took their meal. Many ships had come in from Lemnos carrying wine, sent by Euneus, son of Jason, whom Hypsipyle bore to Jason, shepherd of the people. To the sons of Atreus alone, to Agamemnon and Menelaus, the son of Jason had given a thousand measures of wine to carry over. From these ships the long-haired Greeks bought their wine, some paying with bronze, some with gleaming iron, some with hides, some with whole cattle on the hoof, and some with slaves; and they spread a rich feast. All night long the long-haired Greeks feasted, and so did the Trojans and their allies in the city. And all that night Zeus, the lord of counsel, was plotting evil for them, and he thundered terribly. Pale fear took hold of them, and they poured the wine from their cups onto the ground, and no man dared drink until he had poured an offering to the almighty son of Cronus. Then at last they lay down and took the gift of sleep.
books.title: The Duel of Hector and Ajax

books.label: Book VIII
paragraphs: When Dawn in her saffron robe had spread her light across the earth, Zeus who loves the thunder called the gods to council on the highest peak of jagged Olympus. He spoke, and all of them listened. “Hear me,” he said, “gods and goddesses, while I tell you what is in my mind. Let none of you, female or male, try to cross my will. Obey me, every one, so that I can bring this to its end. If I catch any god slipping off to help the Trojans or the Greeks, he’ll come back to Olympus beaten and ashamed — or I’ll seize him and fling him down into the murk of Tartarus, far off, into the deepest pit under the earth, where the gates are iron and the floor is bronze, as far below Hades as the sky is high above the ground. Then he’ll learn how much the strongest of all I am.

“Test me, if you like, and find out for yourselves. Hang a golden chain from heaven and lay hold of it, all of you, gods and goddesses together — you will never drag Zeus, the high lord of counsel, down from the sky to the earth, pull as you may. But if I cared to haul on it myself, I’d drag you all up, and the earth and the sea along with you. Then I’d tie the chain to a horn of Olympus and leave the whole world dangling in the air. That is how far I am above all gods and men.”

They went silent, all of them, struck by the force of his words. At last bright-eyed Athena spoke up. “Father, son of Cronus, highest of kings — we know your strength is not to be denied. But it grieves us to watch the Greek warriors die, meeting so hard an end. We’ll keep clear of the fighting, since you command it. But let us at least drop a word of good counsel to the Greeks, so they don’t all perish under your anger.”
Zeus who gathers the clouds smiled at her. “Take heart, my child. I don’t mean it as harshly as it sounds; I want to be kind to you.”

With that he yoked his swift horses, their hooves bronze, their manes streaming gold. He wrapped his own body in gold, took up his golden whip, and stepped into the chariot. He cracked the lash, and the horses sprang forward willingly, midway between earth and the starry sky. He came to Ida of the many springs, mother of wild beasts, to Gargarus, where his sacred grove and his fragrant altar stand. There the father of gods and men reined in his horses, freed them from the chariot, and folded a thick cloud around them; and he sat down on the heights in his glory, looking out over the city of Troy and the ships of the Greeks.

The Greeks ate a quick meal among the ships and buckled on their armor. The Trojans armed as well, all through the city — fewer in number, but driven on by need, ready to fight for their wives and their children. The gates were thrown open, and out poured the army, foot and horse, with the tramp of a great host.

When the two sides came together, shield struck shield, spear struck spear, and the fury of armored men met head-on. The bossed shields ground against each other, and the air filled with a great roar — the screams of the dying and the shouts of those who killed them — and the earth ran with blood.

All through the morning, while the day climbed, the weapons bit on both sides and men kept falling. But when the sun stood at the top of the sky, the Father lifted his golden scales. In them he set two fates of death, two heavy dooms — one for the Trojans, one for the Greeks — and he took the balance by the middle and raised it high. The Greeks’ day sank. Their doom settled down to the ground that feeds us all, while the Trojans’ fate rose toward the sky. Then he thundered loud from Ida and hurled the flash of his lightning down on the Greeks; and when they saw it, a pale fear took them, and they were afraid.

Idomeneus did not dare to hold his ground, nor did Agamemnon, nor either of the two named Ajax. Only Nestor, the old horseman of Gerene, stood firm, the bulwark of the Greeks — and not by choice, for one of his horses was crippled. Paris, the husband of lovely Helen, had hit it with an arrow on the crown of the head, where the mane first springs from the skull, the deadliest place. The horse reared in agony as the point drove into its brain and threw the team into chaos. The old man set to slashing the traces with his sword, but Hector’s fast horses came bearing down on him through the rout, with their bold driver — Hector himself. The old man would have died there and then, had Diomedes not seen it in time. He called out to Odysseus with a great shout.

“Odysseus,” he cried, “son of Laertes, where are you running to, with your back turned like a coward? Watch you don’t take a spear between the shoulders in flight. Stay and help me hold off this man from the old one.”

But Odysseus would not hear him; he sped past, on toward the Greek ships. So the son of Tydeus drove in alone, into the thick of it, and pulled up before the horses of old Nestor. “Sir,” he said, “these young fighters are pressing you hard. Your strength is spent, and age weighs on you; your driver is no use to you, and your horses are slow. Up into my chariot — see what the horses of Tros can do, how they fly across the plain in chase or in flight. I took them from Aeneas. Let our squires look after your team, and we’ll drive these straight at the Trojans, so Hector finds out how my spear can rage too.”

Nestor, the horseman of Gerene, did as he said. The two sturdy squires, Sthenelus and kind Eurymedon, took charge of Nestor’s horses, and the two heroes mounted Diomedes’ chariot. Nestor caught up the reins and lashed the horses on, and they closed fast on Hector. The son of Tydeus let fly a spear at him as he charged straight at them. He missed Hector, but struck his driver and squire, Eniopeus son of brave Thebaeus, in the chest by the nipple, the reins still in his hands; and he died on the spot, and the horses shied as he pitched headlong from the car. Grief took Hector for the loss of his driver, but he let him lie for all his sorrow and went looking for another, and his horses did not lack a hand for long: he soon found brave Archeptolemus, son of Iphitus, and set him up behind the team and put the reins in his grip.

Now disaster would have come, past all undoing — the Trojans would have been penned in Troy like sheep — had the father of gods and men not seen it quickly. He thundered and hurled a blazing thunderbolt; it struck the ground just in front of Diomedes’ horses, and a terrible flame of burning sulfur leapt up. The horses cringed and backed under the car, and the reins dropped from Nestor’s hands. He was afraid, and said to Diomedes, “Son of Tydeus, turn the horses and run. Don’t you see that the hand of Zeus is against you? Today he gives the glory to Hector. Tomorrow, if he pleases, he’ll give it back to us. No man, however brave, can turn aside the will of Zeus, for he is far the stronger.”

Diomedes answered, “All of that is true, old man. But here is the grief that cuts me to the heart: someday Hector will say among the Trojans, ‘The son of Tydeus ran from me to the ships.’ That is the boast he’ll make — and on that day, let the earth open and swallow me.”
“Son of Tydeus,” Nestor said, “what are you saying? Even if Hector calls you a coward, the Trojans and the Dardanians won’t believe it, nor the wives of all the strong men you have laid in the dust.”

With that he wheeled the horses back through the press of battle, and the Trojans, with Hector at their head, sent their spears raining after them, screaming in triumph. Hector shouted at him: “Son of Tydeus, the Greeks used to give you the best seat at the table, the choicest meat, your cup filled to the brim. Now they’ll have nothing but contempt for you, for you’ve turned out no better than a woman. Off with you, you trembling girl! You’ll never climb our walls while I flinch aside, never carry our wives off in your ships. Before that, I’ll kill you with my own hand.”

The son of Tydeus was torn — should he turn the horses around and fight him? Three times he was on the point of it, and three times Zeus thundered from the heights of Ida, a sign to the Trojans that he was turning the battle their way. Then Hector called out to his men: “Trojans, Lycians, Dardanians who fight up close — be men, my friends, and fight with all your strength. I can see that Zeus means to grant me the victory and the great glory, and to deal ruin to the Greeks. Fools — to think this flimsy, worthless wall could stop me. My horses will clear that ditch at a bound, and when I’m in among the ships, don’t forget to bring me fire, so I can burn them, and cut the Greeks down beside them, blind and choking in the smoke.”

Then he called to his horses: “Xanthus, Podargus, Aethon, and noble Lampus — pay me back now for your keep, for all the honey-sweet grain Andromache, daughter of great Eetion, has fed you, mixing wine for you to drink whenever you wished, sooner than for me, her own husband. After them, fast — let us take the shield of Nestor, whose fame goes up to heaven, all of it solid gold, the arm-bars and all; and strip from the shoulders of Diomedes the breastplate Hephaestus forged for him. If we can take those two things, the Greeks will be aboard their ships and gone this very night.”

So he boasted; and queen Hera, shaking with anger on her throne, made high Olympus quake. She turned to mighty Poseidon and said, “What now, wide-ruling lord of the earthquake? Doesn’t your heart pity the dying Greeks, who bring you so many welcome gifts at Helice and at Aegae? Wish them the victory, then. If all of us who side with the Greeks were to drive the Trojans back and hold off Zeus, he could sit and sulk by himself up there on Ida.”
Lord Poseidon was troubled, and answered, “Hera, reckless tongue, what are you saying? I will not have the rest of us set ourselves against Zeus. He is far the stronger.”

While they talked, the whole space the ditch enclosed, from the ships out to the wall, was packed with horses and shield-bearers — penned there by Hector, son of Priam, now that Zeus was with him. He would have set the ships ablaze, had not queen Hera put it in Agamemnon’s mind to rouse himself and rally the Greeks. So he went along the ships and the huts, holding a great purple cloak in his hand, and took his stand by the huge black hull of Odysseus’ ship, which lay in the middle of the line, so his voice would carry both ways — to the huts of Ajax, son of Telamon, on the one side, and to those of Achilles on the other; for these two, sure of their own strength, had drawn their ships up at the two ends of the camp. From there he shouted to the Greeks in a voice that reached them all: “Shame on you, Greeks — men in name only, splendid only to look at. Where are all our boasts now, when we swore we were the best, the brave words we threw around on Lemnos, gorging on the meat of cattle and filling the wine bowls to the brim? Each of us vowed he’d stand against a hundred Trojans, two hundred — and now we’re no match for one, for Hector, who’ll soon have our ships in flames. Father Zeus, did you ever so ruin a great king and strip him of his glory? And yet, on this cursed voyage, I never let my ship pass one of your altars without burning the fat and the thigh-bones of oxen on it, so set was I on sacking the strong city of Troy. Grant me this much, Zeus: let us at least escape with our lives, and don’t let the Greeks be broken so utterly by the Trojans.”

So he prayed, and the Father pitied his tears and granted that his people would live and not die. At once he sent an eagle, the surest of all his omens, with a fawn in its talons; and it dropped the fawn beside the splendid altar where the Greeks sacrificed to Zeus, lord of omens. When the men saw that the bird had come from Zeus, they fell on the Trojans with fresh fury and threw themselves back into the fight.

Then, of all the Greeks — and they were many — not one could claim he drove his horses across the ditch and out to the fighting ahead of the son of Tydeus. He was the first by far to kill an armed Trojan, Agelaus son of Phradmon, who had turned his horses to flee; the spear caught him in the back, between the shoulders, and drove on through his chest, and his armor rang around him as he fell forward from the car.

After Diomedes came Agamemnon and Menelaus, the sons of Atreus; then the two named Ajax, clothed in fighting courage; then Idomeneus and his comrade Meriones, a match for the murderous war-god; then Eurypylus, the brave son of Euaemon. Ninth came Teucer with his bow, bent and taking cover behind the shield of Ajax, son of Telamon. Ajax would lift the shield aside, and Teucer would peer out, pick a man in the crowd, and shoot him dead; then he’d duck back to Ajax like a child to its mother, and Ajax would hide him again under the shield.

Which of the Trojans did Teucer bring down first? Orsilochus, then Ormenus and Ophelestes, Daetor and Chromius and godlike Lycophontes, Amopaon son of Polyaemon, and Melanippus. One after another he laid them on the earth, and Agamemnon, lord of men, was glad to see him cutting the Trojans down with his great bow. He came and stood by him and said, “Teucer, my friend, son of Telamon, captain of the host — shoot on. Be the saving of the Greeks and the glory of your father Telamon, who raised you in his own house and cared for you, child though you were born outside his marriage. Win him glory now, far away as he is. And I tell you, and I’ll see it done: if Zeus who wields the storm-shield, and Athena, ever let me sack the strong city of Troy, you’ll have the first prize of honor after my own — a tripod, or a chariot and two horses, or a woman to share your bed.”

Teucer answered, “Most noble son of Atreus, why urge me on when I’m already willing? From the moment we began driving them back toward Troy, I have never stopped watching for men to bring down with my arrows. Eight barbed shafts I’ve let fly, and every one has buried itself in the flesh of some young fighter — but this mad dog, I can’t hit.”

As he spoke he loosed another arrow straight at Hector, set on killing him. He missed again, but the shaft struck Priam’s brave son Gorgythion in the chest — whose mother, lovely Castianeira, fair as a goddess, had come as a bride from Aesyme. His head sank to one side, like a garden poppy heavy with seed and the rains of spring; just so his head drooped under the weight of his helmet.

Again Teucer aimed at Hector, longing to hit him, and again the arrow missed, for Apollo turned it aside. But it struck Hector’s brave driver Archeptolemus in the chest by the nipple as he drove furiously into the fight. The horses shied as he pitched headlong from the car, and the life went out of him. Grief took Hector for the loss of his driver, but he let him lie for all his sorrow and called to his brother Cebriones, who was near, to take the reins. Cebriones did as he was told. And Hector, with a great shout, leapt down from the chariot to the ground, snatched up a great stone, and made straight for Teucer, meaning to kill him. Teucer had just drawn an arrow from his quiver and laid it on the string. But as he drew the string to his shoulder and took aim, Hector struck him with the jagged stone, right where the collarbone joins the neck to the chest, the deadliest place. It snapped the bowstring against his arm; his wrist went numb, and he dropped to his knees, the bow falling from his hand. Ajax saw his brother fall and ran to him, stood astride him, and sheltered him with his shield, while two loyal squires, Mecisteus son of Echius and Alastor, lifted him and carried him to the ships, groaning in his pain.

Now Zeus put fresh heart into the Trojans, and they drove the Greeks back to their deep ditch, Hector in all his glory at their head. As a hound runs down a wild boar or a lion, snapping at its flank or its haunch and watching for the turn, so Hector hung on the heels of the Greeks, always killing the hindmost as they fled in panic. And when they had run back through the stakes and the ditch — leaving many of their own dead at the hands of the Trojans — they halted at the ships and called to one another, and every man lifted his hands and prayed aloud to the gods; while Hector wheeled his horses this way and that, his eyes glaring like the Gorgon’s, or the murderous war-god’s.

Hera saw them and pitied them, and at once she said to Athena, “Ah, child of Zeus who wields the storm-shield — will you and I take no more thought for the dying Greeks, even this last time? Look how they perish, broken by the onset of a single man. Hector, son of Priam, rages past all bearing, and already he’s done terrible harm.”

Athena answered, “I’d gladly see him dead, killed on his own soil by the hands of the Greeks. But my father rages with a black temper — always crossing me, always headstrong and unjust. He’s forgotten how often I saved his son Heracles, worn out under the labors Eurystheus laid on him. He’d cry up to heaven, and Zeus would send me down to help him. If I’d had the sense to foresee all this when Eurystheus sent him down to the house of Hades to fetch the hound of hell out of Erebus, he’d never have come back alive across the deep waters of the Styx. And now Zeus hates me, and gives Thetis her way, because she kissed his knees and took hold of his chin, begging him to honor Achilles. The day will come when he calls me his gray-eyed darling again. Harness our horses for me now, while I go into the house of Zeus and put on my armor. Then we’ll see whether Hector, Priam’s son, is glad to meet us in the lanes of battle — or whether some Trojan will glut the dogs and the vultures with his fat and his flesh, dead by the ships of the Greeks.”

White-armed Hera did as she said, and set about harnessing the horses with their golden gear. And Athena, daughter of Zeus who wields the storm-shield, let her soft embroidered robe fall to her father’s threshold — the robe she had made with her own hands — pulled on the tunic of Zeus, and armed herself for the war that brings tears. She stepped into the flaming chariot and took up the spear, heavy and huge and strong, with which she beats down the ranks of the men who have crossed her. Hera cracked the whip, and the gates of heaven groaned open of their own accord — the gates the Hours keep, who hold the sky and Olympus in their charge, to roll the thick cloud aside or close it again. Through them the two goddesses drove their willing horses.

But Zeus, looking down from Ida, saw them and was filled with rage. He sent golden-winged Iris with a message. “Go, swift Iris, turn them back. Don’t let them come near me — it will be an ugly thing if we come to blows. I tell you plainly what I will do: I’ll cripple the horses under their chariot, throw the two of them out, and smash the car to pieces. Ten full years they’ll not heal the wounds my lightning leaves on them. Then my gray-eyed daughter will learn what it means to fight her own father. With Hera I’m less surprised, less angry — whatever I say, she always contradicts it.”

So Iris went, fast as the wind, from the heights of Ida up to the summits of Olympus. She met the goddesses at the outer gates of its many folded valleys and gave them the message. “Where are you going? What madness is in you? The son of Cronus forbids you to help the Greeks. Here is his threat, and he means to do it: he’ll cripple the horses under your chariot, throw the two of you out, and smash the car to pieces. Ten full years you’ll not heal the wounds his lightning leaves on you — so you’ll learn, gray-eyed goddess, what it means to fight your own father. With Hera he’s less angry; whatever he says, she always contradicts it. But you — you reckless, brazen thing — will you really dare lift that great spear against Zeus?”

With that she left them, and Hera said to Athena, “No, child of Zeus who wields the storm-shield — I’ll not have the two of us fight Zeus over mortal men. Let them live or die as their luck falls, and let him judge between Trojans and Greeks as his own mind tells him; that is his right.”

She turned the horses back. The Hours unyoked them, tied them at their fragrant mangers, and leaned the chariot against the bright wall of the court. And the two goddesses sat down on their golden thrones among the rest of the gods — sick at heart.

Then Zeus drove his chariot up from Ida to Olympus and came among the gathered gods. The great lord of the earthquake unyoked his horses for him, set the car on its stand, and threw a cloth over it; and Zeus sat down on his golden throne, and great Olympus trembled under him. Only Athena and Hera sat apart from Zeus, and neither spoke a word to him or asked him anything. But he knew their minds, and said, “Why so downcast, Athena, Hera? Surely you didn’t tire yourselves killing Trojans, those dear friends you hate so well? Know this: not all the gods on Olympus together could turn me, such is the strength of these hands. You two were shaking before you ever set eyes on the war and its grim work. I tell you, and it would have come true — I’d have struck you with lightning, and your chariot would never have carried you home to Olympus.”

Athena and Hera heard him and groaned, sitting side by side, scheming trouble for the Trojans. Athena held her tongue, though she was boiling with anger at her father and said nothing. But Hera could not contain it. “Dread son of Cronus, what a thing to say. We know your power well enough. Still, we pity the Greek warriors, dying and meeting so hard an end. We’ll keep clear of the fighting, since you command it — but we’ll drop a word of good counsel to the Greeks, so they don’t all perish under your anger.”

Zeus answered, “Wait for the morning, Hera, if you care to watch it: you’ll see the son of Cronus killing Greeks by the thousands. For fierce Hector will not stop fighting until he has roused the son of Peleus — on the day they fight in the worst of straits, by the ships’ sterns, over the body of Patroclus. That is how it is decreed; like it or not, that is how it will be. As for you — go down, if you wish, to the lowest pit beneath the earth and the sea, where Iapetus and Cronus sit with neither a ray of sunlight nor a breath of wind to comfort them, deep in Tartarus; go all the way down, and I won’t care a whit how angry you are. There is no creature on earth more shameless than you.”

Hera said nothing back. And now the sun’s bright disk dropped into the Ocean stream and drew the dark night down over the grain-giving earth. The Trojans were sorry to lose the light — but for the Greeks the darkness came welcome, three times prayed for.

Then Hector led the Trojans back from the ships and held a council on the open ground by the river, where the dead did not lie. They climbed down from their chariots and sat on the bare earth to hear him. In his hand he held a spear eleven cubits long, its bronze point gleaming, ringed at the socket with gold. Leaning on it, he spoke. “Hear me, Trojans, Dardanians, and allies. I thought, just now, I would destroy the ships and all the Greeks with them before I went home to Troy. But darkness came on too soon, and that alone has saved them and their ships on the shore. So now let us give in to the night and see to our supper. Free the horses from the chariots and feed them; then hurry and bring sheep and cattle from the city, and wine, and grain for the horses, and gather plenty of wood, so that all night until the dawn we can keep watchfires burning whose glare reaches the sky. For the Greeks may try to slip away over the sea in the dark, and they must not embark untouched and at their ease. Many a man among them must carry home a wound to nurse — hit with spear or arrow as he leaps for his ship — so that the rest learn to dread bringing war and weeping to the Trojans. And let the heralds cry it through the city: the boys not yet grown and the gray-bearded old men are to camp on the god-built walls; and let every woman light a great fire in her house, and keep a sure watch, so the town isn’t taken by surprise while our army is out on the plain. See to it, brave Trojans — that is enough for now; at daybreak I’ll have more to say. I pray, in hope, to Zeus and the other gods that we may drive these fate-driven dogs from our land, for it is fate that has carried them and their ships here. Tonight we keep watch; with the first light let us arm and rouse hard war at the ships of the Greeks. Then I’ll know whether brave Diomedes, son of Tydeus, will drive me from the ships back to the wall — or whether I’ll cut him down and carry off his bloodied armor. Tomorrow he’ll show his courage, if he dares to stand and face my spear. I think that when the day breaks he’ll be among the first to fall, and many of his men around him. If only I were as certain of being deathless, ageless forever, honored like Athena and Apollo, as I am that this coming day brings ruin to the Greeks.”

So Hector spoke, and the Trojans roared their approval. They loosed the sweating horses from the yokes and tethered each one by its own chariot. They hurried to bring sheep and cattle from the city, and wine, and grain from their houses, and gathered plenty of wood. Then they offered unblemished sacrifices to the immortals, and the wind carried the sweet savor up to heaven — but the blessed gods would not share in it, for they hated Troy, and Priam, and Priam’s people. And so, high in hope, they sat all night long in the lanes of war, and their watchfires burned past counting. As when the stars stand out bright around the moon in a windless sky, and every peak and headland and clearing shows clear, and the high air splits open into endless light, and all the stars can be counted, and the shepherd’s heart is glad — so many were the Trojan fires burning before Troy, between the ships and the streams of the Xanthus. A thousand fires blazed on the plain, and at each one sat fifty men in the glow, while the horses stood by the chariots, champing their barley and grain, and waited for Dawn on her bright throne.
books.title: The Tide of Battle Turns

books.label: Book IX
paragraphs: So the Trojans kept their watch. But Panic, the sister of cold-blooded Rout, had laid hold of the Greeks, and every one of their leaders was sick at heart. As when two winds off Thrace, the north wind and the west, swoop down together on the fish-thronged sea and in an instant heave the dark water into peaks and fling the seaweed scattering up the beach — so were the hearts of the Greeks torn in their breasts.

In his misery the son of Atreus told the heralds to summon the men to assembly — each one called by name, quietly, no shout going up over the camp — and he went among them himself, calling them. They came and sat down heavy-hearted. Agamemnon stood up weeping, the tears running down like a stream of dark water that falls in a sheet from a high cliff, and groaning hard he spoke to the Greeks:

“My friends — leaders and counselors of the Greeks — the hand of Zeus has come down hard on me. The cruel god. Once he bowed his head and promised me I would sack the strong walls of Troy and sail home; now he has played me false, and orders me back to Argos in disgrace, with so many of my men dead. So it must please almighty Zeus, who has thrown down the high crowns of many cities, and will throw down more — his power is the greatest there is. So let us all do as I say: let us run with our ships for our own dear country. We will never take Troy now, with its wide streets.”

He spoke, and for a long while the sons of the Greeks sat without a word, sick at heart and silent. At last Diomedes, master of the war cry, broke it: “Son of Atreus, I'll fight your folly first — it's my right, here in the assembly, so don't take it hard. You attacked my courage once before, in front of the whole army; you called me a coward and no soldier. Every Greek, young and old, knows you said it. The son of crooked-minded Cronus gave you your gifts by halves: he gave you the scepter and the honor of ruling over all of us, but courage — the highest thing there is — he did not give you. You strange man. Do you really think the sons of the Greeks are the cowards you say? If your own heart is set on going home, then go — the road is open, your ships are there on the shore, the whole fleet that came with you from Mycenae. But the rest of us will stay until we've sacked Troy. And if they too want to run — let them sail for their own dear country. Sthenelus and I will fight on, the two of us, until we reach the end of Troy. We came here with a god behind us.”

The sons of the Greeks shouted their approval, struck by the words of Diomedes the breaker of horses. Then Nestor the horseman rose and spoke among them: “Son of Tydeus — in war your strength is beyond question, and in council you are the best of the men your age; no Greek will make light of your words or speak against them. And yet you have not gone all the way to the end of the matter. You're still young — you might be the youngest son I have — but you have spoken sense, and spoken it well, to the kings of the Greeks. So now let me speak; I am older than you, and I will say it all, and no one will make light of it, not even lord Agamemnon. A man who longs for the horror of war among his own people is a man without clan, without law, without a hearth.

“But for now, let us yield to the night and see to our supper. Let the sentries post themselves along the ditch, outside the wall. That is my word to the younger men. And then, son of Atreus, take the lead — you are the most kingly among us. Lay on a feast for the elders; it is right and fitting. Your huts are full of wine, the wine the Greek ships bring across the sea from Thrace every day; you have everything you need to host us, and many men under you. Gather many heads together, and follow the man whose counsel proves best. The Greeks have hard need of good counsel now, wise and shrewd, with the enemy's watchfires burning so close to our ships. What man could look at them and not be afraid? This night will either ruin the army or save it.”

So he spoke, and they heard him gladly and did as he said. The sentries went out under arms — Nestor's son Thrasymedes, shepherd of the people, at their head, and Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, the sons of Ares, and Meriones, and Aphareus, and Deipyrus, and Lycomedes, the noble son of Creon. Seven captains of the watch there were, and a hundred young men with each, gripping their long spears; they took their place between the ditch and the wall, lit their fires, and each man made his supper.

Then the son of Atreus led the elders of the Greeks to his quarters and set a good feast before them, and they reached out their hands to the food. When they had put away their hunger and thirst, old Nestor was the first to weave them his counsel — Nestor, whose advice had always shown the best before. With good will toward them all he spoke:

“Most honored son of Atreus, Agamemnon, lord of men — with you I will begin, and with you I will end, for you are king over many. Zeus has put the scepter in your hand and the law in your keeping, so that you may take thought for your people. So it falls to you above all others both to speak and to listen — and to act on another man's word, when his heart moves him to speak for the good. Whatever a man begins, it comes back to rest on you. So let me say what I judge to be best. No one will think of a better word than the one I have carried in me since the day — yes, royal as you are — that you went into the hut of Achilles and took the girl Briseis, against my own judgment. I argued hard against it, but you gave way to your high temper and dishonored a man the very gods have honored — for you hold his prize still. But even now, let us think how to win him back, with gifts and with gentle words.”

And Agamemnon, lord of men, answered: “Old man, you have not lied; my folly is just as you say. I was blind. I will not deny it. One man, when the gods are with him, is worth a whole army — and Zeus has shown his love for this one by laying the Greeks low. I was blind, I gave way to my own black temper; so now I will make it right, and pay him back with gifts beyond counting. Here, in front of you all, I will name them. Seven tripods never touched by fire. Ten bars of gold. Twenty gleaming cauldrons. Twelve strong horses, prize-winners, who have carried off trophies with their speed — a man would be no poor man, no man short of precious gold, who had as much as these horses have won me. And seven women skilled in fine work, women of Lesbos, that I chose for myself when Achilles took Lesbos — they outshone all their sex in beauty. These I will give him, and with them the one I took from him, the daughter of Briseus. And I will swear a great oath: that I never once went up into her bed, never lay with her, as is the way of men and women.

“All this is his now. And if the gods grant us someday to sack the great city of Priam, let him come when we Greeks are dividing the plunder and load his ship deep with gold and bronze, as much as he likes; and let him pick out for himself twenty Trojan women, the loveliest there are after Helen. And when we reach Greek Argos, the richest land on earth, he will be my son-in-law, and I will hold him in honor like my own son Orestes, who is being raised there in all abundance. I have three daughters in my strong-built house — Chrysothemis, Laodice, and Iphianassa. Let him take whichever he likes, and bring her to the house of Peleus — and no bride-price; I will give him a dowry instead, greater than any man ever gave with his daughter. I will give him seven strong cities: Cardamyle, Enope, and grassy Hire; sacred Pherae, and Antheia in its deep meadows; lovely Aepeia, and Pedasus of the vines. All of them lie near the sea, on the borders of sandy Pylos, and the men who live there are rich in flocks and herds; they will honor him like a god with their gifts, and pay him rich tribute under his rule. All this I will do, if he will let go of his anger. Let him give way. Hades alone is the god who cannot be softened, cannot be turned — and so of all the gods men hate him most. And I am the greater king, and I am the older man.”

Then Nestor the horseman answered: “Most honored son of Atreus, Agamemnon, lord of men — these are no small gifts you offer Achilles. Come, then, let us send chosen men to go without delay to the hut of Peleus's son. The ones I name, let them take it on. First let Phoenix, dear to Zeus, lead the way; then great Ajax and brilliant Odysseus, and let the heralds Odius and Eurybates go with them. Now bring water for our hands, and call for holy silence, while we pray to Zeus, the son of Cronus, to take pity on us.”

So he spoke, and his words pleased them all. The heralds poured water over their hands, and the young men filled the bowls to the brim and served the wine to every man, pouring the first drops out for the gods. When they had poured the offering and drunk what their hearts desired, they set out from the hut of Agamemnon, son of Atreus. And Nestor, the old horseman, sent them off with a long look at each in turn — at Odysseus most of all — pressing on them again and again to do their best to win over the faultless son of Peleus.

The two of them went along the shore of the sounding sea, praying hard to Poseidon, who holds the earth in his arms, that they might easily bend the great heart of Achilles. They came to the ships and huts of the Myrmidons, and found him there, soothing his heart with a clear-toned lyre — a beautiful thing, finely made, with a crossbar of silver. He had taken it from the spoils when he sacked the city of Eetion. With it he was easing his heart now, singing of the glories of men. Patroclus sat across from him, alone with him, silent, waiting for the moment the son of Aeacus would leave off his song. The two envoys came forward, brilliant Odysseus leading, and stood before him. Achilles sprang up, astonished, the lyre still in his hand, and left the seat where he had been sitting; and Patroclus rose too, when he saw the men. Achilles, the swift runner, gave them welcome: “All hail — and welcome. You must come on some pressing need. But you are the dearest of the Greeks to me, even now, in my anger.”

With that brilliant Achilles led them in and sat them down on couches spread with purple cloths, and at once he said to Patroclus, close by him: “Son of Menoetius — set out a larger bowl, mix the wine stronger, and pour a cup for every man. These are the men I love best, here under my roof.”

Patroclus did as his dear friend bade him. He set a great chopping block down in the firelight and laid out on it the back of a sheep, the back of a fat goat, and the chine of a hog rich with fat. Automedon held the meat steady while Achilles carved it, cutting it cleanly and running the pieces onto spits, and the son of Menoetius, a man like a god, built the fire high. When it had burned down and the flame died, he raked the embers flat, laid the spits across them on their racks, and sprinkled the meat with holy salt. When it was roasted he heaped it on platters; Patroclus brought bread to the table in handsome baskets, and Achilles served out the meat. Then he took his own seat against the far wall, across from Odysseus, and told his friend Patroclus to make the offering to the gods, and Patroclus threw the first portions into the fire. So they reached out their hands to the food before them. And when they had put away their hunger and thirst, Ajax nodded to Phoenix. Odysseus saw it, and filling his cup with wine he lifted it to Achilles:

“Your health, Achilles. We have had no want of a good feast — not in the hut of Agamemnon, and not here now; there has been plenty to eat and drink. But it is not feasting we have on our minds. We are looking disaster in the face, my lord, and without you we cannot tell whether our ships will be saved or lost. The Trojans and their allies are camped right up against the wall and the ships; their watchfires are burning all through the camp, and they say nothing can stop them now from falling on the black ships. And Zeus has shown them his sign, the lightning on their right. Hector storms on in his glory, raging, trusting in Zeus, with no fear of god or man left in him — a kind of madness has him. He prays for dawn to come quickly. He swears he will hack the high sterns from our ships, set the hulls ablaze, and slaughter the Greeks where they stand, choking in the smoke. And I am terribly afraid the gods will make good his boast, and our fate will be to die here at Troy, far from the horse-pastures of Argos. Up, then — late as it is, if you mean to save the worn-out sons of the Greeks from the Trojan storm. You yourself will grieve for it later if you don't; once the harm is done, there is no cure for it. Think, while there is still time, how to keep this evil day from the Greeks.

“My friend — when your father Peleus sent you off from Phthia to Agamemnon, did he not charge you, saying: ‘My son, strength is a thing Athena and Hera will give you, if they choose. But you — hold down the high temper in your chest. A kind heart is the better way. Let go of quarreling, the breeder of trouble, and old and young among the Greeks will honor you the more.' That was the old man's charge, and you have let it slip. Even now, let it go — give up this anger that eats the heart. Agamemnon will make you fit amends, if only you give up your rage. Listen, and I will tell you everything he named in his hut. Seven tripods never touched by fire, and ten bars of gold; twenty gleaming cauldrons, and twelve strong horses, prize-winners — a man would be no poor man, no man short of precious gold, who had as much as these horses have won Agamemnon. And seven women skilled in fine work, women of Lesbos, that he chose for himself when you took Lesbos — they outshone all their sex in beauty. These he will give you, and with them the one he took from you, the daughter of Briseus. And he will swear a great oath that he never went up into her bed, never lay with her, as is the way of men and women, my lord. All this is yours at once. And if the gods grant us someday to sack the great city of Priam, you may come when we Greeks are dividing the plunder and load your ship deep with gold and bronze, and pick out for yourself twenty Trojan women, the loveliest there are after Helen. And when we reach Greek Argos, the richest land on earth, you will be his son-in-law, and he will hold you in honor like his own son Orestes, who is being raised there in all abundance. He has three daughters in his strong-built house — Chrysothemis, Laodice, and Iphianassa — and you may take whichever you like, with no bride-price, to the house of Peleus; and he will give a dowry besides, greater than any man ever gave with his daughter. And he will give you seven strong cities: Cardamyle, Enope, and grassy Hire; sacred Pherae, and Antheia in its deep meadows; lovely Aepeia, and Pedasus of the vines, all of them near the sea, on the borders of sandy Pylos, and the men who live there rich in flocks and herds, who will honor you like a god with their gifts and pay you rich tribute under your rule. All this he will do, if you will give up your anger. But if the son of Atreus is too hateful to you, gifts and all, then have pity at least on the rest of the Greeks, worn down through the whole army, who will honor you like a god. You would win great glory in their eyes. You might even kill Hector — he would come right into your reach now, mad as he is, sure there is no man among us the ships have brought who can match him.”

Then Achilles, the swift runner, answered him: “Royal son of Laertes, resourceful Odysseus — I had better say it straight out, the way I see it, the way it is going to be, so you don't sit here cooing at me one after another. I hate that man like the gates of death who says one thing and hides another in his heart. So here is what I think. The son of Atreus will not win me over, and neither will the rest of the Greeks. There is no thanks in it, none — fighting the enemy on and on without rest. The man who hangs back gets the same share as the man who fights his hardest. The coward and the brave man are held in one honor. Death comes the same to the man who has done nothing and the man who has done much. And I have got nothing by it, for all the pain I've put my heart through, day after day staking my life in battle. Like a bird that brings every scrap she finds to her unfledged chicks, and goes hungry herself — that is how it has been with me: long sleepless nights, and bloody days of fighting against men defending their wives. I have sacked twelve cities of men from my ships, and eleven more, I tell you, on foot across the deep soil of Troy. From every one of them I took out great treasure, fine treasure, and carried it all back and put it in the hands of Agamemnon, son of Atreus — and he, hanging back the whole time by his fast ships, would take it, dole out a little, and keep the most for himself.

“Oh, he handed out prizes well enough to the other kings and chiefs, and they have theirs still, untouched. From me alone of all the Greeks he took it — took the woman I loved. Well, let him keep her. Let him lie with her and be glad. But tell me — why must the Greeks make war on the Trojans at all? Why did the son of Atreus gather an army and lead it here? Wasn't it for Helen of the lovely hair? Are the sons of Atreus the only men alive who love their wives? Any man worth anything loves his own woman and cares for her, as I loved mine with my whole heart, spear-won though she was. He has taken her from my hands, cheated me — so let him not try me again. I know him now. He will not move me. No, Odysseus — let him take counsel with you and the other kings how to keep the fire off the ships. He has done a great deal already without me: he has built a wall, and dug a ditch beside it, broad and deep, and driven stakes into it. And even so he cannot hold back man-killing Hector. As long as I was fighting among the Greeks, Hector wouldn't carry the battle far from his own wall — he came only as far as the Scaean gates and the oak tree, and there he once waited for me alone, and barely got away. But now, since I have no will to fight him, tomorrow at dawn I will make sacrifice to Zeus and all the gods, and haul my ships down and load them. And in the morning, if you care to look, you will see my ships at first light riding out over the Hellespont, my men bending hard at the oars. If the great Earthshaker grants me a clear passage, on the third day I will be home in the deep soil of Phthia.

“I have everything there that I left when I came here, to my sorrow — and I'll bring home more besides, gold and red bronze, fine-belted women and gray iron, all I drew by lot — though my prize, the prize that he gave, lord Agamemnon, son of Atreus, in his arrogance has taken back again. Tell him all of it, exactly as I say, and out loud, so the rest of the Greeks may be angry too, if he ever thinks to cheat another of them — shameless as he is to the bone. And yet, dog that he is, he would not dare look me in the eye. No. I will share no counsel with him, no work with him. He cheated me once and wronged me; he will not talk me round a second time. Once is enough. Let him go to his ruin in peace — Zeus has stolen his wits. His gifts are hateful to me; I value them at the price of a single hair. Not if he gave me ten times, twenty times all he has now, and all that might ever come to him from anywhere — not all the wealth that pours into Orchomenus, or into Egyptian Thebes, where the houses are stacked with treasure, Thebes of the hundred gates, two hundred fighters driving out through each with their chariots and horses — not if his gifts were as many as the grains of sand or the dust of the earth, even then Agamemnon will not bend my heart, not until he has paid me back in full for the bitter outrage to my honor.

“And I will not marry the daughter of Agamemnon. Not if she rivaled golden Aphrodite for beauty and gray-eyed Athena for the work of her hands — even so I will not have her. Let him pick some other Greek, a man more his equal, a greater king than I am. If the gods keep me safe and I reach home, Peleus himself will find me a wife. There are Greek women all through Hellas and Phthia, daughters of the lords who hold the towns; I can take any of them I want and make her my wife. My heart has turned that way often, back home — to marry a fit wife, a true bride, and enjoy what my old father Peleus built. For nothing is worth my life — not all they say the great city of Troy held in the old days of peace, before the sons of the Greeks ever came, nor all the treasure locked behind the stone threshold of Apollo the archer at rocky Pytho. Cattle and fat sheep can be had for the taking; tripods and the tawny heads of horses can be won. But a man's life cannot be raided back, cannot be seized or bought, once it has crossed the barrier of his teeth.

“My mother Thetis, the silver-footed goddess, tells me two fates carry me toward the day of my death. If I stay here and fight on around the city of Troy, there is no homecoming for me, but my glory will never die. If I go home, to my own dear country, my glory is lost, but I will live long, and death will be slow in coming. And to the rest of you I say this too: sail home. There is no end of Troy to be reached now. Zeus the wide-thunderer holds his hand over her, and her people have taken heart. So go, and carry my message to the chief men of the Greeks — that is the privilege of elders — and tell them to think of some better plan to save their ships and the army camped beside them, since the one they have hit on cannot serve while my anger holds. As for Phoenix, let him stay and sleep here, so he may sail home with me in the morning, if he is willing. I will not take him by force.”

So he spoke, and they all fell silent, struck dumb by his words; for he had refused them with great force. At last the old horseman Phoenix spoke, bursting into tears, in dread for the ships of the Greeks: “If you really mean to go home, brilliant Achilles — if you will do nothing at all to keep the consuming fire from the ships, because the anger has fallen on your heart — how can I stay here behind you, dear child, all alone? Your father Peleus sent me with you the day he sent you off, a boy still, from Phthia to Agamemnon, knowing nothing of leveling war, nothing of the assembly where men come to stand out among others. He sent me to teach you all of it — to be a speaker of words and a doer of deeds. So I could never be willing to stay behind without you, child — not if a god himself promised to strip the old age from me and make me young and fresh as the day I first left Hellas, the land of lovely women, fleeing the wrath of my father Amyntor, son of Ormenus.

“He was in a fury with me over a beautiful woman, a mistress he loved, while he dishonored his own wife, my mother. And my mother begged me without end, on her knees, to lie with the woman first, so that she would loathe the old man. I did as she asked. My father knew it at once, and cursed me bitterly, calling on the dread Furies, that no son of mine should ever sit on his knees — a son of my begetting. And the gods made the curse good, Zeus of the underworld and dread Persephone. I thought to kill him with the sharp bronze; but some god checked me, and set before my heart the talk of men and all the names they would call me — a father-killer among the Greeks. Yet I could no longer bear to stay in the house of a father so enraged at me. My cousins and kinsmen crowded around, begging me to stay; they killed many fat sheep and shambling oxen, and set many fat hogs to singe and roast over the fire, and drank down jar after jar of the old man's wine. Nine nights running they slept around me, taking the watch in turns, and kept two fires burning — one in the porch of the walled court, one in the hall, before the door of my room. But on the tenth night, in the dark, I broke the close-fitted doors of the chamber, and was over the courtyard wall, slipping past the watchmen and the women slaves before any of them saw me. Then I fled far through the wide land of Hellas and came at last to deep-soiled Phthia, mother of flocks, to King Peleus. And he took me in gladly, and loved me as a father loves his only son, his late-born heir to great wealth. He made me rich and set many people under me, and I lived on the borders of Phthia, lord over the Dolopians.

“And I made you what you are, Achilles, godlike as you are — I loved you from my heart. You would never go off to a feast with another, or eat at home, until I had set you on my knees and cut your meat small for you and held the wine to your lips. Many a time you wet the front of my shirt, spitting up the wine in your helpless little way. I went through a great deal for you, took a great deal of trouble, thinking that since the gods would give me no son of my own, I would make you my son, godlike Achilles, so that one day you might keep the cruel day from me. So master your great spirit, Achilles. You should not have a pitiless heart. Even the gods can be turned, and theirs is the greater excellence, the greater honor and strength. And yet with sacrifices and soft prayers, with libations and the savor of burnt offering, men turn them, begging when a man has gone wrong and overstepped.

“For there are Prayers, too — the daughters of great Zeus. Lame, and wrinkled, and their eyes turned aside, they come limping along behind Ruin. But Ruin is strong, and quick on her feet, and so she outruns them all by far and gets first to every land, and there she does her harm to men; and the Prayers come after, healing what she has done. Now, the man who reveres these daughters of Zeus when they come near — him they help, and they hear him when he prays. But the man who refuses them, who hardens against them and turns them away — they go to Zeus, son of Cronus, and ask that Ruin walk with that man, so that he is hurt, and pays. So you, Achilles — see that you too grant the daughters of Zeus the honor that bends the minds of other good men. If the son of Atreus were not bringing gifts and naming more for later, if he were still hot in his anger, I would not be the one to tell you to throw your wrath aside and stand by the Greeks, however hard their need. But he is giving much now, and pledging more to come, and he has sent the best men to plead his cause, picked out from the whole army, the men dearest to you of all the Greeks. Don't shame their words or their coming. Until now no one could blame your anger. But of the heroes of old we have heard the same — that even men in a towering rage could be won by gifts and turned by words.

“There is an old tale I remember — an old one, not a new one — and since you are all friends here, I'll tell it. The Curetes and the Aetolians were fighting, killing each other around the city of Calydon, the Aetolians defending it, the Curetes burning to bring it down. Artemis of the golden throne had set this evil on them, angry that Oeneus had not offered her the first fruits of his orchard. The other gods all feasted on his sacrifices; to her alone, the daughter of great Zeus, he gave nothing — he forgot, or it slipped his mind somehow, and his heart went badly astray. So in her anger the archer goddess sent a wild boar against him, a great white-tusked thing, and it did much harm to Oeneus's orchard, throwing tall apple trees flat on the ground, roots and blossoms and all. Meleager, the son of Oeneus, killed it at last, gathering hunters and hounds from many cities — for it was no small band that could bring down a beast so huge; it set many a man on the bitter funeral pyre. But over its body the goddess raised a clash and an uproar, the Curetes and the great-hearted Aetolians fighting for the boar's head and its shaggy hide.

“Now, as long as Meleager, dear to Ares, was in the fighting, it went badly for the Curetes, and for all their numbers they could not hold their ground outside the wall. But there came a time when anger swelled in Meleager — the anger that swells the breast even of wise men. He was enraged at his mother Althaea, and so he lay idle beside his wedded wife, lovely Cleopatra. She was the daughter of Marpessa of the fine ankles and of Idas, the strongest man on earth in his day — Idas, who took up his bow against lord Apollo himself for the sake of fair Marpessa. Her father and mother in their house had named the girl Alcyone, the halcyon, because her mother had wept like the halcyon bird, the bird of grief, when Apollo the far-shooter carried her off. Beside this Cleopatra Meleager lay, nursing the bitter anger of his mother's curse. For she, in her grief over her dead brother, prayed to the gods, beating the nourishing earth with her hands, calling on Hades and dread Persephone, down on her knees, her breast wet with tears, that they should bring death to her son. And the Fury that walks in the dark, the one whose heart knows no pity, heard her out of Erebus.

“Soon the noise of battle was at the gates, the thudding of the Curetes against the towers. The elders of the Aetolians sent the holiest of their priests to Meleager, begging him to come out and save them, and promising a great gift: wherever the richest land lay in the plain of lovely Calydon, there they bade him cut himself fifty acres, half vineyard, half open plowland. The old horseman Oeneus pleaded with him, standing on the threshold of his high room, rattling the close-fitted doors, begging his son. His sisters pleaded, and his honored mother; he refused them harder still. His comrades pleaded, the ones nearest and dearest to him of all; not even they could move his heart — not until his own room was being battered, and the Curetes were climbing the towers and setting the great city alight. Then at last his wife, in her grief, begged him, and laid out for him all the sorrows that fall on a people whose city is taken: the men cut down, the city burned to ash, the children and the deep-belted women dragged away. His heart stirred as he heard those evils, and he rose and went out and put on his shining armor. So Meleager kept the day of ruin from the Aetolians, giving way to his own heart — but they never gave him the rich and gracious gifts; he saved them, and got nothing.

“So don't you think that way, dear child; let no god turn your mind down that road. It will be a harder thing to save the ships once they are burning. Come for the gifts. The Greeks will honor you like a god. But if you go into the slaughter later, without the gifts, you will not be held in the same honor, even if you beat the war back.”

Then Achilles, the swift runner, answered him: “Phoenix, old father, dear to Zeus — I have no need of that kind of honor. I think I am honored already by the will of Zeus, and that honor will keep me here by the curved ships as long as the breath is in my chest and my knees have their spring. And I'll tell you another thing — fix it in your mind. Don't go confusing my heart with this weeping and grieving, doing it all for the son of Atreus. You shouldn't love that man; you'll lose the love I bear you if you do. It would be the fine thing to wound, with me, the man who wounds me. Be king at my side, share half my honor. These men will carry the answer back. You stay here, sleep on a soft bed, and at first light we'll decide whether to go home or stay.”

And he gave a quiet nod to Patroclus, with his brows, to spread a thick bed for Phoenix — a sign for the others to think about leaving. Then Ajax, the godlike son of Telamon, spoke: “Royal son of Laertes, resourceful Odysseus — let's go. I don't think we'll reach the end of this errand on this road. We had better take the answer back, hard as it is, to the Greeks who sit there waiting for it. Achilles has turned the great heart in his chest savage and proud — a hard man, who cares nothing for the love of his comrades, the love we gave him at the ships beyond all others. Pitiless. Why, a man takes a blood-price even for a brother killed, even for his own dead son; the killer pays it and stays on among his people, and the other holds back his heart and his pride once he's taken it. But in you the gods have set a hard, unyielding spirit, and all of it for one girl, a single one — when here we are offering you seven, the best there are, and a great deal more besides. Let your heart turn gentle. Respect your own roof. We are under it as messengers of the whole Greek host, and we would be the nearest and dearest to you of all the Greeks.”

Then Achilles, the swift runner, answered: “Ajax, royal son of Telamon, lord of the people — everything you've said is close to my own mind. But my heart swells with anger every time I think of it, the way the son of Atreus shamed me in front of the Greeks, as if I were some worthless drifter with no rights at all. So go, the two of you, and carry the message. I will give no thought to bloody war until the son of wise Priam, until Hector himself comes through, killing as he comes, to the huts and the ships of the Myrmidons, and sets them on fire. But at my own hut, by my own black ship, I think I will hold Hector, hungry for battle though he is.”

So he spoke, and each of them took up a double cup, poured the offering, and went back along the line of ships, Odysseus leading. Patroclus told his men and the serving women to make up a thick bed for Phoenix at once, and they laid it down — fleeces, a coverlet, and a sheet of fine linen — and there the old man lay and waited for the bright dawn. But Achilles slept in the inner room of the well-built hut, and beside him lay a woman he had carried off from Lesbos, Diomede, the lovely daughter of Phorbas. Patroclus lay across the room, and with him fair-belted Iphis, whom brilliant Achilles had given him when he took steep Scyros, the city of Enyeus.

When the envoys came back to the huts of the son of Atreus, the Greeks rose to meet them, lifting cups of gold all down the line, and pressed them with questions.
