Agamemnon, lord of men, asked first: “Tell me, Odysseus, glory of the Greeks — will he keep the consuming fire off the ships, or did he refuse, and is the anger still in his proud heart?”

And the long-suffering, brilliant Odysseus answered: “Most honored son of Atreus, Agamemnon, lord of men — that man has no will to put out his anger. He is fuller of rage than ever, and he waves you off, you and your gifts. He tells you to take counsel with the Greeks yourself, how to save the ships and the army. As for himself, he threatens that at first light he will haul his ships down to the sea. And he said he'd advise the rest of us to sail home too, since we will never reach the end of Troy now. ‘Zeus the wide-thunderer holds his hand over her,' he said, ‘and her people have taken heart.' That is what he said; and these who came with me will tell you the same — Ajax, and the two heralds, both of them men of sense. Old Phoenix stayed behind to sleep there, for so Achilles wanted it, that he might sail home with him in the morning, if he is willing; but he will not take him by force.”

So he spoke, and they all fell silent, struck dumb by his words; for he had brought back a hard answer. For a long while the sons of the Greeks sat in silence, sick at heart. At last Diomedes, master of the war cry, spoke: “Most honored son of Atreus, Agamemnon, lord of men — you should never have begged the great-hearted son of Peleus, nor offered him gifts beyond counting. He is proud enough on his own; now you have driven him deeper into his pride. But let him be — let him go or stay as he pleases. He will fight again, soon enough, when the heart in his chest stirs him and a god drives him to it. So now let us all do as I say. Lie down and sleep — you have had your fill of food and wine, and in those a man finds strength and heart. But when lovely rosy-fingered Dawn shines out, get the army and the horsemen drawn up before the ships, and rouse them on; and you yourself, fight in the front line.”

So he spoke, and all the kings approved his words, marveling at Diomedes the breaker of horses. Then they poured the offering and went, each man to his own hut, and lay down and took the gift of sleep.
books.title: The Embassy to Achilles

books.label: Book X
paragraphs: All the other Greek captains slept soundly the whole night through, but sleep would not come to Agamemnon, son of Atreus; his mind churned. As when the lord of fair-haired Hera throws his lightning to signal a great storm of rain, or hail, or snow that whitens the fields, or else to open wide the hungry jaws of war — so Agamemnon groaned again and again from the depths of his chest, and his heart shook within him. When he looked out across the plain of Troy he was amazed at all the watchfires burning in front of the city, and at the cry of pipes and flutes and the murmur of men. But when he turned back to his own ships and his own army, he tore at his hair by the handful, calling on Zeus on high, and the great heart in him groaned aloud.

In the end this seemed best to him: to go first to Nestor, son of Neleus, and see whether the two of them together could devise some defense against ruin for the Greeks. So he rose, pulled on his tunic, bound the fine sandals to his feet, and threw over his shoulders the tawny skin of a great lion that hung to his heels, and took up his spear.

Menelaus could not sleep either. He too feared for the Greeks, who for his sake had crossed the wide water to make war on the Trojans. He covered his broad back with the dappled hide of a leopard, set a helmet of bronze on his head, took a spear in his strong hand, and went to wake his brother — the most powerful of all the Greeks, a man the army honored like a god. He found him at the stern of his ship, already settling his armor about his shoulders, and was glad to see him coming.

Menelaus spoke first. “Why are you arming, brother? Are you going to send one of our men to scout the Trojans? I am afraid no one will do you this service — to spy on the enemy alone, in the dead of night. That takes a hard kind of courage.”

Agamemnon, lord of men, answered: “Menelaus, the two of us need sharp counsel, something that will save the Greeks and their ships. Zeus has turned his mind; he leans now toward Hector's offerings, not ours. I have never seen or heard of any man working such ruin in a single day as Hector has worked against the sons of the Greeks — and all of it alone, son to no god or goddess. The Greeks will remember this grief for a long time. Now run, fast as you can, down the line of the ships, and call Ajax and Idomeneus. I will go to Nestor and tell him to rise and walk among our sentry companies and give them their orders. They will listen to him sooner than to anyone, for his own son and Meriones — Idomeneus's man — are the captains over them. To them above all we gave that watch.”

Menelaus said: “How do I take your meaning? Am I to wait there with them for you, or come back here once I have given the order?” “Wait,” said Agamemnon, lord of men. “There are so many paths through the camp that we could miss each other in the dark. And call out to every man as you go; wake them. Name each by his lineage and his father's name; give every man his honor, and do not stand too proudly on your own. We must take our full share of the work. This was the heavy load Zeus laid on us at our birth.”

With that he sent his brother off and went on himself to Nestor, shepherd of his people. He found the old man asleep in his hut by his black ship. His fine armor lay beside him — his shield, his two spears, his helmet — and beside him too the gleaming war-belt the old man buckled on when he armed to lead his men into battle; for age did not hold him back. He raised himself on one elbow, lifted his head, and called out to Agamemnon: “Who is this, going alone through the camp and the ships in the dead of night, when other men are sleeping? Are you looking for a stray mule, or for some friend? Speak — don't just stand there in silence. What do you want?”

Agamemnon, lord of men, answered: “Nestor, son of Neleus, glory of the Greeks — you see Agamemnon, son of Atreus, on whom Zeus has heaped trouble and grief beyond all others, so long as there's breath in my body and my legs hold me up. I am wandering here because sleep will not settle on my eyes; the war weighs on me, and the danger to the Greeks. I am sick with fear for them. My heart will not stay in its place; it pounds as if it would leap out of me, and my limbs give way beneath me. If you too cannot sleep, then come — let us go down to the sentries and see whether they have not dropped off, worn out, and forgotten their watch. The enemy is camped close by, and we have no way of knowing he will not strike in the night.”

Nestor, the horseman of Gerene, answered: “Most honored son of Atreus, Agamemnon, lord of men — Zeus will not grant Hector everything he hopes for. He will have his own share of troubles yet, and more of them, if Achilles ever turns his heart back from this bitter anger. I will go with you gladly, and we'll rouse the others too — the son of Tydeus, and Odysseus, and quick Ajax, and the brave son of Phyleus. And someone should go and call great Ajax and King Idomeneus, whose ships lie farthest off of all, not near at hand. But I will say this plainly, even if it stings — I love and honor Menelaus, but I have to blame him for sleeping and leaving all this trouble on your shoulders alone. He should be out among all the captains, begging their help, now that the need is so dire.”

Agamemnon, lord of men, answered: “Old man, there are times you would be right to blame him. He is often slack, unwilling to put himself forward — not from laziness, not from carelessness, but because he looks to me and waits for me to lead. This time, though, he woke before I did, and came to me on his own. I have already sent him off to call the very men you named. So let us go. We will find them out beyond the gates with the watch; that is where I told them to meet.”
Nestor, the horseman of Gerene, answered: “If so, no Greek will blame him or refuse him, when he urges them on or gives them orders.”

With that he pulled on his tunic, bound the fine sandals to his feet, and clasped about him a purple cloak, doubled over, wide, with a thick shaggy nap. He took up a strong bronze-headed spear and set off down the line of the Greek ships. First he came to Odysseus, the equal of Zeus in counsel, and woke him with a shout — quickly the cry pierced his sleep, and he came out of his hut and said: “Why are you wandering alone like this, down the line of the ships, in the still of the night? What is so urgent?” And Nestor, the horseman of Gerene, answered: “Royal son of Laertes, resourceful Odysseus — don't take it amiss. The Greeks are in dire straits. Come with me; let us wake another man, one who can help us decide whether to fight or to run.”

At that Odysseus stepped back into his hut, slung his shield over his shoulders, and went with them. They came first to Diomedes, son of Tydeus, and found him outside his hut in his armor, his men sleeping around him with their shields beneath their heads. Their spears stood upright, butt-spikes driven into the ground, and the bronze of them flashed far off like the lightning of Father Zeus. The hero himself was sleeping on an ox-hide, with a bright rug folded under his head. Nestor went and stirred him with his heel and woke him, prodding him, scolding him on: “Up, son of Tydeus. How can you sleep the whole night through? Don't you see the Trojans are camped on the rise of the plain, close by the ships, with only a little ground left between us?”

At that Diomedes sprang up at once and said: “Old man, you are made of iron. You never rest a moment from your labors. Are there no younger Greeks who could go around and rouse the captains? There is no wearing you out.”

Nestor, the horseman of Gerene, answered: “My son, everything you say is true. I have good sons, and plenty of men who could call the chieftains. But the Greeks stand in the gravest danger; right now everything balances on a razor's edge — life or death for all of us. Go then, since you are younger than I am, and wake quick Ajax and the son of Phyleus. Be good enough to do it.”

Diomedes threw the skin of a great tawny lion about his shoulders — a skin that hung to his heels — took up his spear, and went. When he had roused the heroes he brought them back, and together they went the round of the watch. They found the captains not asleep at their posts but awake, sitting alert, their weapons in their hands. As sheepdogs keep an anxious watch over the fold when they catch a wild beast coming down through the mountain woods — a clamor of dogs and men breaks out, and sleep is gone — so sleep was driven from the eyes of the men keeping the cruel night's watch; they kept turning toward the plain, listening for any stir from the Trojans. The old man was glad to see it, and spoke to lift their hearts: “That's the way, my children. Stay awake, every one of you; let no sleep take hold, or we'll be the laughter of our enemies.”

With that he crossed the trench, and the other chiefs who had been called to the council went with him — and Meriones too, and Nestor's brave son, for the princes asked them along. Beyond the dug trench that ran around the wall they came to clear ground, a space free of the dead, where Hector had turned back from killing Greeks when night came down. There they sat and held their council.

Nestor, the horseman of Gerene, spoke first: “My friends — is there a man bold enough to trust his own daring heart and go among the Trojans? He might cut off some straggler on the edge of the camp, or hear what the enemy means to do — whether they plan to hold their ground here by the ships, far from the city, or fall back behind their walls now that they've beaten us. If he could learn all this and come back safe, his fame would rise high as heaven in the mouths of men, and his reward would be rich: every captain who commands a ship would give him a black ewe with her lamb at the udder — no possession is worth more — and he would have his place at every feast and gathering.”

They all sat silent. Then Diomedes, master of the war cry, spoke: “Nestor, my heart and my proud spirit drive me to go among the enemy, the Trojans, so close at hand. But I'd go with far more confidence if another man went with me. When two go together, one sees the chance before the other; alone, a man's sight is narrower and his wits are slower.”

At that, many offered to go with Diomedes. Both Ajaxes, fighters in Ares' company, wanted to go, and Meriones, and Nestor's son above all; Menelaus, son of Atreus, wanted to go; and patient Odysseus too, for his heart was always eager to dare. Then Agamemnon, lord of men, said: “Diomedes, son of Tydeus, dear to my own heart — choose your companion yourself. Take the best of those who have offered, for many are willing. And do not, out of some misplaced respect, leave the better man behind and take the worse for the sake of his royal blood.” He said this because he was afraid for Menelaus.

Diomedes, master of the war cry, answered: “If you tell me to choose the man myself, how could I overlook Odysseus? His heart and his bold spirit are equal to any danger, and Pallas Athena loves him. With him beside me, we could come back through fire itself — there is no one quicker to see and to understand.”

Patient, brilliant Odysseus said: “Son of Tydeus, don't praise me too much, and don't run me down. You are speaking among Greeks who know me well. Let us go. The night is wearing on, and dawn is near. The stars have wheeled across the sky; two parts of the night are gone, and only the third is left to us.”

Then the two of them armed. Brave Thrasymedes gave the son of Tydeus a two-edged sword — for his own was back at the ship — and a shield, and set on his head a helmet of bull's hide, without ridge or crest, the kind they call a skullcap, that guards the heads of strong young men. Meriones gave Odysseus a bow, a quiver, and a sword, and set on his head a helmet made of leather, drawn tight inside with thongs and on the outside set thick with the white tusks of a boar, packed close and skillfully worked all around, with a lining of felt fitted in the middle. This helmet had a long history: Autolycus had once stolen it out of Eleon, when he broke into the strong house of Amyntor, son of Ormenus; he gave it to Amphidamas of Cythera to carry to Scandeia; Amphidamas gave it as a guest-gift to Molus, who gave it to his son Meriones; and now it was set on the head of Odysseus.

When the two of them had armed, they set out, leaving the other captains behind. And Pallas Athena sent them a sign — a heron, close by the path on their right. They could not see it in the dark, but they heard its cry. Odysseus was glad at the omen, and prayed to Athena: “Hear me, daughter of Zeus who holds the storm-shield, you who stand beside me in all my labors and miss nothing I do — befriend me now, more than ever. Grant that we come back to the ships covered in glory, having done some great deed the Trojans will not forget.”

Then Diomedes, master of the war cry, prayed as well: “Hear me too, unwearying daughter of Zeus. Come with me now, as you went with my father, brave Tydeus, to Thebes, when the Greeks sent him there as their envoy. He left them on the banks of the Asopus and carried his message of peace to the Cadmeians — and on his way back he did great and terrible things, with you beside him, gracious goddess, ready at his side. So stand by me now, and keep me safe. In return I will sacrifice to you a broad-browed heifer of a year, unbroken, never yet led under the yoke by any man. I will sheathe her horns in gold and offer her to you.”

So they prayed, and Pallas Athena heard them. When they had finished their prayer to the daughter of mighty Zeus, the two went forward like a pair of lions through the black night, through the slaughter and the corpses and the scattered arms and the dark blood.

Meanwhile Hector would not let the Trojans sleep either. He had called together all the leaders and counselors of the Trojans, and laid his plan before them: “Who will undertake the task I have in mind, for a great reward? His pay will be enough. I will give him a chariot and two horses, the finest at the Greek ships, to anyone who will dare it and win glory for himself besides. Let him go to the fast ships and find out whether they are still guarded as before, or whether the Greeks, beaten now, are planning their escape and are too worn out to keep their watch.”

They all sat silent. But there was among the Trojans a man named Dolon, son of Eumedes the herald, a man rich in gold and bronze. He was ugly to look at but quick on his feet, an only son among five sisters. He spoke now to Hector and the Trojans: “Hector, my heart and my proud spirit drive me to go to the fast ships and spy on them. But first hold up your scepter and swear to me you will give me the horses and the chariot, bright with bronze, that carry the matchless son of Peleus. I'll be no useless scout to you, and I won't fall short. I'll go straight through their camp until I reach the ship of Agamemnon, where I expect the captains are taking counsel — whether to fight or to run.”

He spoke, and Hector took the scepter in his hands and swore: “Let Zeus himself be my witness, the loud-thundering husband of Hera — no other Trojan shall ride behind those horses. They are yours; you alone shall have the glory of them, for as long as you live.”

So he swore — an empty oath, but it spurred Dolon on. At once he slung his curved bow over his shoulder, pulled the gray hide of a wolf over his back, set a cap of weasel-skin on his head, took up a sharp javelin, and left the camp for the ships. But he was never to come back from the ships with word for Hector. When he had left the press of men and horses behind, he hurried eagerly down the path — and Odysseus saw him coming, and said to Diomedes: “Diomedes, here is someone from the camp. I can't tell whether he's a spy sent for our ships, or a man come to strip the dead. Let him get a little past us along the open ground; then we'll rush him and run him down. And if he outruns us, keep pressing him toward the ships, away from his own camp, with your spear, so he can't slip back to the city.”

With that the two of them lay down off the path among the dead. Dolon, suspecting nothing, ran straight past them. But when he had got about as far ahead as the width of a field a team of mules can plow in a day — for mules outwork oxen at dragging the jointed plow through deep fallow — the two ran after him. He heard their feet and stopped, sure they were friends from the Trojan camp, sent by Hector to call him back. But when they were a spear's throw off, or less, he saw they were enemies and bolted, his legs flying, and they tore after him. As two sharp-toothed hounds, trained to the hunt, press hard on a fawn or a hare through wooded country while it runs squealing before them, so the son of Tydeus and Odysseus, the sacker of cities, ran Dolon down, cutting him off from his own people. But when, in his flight toward the ships, he had nearly reached the sentries, Athena put fresh strength into the son of Tydeus, so that no other Greek might strike first and rob him of the glory, leaving him second. Diomedes sprang on with his spear and shouted: “Stop, or I'll run you through. You won't escape death from my hand for long.”

He threw the spear, but missed on purpose. The point passed over the man's right shoulder and stuck fast in the ground beyond him. Dolon stopped dead, shaking, his teeth chattering in his head, his face gone white with terror. The two came up to him panting and gripped his hands, and he burst into tears: “Take me alive — I'll ransom myself. There is gold in my father's house, and bronze, and hard-wrought iron; he will pay you a boundless ransom if he hears I'm alive at the Greek ships.”

Resourceful Odysseus answered him: “Take heart. Let no thought of death weigh on you. But tell me this, and tell it true: where are you going, alone, away from your camp toward the ships, in the dead of night, while other men sleep? Did you come to strip the bodies of the dead, or did Hector send you to spy out everything at the ships? Or did some impulse of your own bring you here?”

Dolon answered, his knees trembling under him: “Hector led me astray, out of all good sense, with his promises. He swore he would give me the strong-hoofed horses of the matchless son of Peleus and his chariot bright with bronze. He sent me through the fast black night to get close to the enemy and find out whether the ships are still guarded as before, or whether the Greeks, beaten now, are planning their escape and are too worn out to keep their watch.”

Resourceful Odysseus smiled at him and said: “You had set your heart on a great prize indeed — the horses of warlike Achilles. They are hard for any mortal man to master or to drive, any man but Achilles himself, whose mother is a goddess. But tell me this now, and tell it true: where did you leave Hector when you came? Where is his war-gear lying, and his horses? How are the watches set among the other Trojans, and where do they sleep? What are they planning? Will they hold their ground here by the ships, away from the city, or fall back behind their walls now that they've beaten us?”

Dolon, son of Eumedes, answered: “I will tell you the whole truth. Hector and his counselors are holding their council apart from the noise, beside the tomb of great Ilus. As for the guards you ask about — there is no chosen watch set over the camp. The Trojans themselves keep their fires burning, since they must, and they stay awake and call each other to their posts. But the allies, who have come from many lands, are asleep; they leave the watching to the Trojans, for their own wives and children are not here.”
Resourceful Odysseus said: “And these allies — do they sleep mingled in among the Trojan horsemen, or apart? Tell me clearly; I want to understand.”

Dolon, son of Eumedes, answered: “I'll tell you the whole truth of that as well. Toward the sea lie the Carians, and the Paeonians with their curved bows, and the Leleges and Cauconians and the noble Pelasgians. Toward Thymbra are the Lycians, and the proud Mysians, and the Phrygians and the Maeonians, masters of horses. But why ask all this? If you mean to slip into the Trojan host — there, at the very edge of the camp, apart from the rest, lie the Thracians, newly come. Among them is their king, Rhesus, son of Eioneus. I have never seen horses like his, so fine, so tall — whiter than snow, swift as the winds when they run. His chariot is worked with gold and silver, and he came carrying golden armor, a marvel of craft, too splendid for mortal men to wear — fit only for the deathless gods. Now take me to the fast ships, or tie me up and leave me here, until you go and prove for yourselves whether what I've told you is true or false.”

Diomedes, master of the war cry, glared at him and said: “Don't imagine you'll get away now, Dolon, useful as your news has been, once you're in our hands. If we let you go or ransom you, you'll be back at the Greek ships another time — to spy again, or to fight us in the open. But if my hand takes your life, you'll never trouble the Greeks again.”

Dolon reached up, about to take him by the chin and beg for his life — but Diomedes struck him across the middle of the neck with his sword and cut through both tendons. Dolon's head rolled in the dust while he was still trying to speak. They stripped from him the weasel-skin cap, the wolf hide, the bent bow, and the long spear. Odysseus, sacker of cities, lifted them high in his hands to Athena, giver of spoils, and prayed: “Take these, goddess, and rejoice. Of all on Olympus, you are the first we call on. Now guide us once more — to the horses and the sleeping-ground of the Thracian men.”

With that he lifted the spoils and set them on a tamarisk bush, and marked the spot by pulling up reeds and breaking off branches of the tamarisk, so they would not miss it coming back through the swift dark of the night. Then the two went on, through the scattered arms and the black blood, and came quickly to the band of Thracian men. They were asleep, worn out with the day's labor; their fine armor lay beside them on the ground in three good rows, and each man had his pair of horses by him. Rhesus slept in the middle, his swift horses tied with their reins to the topmost rail of his chariot. Odysseus saw him first and said: “Diomedes, this is the man, and these are the horses Dolon told us of, the one we killed. Now show your full strength. It is no time to stand idle in your armor. Loose the horses — or kill the men, and leave the horses to me.”

He spoke, and bright-eyed Athena breathed fury into Diomedes, and he killed to the left and the right. Hideous groans rose from the men as the sword went through them, and the ground ran red with blood. As a lion comes on a flock of sheep or goats left without their shepherd and leaps among them, bent on slaughter, so the son of Tydeus fell on the Thracian men until he had killed twelve. And each man Diomedes cut down with his sword, Odysseus, the master of strategy, took by the foot and dragged aside, clearing a way, so the fair-maned horses could pass through without shying — for they were not yet used to walking over the dead. Then the son of Tydeus came to the king himself, and Rhesus made the thirteenth life he took with his sword — Rhesus, gasping in his sleep. For an evil dream had stood that night above his head: the grandson of Oeneus himself, by the design of Athena. Meanwhile Odysseus, the man of patience, loosed the strong-hoofed horses, tied them together with the reins, and drove them clear of the camp, herding them with his bow — for he had forgotten to take the bright whip from the chariot. Then he whistled, a signal to brilliant Diomedes.

But Diomedes stood there still, turning over what bolder thing he might do — whether to seize the chariot, with the king's fine armor lying in it, and drag it off by the pole, or hoist the armor out and carry it away; or whether to take still more Thracian lives. And while he stood weighing it, Athena came and stood beside him: “Think of going back to the ships, son of great-hearted Tydeus, or you may go back driven before the enemy — should some other god wake the Trojans.”
He knew the voice of the goddess, and swung up at once onto a horse. Odysseus whipped them on with his bow, and they flew toward the fast ships of the Greeks.

But Apollo of the silver bow was keeping no idle watch. He had seen Athena going with the son of Tydeus, and in his anger at her he slipped into the great host of the Trojans and woke a Thracian counselor, Hippocoon, a noble kinsman of Rhesus. The man started up out of sleep, and when he saw the empty ground where the swift horses had stood, and the men gasping out their lives in the bloody slaughter, he cried aloud and called his dear comrade by name. And an uproar rose through the Trojan camp, a confused rush of men running together, and they stared in horror at the deeds those two had done before they got away to the ships.

When the two reached the place where they had killed Hector's spy, Odysseus, dear to Zeus, reined in the horses, and the son of Tydeus leaped to the ground, put the bloody spoils into Odysseus's hands, and climbed back up. Then he lashed the horses on, and they flew willingly toward the hollow ships, glad to be going home. Nestor was the first to hear the beat of their hooves, and said: “Friends, leaders and counselors of the Greeks — am I wrong, or am I right? My heart tells me to speak. The sound of swift horses' hooves is in my ears. I pray it is Odysseus and brave Diomedes driving the strong-hoofed horses back from the Trojans now — but I am terribly afraid the bravest of the Greeks may have come to harm in the uproar of the enemy.”

He had not finished speaking when the two arrived. They dismounted, and the others welcomed them gladly, with handclasps and warm words. Nestor, the horseman of Gerene, was the first to ask: “Tell me, Odysseus, glory of the Greeks — how did the two of you take these horses? Did you slip into the Trojan host, or did some god meet you and give them to you? They are like the rays of the sun. I am always going among the Trojans — old as I am, I never hang back by the ships — but I have never seen or imagined horses like these. Some god must have met you and made you this gift; for Zeus who gathers the clouds loves you both, and so does his daughter, bright-eyed Athena.”

Resourceful Odysseus answered him: “Nestor, son of Neleus, glory of the Greeks — a god, if he wished, could easily give us finer horses than these, for the gods are far stronger than we are. But these horses you ask about, old man, are newcomers from Thrace. Brave Diomedes killed their king and twelve of his men beside him, the best of them. And we took a thirteenth close to the ships — a scout Hector and the other proud Trojans had sent to spy on our camp.”

So he spoke, and he laughed as he drove the strong-hoofed horses across the trench, and the other Greeks went with him, glad at heart. When they reached the well-built quarters of the son of Tydeus, they tied the horses with cut leather reins at the manger, where Diomedes's own swift horses stood feeding on sweet barley. And Odysseus hung Dolon's bloody spoils at the stern of his ship, until they could ready a holy offering for Athena. Then the two of them waded into the sea and washed the heavy sweat from their shins and necks and thighs. And when the swell of the sea had rinsed the sweat from their bodies and the heart in each man eased, they stepped into the polished tubs and bathed. Washed and rubbed with oil, they sat down to eat, and from a full mixing-bowl they drew sweet wine and poured the first of it out to Athena.
And so the night, which had begun in sleepless dread, ended in the salt water and the wine — the only Greek victory in many days, and it had cost them nothing.
books.title: The Night Raid

books.label: Book XI
paragraphs: Dawn rose from her bed beside Tithonus to bring her light to gods and men, and Zeus sent Strife down to the fast Greek ships — grim Strife, with the war-sign of battle in her hands. She took her stand at the great black hull of Odysseus's ship, the one in the middle of the line, so her cry would carry both ways at once — to the huts of Telamonian Ajax at one end, and to those of Achilles at the other, for those two had drawn up their ships at the far edges, trusting their own strength. There she stood and let loose a cry, loud and shrill, and it poured courage into the heart of every Greek, the will to fight on without stopping. War was suddenly sweeter to them than the voyage home in the hollow ships.

The son of Atreus shouted to the Greeks to gird themselves, and he put on his own gleaming bronze. First he fastened the fine greaves around his shins, clasping them at the ankle with silver. Then he buckled on the breastplate Cinyras had once given him as a guest-gift, far off in Cyprus, when word came even there that the Greeks were about to sail for Troy. It had ten bands of dark blue enamel, twelve of gold, and twenty of tin; three blue serpents reared toward the neck on either side, like the rainbows the son of Cronus sets in the clouds as a sign to mortal men. Over his shoulders he slung the sword, studded with gold, its scabbard silver, hung from a chain of gold. He took up the great shield that covered his whole body, splendid to see, ringed with ten circles of bronze, twenty bosses of white tin on its face and one of dark blue at the center — and on that center a Gorgon's head, glaring and terrible, with Rout and Terror flanking it. On his head he set a helmet, two-ridged, four-plumed, the horsehair nodding above it. He gripped two heavy bronze-shod spears, and the light off his armor leapt up to the sky like fire, while Hera and Athena thundered overhead in honor of the king of golden Mycenae.

Each man left his horses with his charioteer to wait in line at the trench, and went forward on foot in full armor, and a great roar climbed into the breaking day. The fighters reached the trench ahead of the horses, and the chariots came up behind. The son of Cronus stirred an evil din over them, and sent down dew thick with blood, for he was about to hurl many strong heads down to the house of the dead.

Across from them, on the rising ground of the plain, the Trojans gathered around great Hector and noble Polydamas, and Aeneas, whom the Trojans honored like a god, and the three sons of Antenor — Polybus, godlike Agenor, and young Acamas, beautiful as the immortals. Hector showed his round shield in the front rank, and like a baleful star that flashes for a moment through a tear in the clouds and is gone again under them, so he flickered — now blazing among the foremost, now among the last — and his bronze flashed like the lightning of Zeus who carries the storm-shield.

Like reapers driving their swathes toward each other across a rich man's field of wheat or barley, the sheaves dropping thick under them, so the Trojans and the Greeks fell on one another and cut each other down. Neither side gave a thought to ruinous flight; they held even, fighting like wolves. And Strife rejoiced to watch them — she alone of the gods was there in the killing. The others kept apart, quiet in their own houses among the folds and valleys of Olympus, and all of them blamed the son of Cronus for meaning to hand the Trojans victory. But Father Zeus paid them no mind. He sat apart from the rest, alone in his glory, gazing down at the city of Troy and the Greek ships, at the glint of bronze, at the killers and the killed.

All morning, while the light grew, the spears bit on both sides and the men kept falling. But at the hour when a woodcutter in a mountain forest sets out his midday meal — his arms worn out from felling the tall trees, weariness on him, hunger for food in his heart — at that hour the Greeks broke the enemy line with a cry that ran down their whole front. Agamemnon led the way. First he killed Bienor, a leader of his people, and then his comrade and driver Oileus, who had jumped from the chariot to come straight at him; Agamemnon caught him full in the forehead with his spear, and the bronze visor of his helmet did not hold — the point drove through bronze and bone, and his brains were spattered inside, and he went down.

Agamemnon left them there, their chests bared to the sky, and went on to kill Isus and Antiphus, two sons of Priam — one a bastard, one trueborn — riding together in one chariot, the bastard at the reins, noble Antiphus fighting beside him. Achilles had once caught the pair of them on the slopes of Ida, tied them with fresh-cut willow shoots while they herded their flocks, and let them go for a ransom. Now the son of Atreus struck Isus in the chest above the nipple, and ran Antiphus through by the ear and pitched him from the car. He stripped their fine armor fast — and knew their faces, for he had seen them by the ships when Achilles brought them down from Ida. As a lion takes the helpless fawns of a running deer, snapping them up in his strong jaws and crushing the soft life out of them, and the doe, though she is near, can do nothing — terror runs through her, and she bolts through the thick brush, sweating, straining, away from the beast — so not one of the Trojans could help those two, for they themselves were running before the Greeks.

Then Agamemnon came on the two sons of Antimachus, Pisander and brave Hippolochus. Their father was the man who, more than any, had argued against giving Helen back to Menelaus — heavily bribed by Paris to say it. Now Agamemnon took his two sons, both in the one chariot, fighting to rein in their bolting team; the reins had slipped from their hands and the horses had gone wild. The son of Atreus sprang at them like a lion, and the two of them reached out from the car and begged: "Take us alive, son of Atreus, and you'll have a rich ransom. Our father Antimachus has gold and bronze and worked iron stored up — he'll pay you handsomely if he hears we're alive at the Greek ships."

So they pleaded, with tears, in soft words — and got back no soft answer. "If you are the sons of Antimachus," Agamemnon said, "the man who once, in the Trojan council, urged that Menelaus and Odysseus, who had come to you as envoys, be killed on the spot and never let go home — then you'll pay now for your father's filthy crime."

With that he drove Pisander from the chariot to the ground, the spear in his chest, and he fell flat on his back. Hippolochus leapt down to run, but Agamemnon cut him too — lopped off his hands, struck off his head, and sent it rolling through the press like a log. He left them there and went where the ranks were thickest, and the rest of the Greeks came after. Foot soldiers killed the foot soldiers driven before them, horsemen killed horsemen, and the trampling hooves beat a cloud of dust off the plain. King Agamemnon kept on, killing, shouting his men forward. As a fire falls on a dry forest and the wind whirls it everywhere, and the thickets shrivel and go down under the rush of the flame — so the heads of the running Trojans went down before Agamemnon, son of Atreus, and many a fine team dragged an empty chariot rattling down the lanes of war, missing the drivers who lay on the ground, dearer now to the vultures than to their wives.

Zeus drew Hector out of the spears and the dust, out of the carnage and the din. But the son of Atreus pressed on, roaring to the Greeks. Past the tomb of old Ilus, son of Dardanus, in the middle of the plain, past the wild fig tree they swept, always making for the city — Agamemnon still shouting, his hands fouled with gore. But at the Scaean gates and the oak tree they halted, and waited for the rest to come up. Out on the open plain the Trojans were still running like a herd of cattle scattered by a lion that has fallen on them in the dead of night — he springs at one, breaks her neck in his jaws, then laps the blood and tears out the guts — so Agamemnon harried them, always killing the last man as they fled headlong, and many were flung from their chariots face-first into the dust under his hand, for his spear raged on ahead of him.

But just as he was about to reach the high wall and the town, the father of gods and men came down from the sky and took his seat, thunderbolt in hand, on the peak of Ida of the many springs. He called golden-winged Iris and sent her with a word: "Go, swift Iris, and tell Hector this. As long as he sees Agamemnon out in front, raging, mowing down the ranks, let him hold back and order the others to bear the brunt. But the moment Agamemnon is wounded — by spear or by arrow — and climbs into his chariot, then I will hand Hector the strength to kill, all the way to the ships, until the sun goes down and the dark comes on."

Iris obeyed. Down she came from the crests of Ida to sacred Troy, and found Hector, son of Priam, standing by his chariot and horses. She came near and said: "Hector, son of Priam, equal to Zeus in counsel — Father Zeus has sent me to you with this. As long as you see Agamemnon out in front, raging, cutting down the ranks, hold off from the fighting and send the rest in to take the worst of it. But the moment he's wounded — by spear or arrow — and takes to his chariot, Zeus will give you the strength to kill, all the way to the ships, until the sun goes down and the dark comes on."

Iris said it and was gone, and Hector leapt from his chariot to the ground in full armor, brandishing his two spears, ranging everywhere through the army, rousing the men to fight, waking the terrible work of war. They wheeled and stood and faced the Greeks, and the Greeks closed their own ranks to meet them. The line was set; they stood front to front — and Agamemnon, hungry to be first of all, pressed forward ahead of them.

Tell me now, you Muses who hold the halls of Olympus — which of the Trojans, or of their famous allies, was first to come against Agamemnon? It was Iphidamas, son of Antenor, a big man and a brave one, raised in fertile Thrace, the mother of flocks. His mother's father Cisses brought him up from a child in his own house — Cisses, father of lovely Theano. When he came to the glory of manhood, Cisses tried to keep him there and gave him his daughter in marriage; but no sooner had he wed than word of the Greeks' coming pulled him away, and he sailed with twelve ships of his own. He left the ships at Percote and came on to Troy by land. This was the man who now met the son of Atreus. When they were close, Agamemnon's cast went wide. Iphidamas struck him on the belt below the breastplate and threw his whole weight behind it, trusting his strong arm — but the belt held; the point never got near, turned aside on the silver like lead. Agamemnon caught the spear in his hand, dragged it toward him with a lion's fury, wrenched it from his grip, then drew his sword and struck him across the neck and dropped him. So he fell there and slept the sleep of bronze, poor man, killed defending his own people, far from the bride he had wed and never had joy of, though he had paid so much for her — a hundred cattle down, a thousand sheep and goats promised after, out of the countless flocks he owned. Agamemnon, son of Atreus, stripped him and carried the fine armor back into the Greek host.

When Coon, Antenor's eldest son, saw it, grief darkened his eyes at the sight of his fallen brother. He came at Agamemnon from the side, unseen, spear in hand, and stabbed him in the middle of the arm, below the elbow, the bright point driving clean through. Agamemnon shuddered with the pain — but even then he did not quit the fight. He went for Coon with his wind-swift spear as the man was hauling his brother off by the foot — his own father's son — and crying out to the best of his comrades for help; and Agamemnon caught him under his shield with the bronze and killed him, standing over the body of Iphidamas, and cut off his head there. So the sons of Antenor, at the hands of the son of Atreus, filled out their fate and went down to the house of Hades.

As long as the blood still ran warm from the wound, Agamemnon ranged the enemy ranks with spear and sword and great heaved stones. But once the blood stopped and the gash dried, sharp pains broke over him — like the piercing pangs the Eilithyiae send on a woman in labor, the goddesses of childbirth, daughters of Hera, keepers of bitter pain — so sharp were the pangs that broke over the son of Atreus. He climbed into his chariot and told his driver to make for the hollow ships, for the agony was on him; and with a great clear shout he called to the Greeks: "Friends, captains and counselors of the army — it falls to you now to fight off the ships, since Zeus will not let me battle the Trojans all day long."
His driver lashed the horses toward the ships, and they flew on willingly, their chests white with foam, their bellies grey with dust, carrying the wounded king out of the war.

When Hector saw Agamemnon leave the field, he shouted to the Trojans and Lycians: "Trojans, Lycians, Dardanian fighters — be men, friends, remember your courage! Their best man is gone. Zeus has handed me a great prize. Drive your horses straight at the Greeks and win yourselves still greater glory."

With those words he put fire into every man. As a hunter sets his white-toothed hounds on a wild boar or a lion, so Hector, the equal of Ares, set the proud Trojans on the Greeks; and full of fight he plunged in among the foremost and fell on the battle like a screaming squall that swoops down and lashes the wine-dark sea to fury.

Who, then, were the first and the last that Hector killed, in the hour Zeus gave him the glory? Asaeus first, then Autonous and Opites; Dolops, son of Clytius, and Opheltius, and Agelaus; Aesymnus, and Orus, and Hipponous steady in the fight. These were the captains he cut down, and then he fell on the ranks behind them. As when the west wind drives the white clouds of the south and beats them down in its blasting rage, and the swells roll big and the spray is flung high under the wandering wind — so thick were the heads that fell under Hector's hand.

Now ruin would have come, with no way out, and the Greeks would have been driven in a rout back to their ships — if Odysseus had not called to Diomedes: "Son of Tydeus, what's wrong with us, that we forget our fighting strength? Come here, friend, stand at my side. We'll be shamed forever if Hector takes the ships."
And strong Diomedes answered: "I'll stand, and I'll hold. But there'll be little joy in it — Zeus means to give the Trojans the day, and not us."

With that he struck Thymbraeus from his chariot to the ground, the spear in his left breast, while Odysseus killed Molion, the man's squire. They left those two, done fighting now, and the pair of them tore through the Trojans like two wild boars that round on the hounds that hunt them — and the Greeks, fleeing before Hector, were glad of the breath it bought them.

Next they took two men with their chariot, the two sons of Merops of Percote, the best of all men at reading what is to come. He had forbidden his sons to go to the war, but they would not listen — their own death drew them on. Diomedes, son of Tydeus, killed them both and stripped them, and Odysseus killed Hippodamus and Hypeirochus.

And the son of Cronus, looking down from Ida, held the scales level between them, and they went on killing one another. The son of Tydeus speared Agastrophus, son of Paeon, through the hip — his chariot was not at hand to carry him off, so blind had his confidence made him; his squire had it back at a distance while he himself fought on foot among the front rank, until he lost his life. Hector was quick to see the havoc Diomedes and Odysseus were making, and he bore down on them with a shout, the Trojan ranks behind him. Brave Diomedes felt a chill at the sight, and said to Odysseus beside him: "Here comes great Hector, rolling down on us — we're for it. Stand fast, and we'll take his charge where we are."

He balanced his spear and let it fly, and he did not miss: he hit Hector full on the head, high on the helmet — but bronze turned bronze, and Hector was not touched, for the point was stopped by the visored helmet of three plates that Phoebus Apollo had given him. Hector sprang far back into the cover of his men, dropped to one knee, and braced himself with a heavy hand against the ground, and the dark came down over his eyes. While the son of Tydeus chased his own spear far through the front ranks to where it had stuck in the earth, Hector got his breath, swung back into his chariot, and drove into the crowd, and so escaped death. But Diomedes came after him with his spear and called: "Dog — you've slipped death again, close as it came. Phoebus Apollo saved you once more, the god you must pray to before you walk into the spears. But I'll finish you yet, the next time we meet — if there's any god who'll stand by me too. For now I'll go after whoever else I can reach."

And he bent to strip the son of Paeon — but Paris, the husband of lovely Helen, was drawing on him with his bow, leaning against a pillar on the barrow men had raised long ago for Ilus, son of Dardanus, a lord of the old days. Diomedes had just lifted the breastplate from Agastrophus's chest, the heavy helmet, the shield from his shoulders, when Paris pulled the string and let the arrow go — and it did not leave his hand for nothing. It pierced the flat of Diomedes' right foot, drove clean through, and stuck in the ground. With a happy laugh Paris jumped up from his cover and crowed: "You're hit! My shot was not wasted. I only wish I'd caught you in the gut and killed you — then the Trojans, who fear you the way goats fear a lion, might have had a rest from their troubles."

But Diomedes, not shaken at all, answered him: "Archer — you with your bow, your foul tongue, your pretty hair, you ogler of girls — if you ever faced me man to man in armor, your bow and your arrows would do you no good at all. You scratched the flat of my foot, and you boast of it. I no more feel it than if a woman or a foolish child had struck me — a worthless coward's dart raises a feeble wound. When I hit a man, it's another matter: even a graze lays him out dead. His wife claws her cheeks, his children are left fatherless, and he rots there reddening the ground, with more vultures around him than women."

He spoke, and Odysseus the spearman came up and stood over him as cover, and Diomedes sat down behind him and drew the arrow from his foot, and a sharp pain shot through his flesh as it came. Then he climbed into his chariot and told his driver to make for the hollow ships, for his heart was heavy.

Now Odysseus was alone. Not one of the Greeks stood with him; fear had taken them all. Troubled, he spoke to his own brave heart: "What is happening to me? It's a bad thing to run from these numbers — but a worse thing to be caught alone, now that Zeus has scattered the rest in panic. Yet why do I argue it out with myself? I know well enough: the coward leaves the field, but the man of worth must hold his ground hard, whether he wounds or is wounded."

While he turned it over, the Trojan ranks came on and closed around him — and they hemmed in their own grief. As hounds and strong young men set on a boar that breaks from his lair, gnashing his white tusks, and they press in from every side, and the gnashing rings out, and fierce as he is they hold their ground — so the Trojans crowded around Odysseus. First he lunged with his spear and wounded faultless Deiopites in the shoulder from above; then he killed Thoon and Ennomus; then he caught Chersidamas in the belly below the shield as the man dropped from his chariot, and he fell in the dust and clutched the earth in his hand. He left them and ran Charops, son of Hippasus, the brother of noble Socus, through with the spear. And Socus came to help his brother — a hero — and stood close and said: "Far-famed Odysseus, never filled with cunning or with toil — today you'll either boast you killed both sons of Hippasus and stripped their armor, or you'll fall on the end of my spear."

With that he struck the shield of Odysseus. The spear punched through the shield and on through the worked breastplate and tore the flesh off his side — but Pallas Athena would not let it reach his guts. Odysseus knew the wound was not his death, and he gave ground and said to Socus: "Poor wretch, your end has come. You've stopped me fighting the Trojans for a moment — but now you'll go down on my spear, and hand the glory to me and your soul to Hades of the fine horses."

Socus had turned to run; and as he turned, the spear caught him in the back between the shoulders and drove on through his chest. He fell with a crash, and Odysseus stood over him and cried: "Socus, son of Hippasus the horse-tamer — death came too fast for you; you didn't outrun it. Poor man — your father and mother won't be there to close your eyes; the carrion birds will wrap you in the beating of their dark wings and tear you. But if I die, the Greeks will give me my burial."

He drew Socus's heavy spear out of his flesh and out of the shield, and the blood spurted when it came free, and his heart sank at the sight of it. When the Trojans saw Odysseus bleeding, they raised a great shout and rushed at him together, and he gave ground and called his comrades to him. Three times he shouted, as loud as a man's head can hold, and three times Menelaus heard him; and at once he turned to Ajax beside him and said: "Ajax, son of Telamon, born to lead — the cry of Odysseus is in my ears, and it sounds as if the Trojans have cut him off and are wearing him down, alone, in the thick of them. Let's drive through the crowd. Better to stand by him. I'm afraid for him, brave as he is, alone among that many — and the Greeks would feel the loss of him hard."

He led the way, and great Ajax went with him. They found Odysseus ringed by Trojans, like tawny jackals in the hills around a wounded stag that a hunter has hit with an arrow — the stag ran on while the blood was warm and his legs would hold him, but when the shaft has worn him down the jackals fall to tearing him in a shaded glen — until some power sends a lion their way, and the jackals scatter in terror and the lion has the meat. So the Trojans, many and brave, crowded around cunning Odysseus, and the hero stood at bay and held them off with his spear. Then Ajax came up with his shield like a wall before him and stood beside him, and the Trojans broke and ran in all directions. Menelaus took Odysseus by the hand and led him out of the press while his squire brought up the chariot; and Ajax fell on the Trojans and killed Doryclus, a bastard son of Priam, and then wounded Pandocus, and Lysandrus, and Pyrasus, and Pylartes. As a swollen river comes roaring down from the mountains onto the plain, fat with the rain of the sky, sweeping dry oaks and pines along with it, and flinging the mud out into the sea — so glorious Ajax stormed across the plain, killing men and horses both.

Hector did not yet know any of this, for he was fighting away on the far left of the line, by the banks of the Scamander, where the dying was thickest and the war-cry rose loudest around Nestor and brave Idomeneus. There Hector worked among them with his spear and his driving, wrecking the ranks set against him; and even so the Greeks would not have given ground — if Paris, the husband of lovely Helen, had not stopped Machaon, shepherd of his people, in his stride, hitting him in the right shoulder with a three-barbed arrow. The Greeks, with the fight already turning, were afraid the Trojans might take him; and Idomeneus said to Nestor: "Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Greeks — get up into your chariot, take Machaon, and drive your horses to the ships as fast as they'll go. A healer is worth many other men, for he can cut out arrows and lay on the soothing herbs."

Nestor, the Gerenian horseman, did as Idomeneus said. He climbed into his chariot at once, and Machaon, son of the great healer Asclepius, climbed up beside him. Nestor laid on the whip, and the horses flew toward the ships, glad enough to go.

Then Cebriones, riding beside Hector, saw the Trojans thrown into confusion, and said: "Hector, here we are fighting on the very edge of the battle, out at the rim — while the rest of the Trojans are routed, men and horses tangled together. Ajax, son of Telamon, is driving them; I know him by the breadth of his shield. Let's turn the chariot and horses there, where the fighting is worst, horse and foot, and the war-cry is loudest."

With that he lashed the fine team, and at the stroke they tore the chariot in among the Greeks and Trojans, over bodies and over shields, and the axle below was sprayed with blood, and the rail around the car splashed with the gore the hooves and the wheel-rims threw up. Hector cut his way in and flung himself into the thick of it, scattering the Greeks, his spear never long idle. He ranged the ranks with sword and spear and great stones — but he kept clear of Ajax, son of Telamon, for Zeus would have been angry to see him take on a better man than himself.

Then Father Zeus, on his high seat, put fear into the heart of Ajax, so that he stood stunned, slung his great shield behind him, and gave ground, glancing about at the crowd of his enemies like a cornered beast, turning this way and that, drawing slowly back. As farmers and their dogs drive a lion off from the cattle-yard, keeping the night-long watch so he won't carry off the best of the herd — he lunges, hungry, and gets nothing, for the darts come thick from the bold hands against him, and the burning brands that scare him for all his rage, and at dawn he slinks away sullen and balked — so Ajax drew back from the Trojans, against all his will, in dread for the ships of the Greeks. Or as a stubborn donkey gets the better of the boys in a field — one who has had many a stick broken across his back — and pushes into the standing grain and eats his fill, and they beat him with their sticks but their strength is a child's strength, and only when he's had enough do they at last drive him out — so the Trojans and their allies pressed on great Ajax, jabbing always at the center of his shield. Now and then he would round on them and turn the whole Trojan front back, and then again he gave ground — but he kept any of them from breaking through to the ships. He stood alone between the two armies, and the spears flung from their hands stuck in his great shield, while many, thirsting for his flesh, fell short in the dirt before they could taste it.

Now when Eurypylus, the brave son of Euaemon, saw Ajax being worn down under the storm of arrows, he came and stood beside him and let his spear fly. He hit Apisaon, son of Phausius, in the liver below the midriff and dropped him on the spot, and sprang to strip the armor off his shoulders. But Paris saw him and drew on him, and the arrow caught Eurypylus in the right thigh; the shaft broke off, and the point dragged in the wound. He fell back into the cover of his comrades to save his life, shouting to the Greeks as he went: "Friends, captains and counselors of the army — turn back, stand, defend Ajax. He's overwhelmed, and I doubt he'll come out of this alive. Here — to the rescue of great Ajax, son of Telamon!"

So the wounded man cried, and the others came up and gathered around him, bracing their shields against their shoulders to give him cover; and Ajax made his way toward them, and turned to stand at bay once he had reached his own men.

So they fought on, like a blaze of fire. Meanwhile the mares of Neleus, lathered with sweat, were carrying Nestor out of the battle, and Machaon, shepherd of his people, with him. Achilles saw it and took note, for he was standing on the high stern of his ship, watching the bitter labor of the rout. He called from the ship to his comrade Patroclus, and Patroclus heard him in the hut and came out looking like Ares himself — and here was the beginning of the evil that would soon come on him. "Why do you call me, Achilles?" he said. "What do you want of me?" And swift-footed Achilles answered: "Noble son of Menoetius, dear to my heart — now, I think, the Greeks will be at my knees, begging, for they're in real straits. Go, Patroclus, dear to Zeus, and ask Nestor who it is he's carrying wounded from the field. From behind I'd say it's Machaon, son of Asclepius, but I couldn't see the man's face — the horses went past me too fast."
Patroclus did as his dear comrade told him, and set off running along the line of huts and ships.

When Nestor and Machaon reached the huts of the son of Neleus, they got down, and a squire, Eurymedon, unhitched the horses. The two of them stood in the breeze by the shore to dry the sweat from their shirts, then came inside and took their seats. Lovely Hecamede mixed them a draught — the woman Nestor had been given out of Tenedos when Achilles sacked it; she was the daughter of great-hearted Arsinous, and the Greeks had picked her out for Nestor because he was the best of them in counsel. First she drew up a fine table with feet of blue enamel, and set on it a bronze dish with an onion to give an edge to the drink, and pale honey, and the sacred barley-meal, and beside them a magnificent cup the old man had brought from home, studded with gold, with four handles, and two golden doves feeding at each, and two supports beneath. Anyone else would have strained to lift it from the table when it was full, but old Nestor raised it easily. In it the woman, lovely as a goddess, mixed them the draught with Pramnian wine — she grated goat cheese into it with a bronze grater, scattered white barley over it — and when it was ready she told them to drink. When they had drunk and put off their parching thirst, they fell to talking with one another, and just then Patroclus appeared in the doorway.

When the old man saw him, he sprang up from his shining seat, took him by the hand, led him in, and pressed him to sit. But Patroclus held back and said: "No seat for me, old sir — you won't talk me in. The man who sent me is not one to take lightly, and he sent me to ask who it is you've carried wounded from the field. But I can see for myself now — it's Machaon, shepherd of his people. I'll go back and tell Achilles. You know yourself, old sir, what a hard man he is — quick to find fault even where no fault lies."

And Nestor, the Gerenian horseman, answered: "Why should Achilles care now which of the Greeks have been hit? He has no notion of the grief that's loose in this camp. Our best men are down, struck and wounded. Brave Diomedes, son of Tydeus, is wounded; Odysseus is wounded, and Agamemnon too; Eurypylus has an arrow in the thigh; and I have just brought this man here out of the fighting, hit by an arrow as well. And still Achilles, for all his courage, feels nothing for us, has no pity. Will he wait until the ships are burning at the water's edge, do what we can, and we are killed one on top of another? I have no strength left in my limbs as I once had. If only I were young again, and my power were what it was in the days of the cattle-raid, when there was a war between us and the men of Elis. I killed Itymoneus then, the brave son of Hypeirochus, who lived in Elis, as I was driving off the spoil — he was hit by a dart from my hand as he stood in the front rank defending his herds, and he fell, and the country people around him scattered in fear. We drove a vast plunder off that plain — fifty herds of cattle, as many flocks of sheep, as many droves of pigs, as many wide-ranging flocks of goats, and a hundred and fifty horses, all of them mares, many with foals running beside them. We drove the whole of it into Pylos, the city of Neleus, by night, and the heart of Neleus was glad that I had taken so much my first time out. At daybreak the heralds went round crying that anyone owed a debt in Elis should come; and the leading men of Pylos gathered to divide it — for the Epeians owed many of us, since we of Pylos were few and had been wronged. In years past Heracles had come and laid us low, and our best men had died. Neleus had twelve sons, and I alone was left; all the others were gone. The Epeians grew arrogant on that and worked us much harm. So my father chose out a herd and a great flock — three hundred head, with their herdsmen — for a heavy debt was owed him in Elis: a team of four prize horses, with their chariot, that had gone to the games to run for a tripod, and King Augeas had kept them, and sent the driver home grieving for his horses. Angered by all this, in word and in deed, Neleus took great recompense, and divided out the rest, so that no man should go without his fair share.

"So we set everything in order and made sacrifice to the gods throughout the city. But on the third day the Epeians came against us in force, men and chariots together, and with them the two Molione in their armor, still only boys then, untried in war. There is a city, Thryoessa, set on a steep hill far off on the Alpheus, on the border of sandy Pylos. This they meant to destroy, and they ringed it about. But when they had crossed the whole plain, Athena came down to us in the night from Olympus to call us to arms — and she found the men of Pylos willing, hungry for the fight. Neleus would not let me arm; he hid my horses, saying I knew nothing of war yet. Even so, on foot among our own horsemen, I made my mark, for Athena ordered the fight that way. There is a river, the Minyeius, that runs into the sea near Arene, and there we who had horses waited for the holy Dawn, while the companies of foot came up behind us. From there, in full armor, we came at midday to the sacred stream of the Alpheus. We made fine sacrifices to almighty Zeus there, a bull to the Alpheus, a bull to Poseidon, and an unbroken heifer to Athena. Then we took our supper by companies, and lay down to sleep, each in his armor, along the river.

"The Epeians were closing on the city, set on taking it — but a great fight stood between them and that. When the sun's first light struck the earth, we joined battle, praying to Zeus and Athena. And when the two armies met, I was the first to kill my man and take his horses — the spearman Mulius, son-in-law of Augeas, who had married the eldest daughter, golden-haired Agamede, who knew every healing herb the wide earth grows. I speared him as he came at me, and when he fell in the dust I leapt up into his chariot and took my place in the front rank. The Epeians broke and ran in every direction when they saw the captain of their horsemen, their best man, go down. And I came down on them like a black whirlwind. I took fifty chariots, and at each of them two men bit the dust on my spear. I would have killed the two young Molione, sons of Actor, if their true father, Poseidon who shakes the earth, had not hidden them in a thick mist and carried them out of the war. Then Zeus handed the men of Pylos a great victory, and we chased the enemy far across the plain, killing them and gathering their armor, until we drove our horses to Buprasium rich in wheat, and the Olenian rock, and the hill they call Alesium — and there Athena turned the army back. There I killed the last man, and left him; and the Greeks drove their horses back from Buprasium to Pylos, and gave thanks to Zeus among the gods, and to Nestor among men.

"That is the man I was among my people, when I was a man. But Achilles will keep all his courage for himself alone — and bitterly he'll weep for it later, when the army has been cut to pieces. My friend, didn't Menoetius give you this very charge the day he sent you out of Phthia to Agamemnon? Odysseus and I were inside the house, and we heard every word of it. We had come to the fine house of Peleus, gathering men through the length of Achaea, and there we found Menoetius, and you, and Achilles beside you. Old Peleus was in the courtyard, burning the fat thighs of an ox to Zeus the thunderer, holding a golden cup and pouring bright wine over the burning offering, and the two of you were busy carving the ox. We stood at the gate, and Achilles sprang up startled, took us by the hand and led us in, sat us down, and set before us all that guests are owed. When we'd had our fill of food and drink, I made my case and urged you both to come with us. You were eager enough — and the two old men charged you hard. Old Peleus told his son Achilles always to be the best, to outdo the rest; and Menoetius, son of Actor, said this to you: 'My son, Achilles is the higher born, but you are the elder, though he is far the stronger in his hands. Counsel him well, guide him the right way, advise him — and he'll follow you to his own good.' That is what your father charged you, and you have forgotten it. Even now you might say all this to Achilles, and he might listen. Who knows but you could win him over — a friend's word has its own power. And if some prophecy holds him back, or his mother has told him something from Zeus, then let him send you out, and the rest of the Myrmidons with you, in case you might be the light and the saving of the Greeks. And let him send you into the fighting in his own armor, so the Trojans take you for him and pull back, and the Greeks, hard pressed and barely able to breathe, get a moment's rest. You, fresh, could easily drive worn-out men back from the ships and the huts, back to their own walls."

So he spoke, and stirred the heart in Patroclus, and he set off running back along the line of ships toward Achilles, son of Aeacus. But when he came level with the ships of Odysseus, where the men held assembly and gave judgment and where the altars of the gods were set, there Eurypylus met him — Euaemon's son, wounded in the thigh with an arrow, limping out of the fight. The sweat poured down his head and shoulders, and the dark blood welled from his cruel wound, but his mind was still clear. The son of Menoetius saw him and pitied him, and said in grief: "You poor men — captains and counselors of the Greeks — was this your fate, far from your friends and your own land, to feed the dogs of Troy with your white fat? But tell me, Eurypylus, can the Greeks still hold great Hector off, or will they go down now under his spear?"

And the wounded Eurypylus answered: "No hope left for the Greeks now, noble Patroclus. They'll be driven back against the black ships. All the men who were our best are lying there, struck and wounded at the Trojans' hands, and the Trojans grow stronger and stronger. But save me — get me to my ship, cut the arrow out of my thigh, wash the dark blood off it with warm water, and lay on those soothing herbs they say you learned from Achilles, who learned them from Chiron, the most honest of the Centaurs. For of our two healers, I hear Machaon is lying wounded in the huts, in need of a healer himself, and Podalirius is still out on the plain, facing the Trojans."

And the brave son of Menoetius answered: "How can this be, Eurypylus? What am I to do? I'm on my way to carry a message to Achilles from Nestor of Gerene, bulwark of the Greeks. But even so — I won't leave you in your pain." With that he put his arm around him and led him into the hut, and a servant, seeing them, spread ox-hides on the ground. Patroclus laid him out full length, and with a knife cut the sharp arrow from his thigh, and washed the dark blood from the wound with warm water; then he crushed a bitter root between his hands and rubbed it on — a root that takes away all pain — and the wound dried, and the bleeding stopped.
books.title: The Day of Agamemnon

books.label: Book XII
paragraphs: So inside the hut the son of Menoetius was tending the wound of Eurypylus, while out beyond, the Greeks and Trojans fought on without let. And now the ditch was not going to hold the Trojans back any longer, nor the high wall above it. The Greeks had raised it to shield their ships, and dug the trench around it to guard the ships and the rich spoils they had taken — but they had not made the gods their burnt offerings. It went up without the blessing of the immortals, and so it was not built to last.

While Hector lived and Achilles nursed his rage, and while Priam's city stood unsacked, the great Greek wall held firm. But once the bravest of the Trojans had fallen, and many of the Greeks with them — once, in the tenth year, the city was sacked and the Greeks had sailed home in their ships — then Poseidon and Apollo laid their plans to tear the wall down. They turned against it every river that runs from the heights of Ida down to the sea: Rhesus, Heptaporus, Caresus, Rhodius, Grenicus, Aesopus, and bright Scamander, and Simois too, where so many shields and helmets had dropped in the dust, and so many men of the half-divine generation had fallen. Apollo swung all their mouths together and drove them against the wall for nine days, while Zeus rained without pause to wash it the sooner into the sea. Poseidon himself went before them, trident in hand, and swept into the surf every foundation of log and stone the Greeks had laid with such labor; he leveled it all along the rushing Hellespont, then buried the whole stretch under a wide beach of sand. When the wall was gone, he turned the rivers back into their old channels.

That was what Poseidon and Apollo would do, in time to come. For now the fighting and the uproar still raged around the wall, and its timbers groaned under the blows raining on them. The Greeks, broken down under the lash of Zeus, were penned against their ships in dread of Hector, that master of rout, who fought as he always did, with the force and fury of a whirlwind. As a lion or a wild boar wheels among the dogs and hunters that close on him, and they lock themselves into a wall of bodies and pour their javelins at his face — and his great heart never flinches, though that same high spirit will be the death of him; again and again he charges to scatter them, and wherever he drives, they give way — so Hector ranged through the ranks, urging his men on, pressing them to cross the ditch.

But the horses would not. They balked at the brink, neighing, frightened by the width of it. They could neither leap the trench nor pick their way across, for it ran with steep overhanging banks on both sides, and set close along the top were the sharp stakes the Greeks had planted thick and strong against any assault. A horse could not go down into it and haul a chariot after, but the men on foot kept straining to do what they could. Then Polydamas came up to Hector and said, "Hector, and you other captains of the Trojans and the allies — it is madness to drive our horses across the ditch. It will fight us every step: it bristles with stakes, and just beyond them is the wall. There is no room for chariots down there, and no use for them; it is a narrow place, and we would only be cut to pieces. If Zeus in his anger truly means to help us and destroy the Greeks, then let it come now, here, far from Argos. But if they turn and we are driven back from the ships in a rout, back into the trench — not one of us will make it home to tell the city. So do as I say. Let the squires hold the horses at the ditch, and the rest of us follow Hector on foot, in full armor, in one mass. If their day of doom has come, the Greeks will not stand against us."

Polydamas had spoken well, and it pleased Hector. He leapt down from his chariot to the ground in full armor, and when the other Trojans saw it, they too left their chariots. Each man handed his horses to his driver to hold ready at the ditch. Then they sorted themselves into companies, armed, and went forward behind their leaders in five bodies. The largest and the bravest, the ones most set on breaking through and fighting at the ships, marched with Hector and Polydamas, and Cebriones was their third in command, for Hector had left a lesser man in charge of his chariot. The second company was led by Paris, Alcathous, and Agenor; the third by two sons of Priam, Helenus and Deiphobus, and with them the hero Asius — Asius son of Hyrtacus, whom the great tawny horses of the Selleis breed had carried from Arisbe. Aeneas, the brave son of Anchises, led the fourth, and with him the two sons of Antenor, Archelochus and Acamas, men skilled in every kind of fighting. And Sarpedon was captain of the allies; he took with him Glaucus and Asteropaeus, whom he judged the best men after himself — for he was far the best of them all. They locked their ox-hide shields together and drove straight at the Greeks, certain they could hold out no longer and would break before the ships.

The rest of the Trojans and their allies did as Polydamas advised. But Asius, son of Hyrtacus, would not leave his horses and his driver behind. In his recklessness he took them on toward the ships — and so he came to his death, and never again returned to windy Ilium, glorying in his chariot and his horses. Before that, doom with its dark name closed over him, and he fell to the spear of Idomeneus, the lordly son of Deucalion. He had driven for the left wing of the ships, the way the Greeks came back from the plain with their chariots and horses, and there he found the gates flung wide and the great bar drawn — for the gatemen kept them open to let in any of their own who came fleeing toward the ships. That was the road Asius chose, on purpose, and his men charged behind him with a shout, sure the Greeks would not hold. They did not know that two of the bravest fighters stood at the gates: the proud sons of the warlike Lapiths, Polypoetes, the strong son of Pirithous, and Leonteus, the equal of murderous Ares. The two of them waited there like a pair of high oaks on the mountains, that stand on their wide-spreading roots and year after year ride out the wind and the rain — so these two awaited the charge of great Asius, steady and unafraid. The Trojans came on under Asius and Iamenus and Orestes, and Adamas son of Asius, and Thoon and Oenomaus, raising the war cry, their shields of dry ox-hide held over their heads, straight for the wall. For a while the two defenders stayed within and rallied the Greeks to fight for the ships. But when they saw the Trojans storming the wall and their own men crying out and breaking, they burst out and fought in front of the gates like two wild boars in the hills that take the rush of men and dogs, and charging from both sides snap the brush around them, tearing it up by the roots, and you can hear the gnashing of their tusks — until a man strikes them down. So the bright bronze rang on the breasts of the two as the blows came at them; for they fought hard, trusting their own strength and the men on the wall above. And those men hurled great stones from the heights in defense of themselves and their tents and their ships. The stones fell thick as snowflakes that a screaming wind drives down from the dark clouds and pours in sheets on the earth — so thick flew the missiles from the hands of Trojans and Greeks alike. Helmet and shield boomed under the pounding of the great stones, and Asius, son of Hyrtacus, struck both his thighs in dismay and cried out, "Father Zeus — so you too are a friend to lies. I was certain the Greeks could never stand against our fury, and here, like wasps with narrow waists, or bees that nest in a rock by the road, they will not abandon the hollow they have built but fight for their young against every raider — two men, only two, and they will not be moved from the gates until they kill or are killed."

So he spoke, but he did not move the mind of Zeus, whose purpose now was to give the glory to Hector. Meanwhile, around the other gates, the rest of the fighting raged on — and I am no god, to tell all of it; everywhere the battle blazed about the stone wall like a furnace. The Greeks, hard pressed, were forced to fight for their ships, and all the gods who stood for them grieved in their hearts. But the Lapiths fought on with all their strength.

There Polypoetes, the strong son of Pirithous, struck Damasus through the bronze-cheeked helmet with his spear; the helmet did not hold, the point drove through and shattered the bone, and the brain was scattered inside it, and Damasus went down in mid-charge. Then Polypoetes killed Pylon and Ormenus. And Leonteus, of the line of Ares, ran Hippomachus, son of Antimachus, through the belt with his spear; then he drew his sword and came first on Antiphates, cut him down hand to hand, so that he fell on his back in the dust, and after him killed Menon, Iamenus, and Orestes, one upon another, and laid them in the earth.

While the two were stripping the armor from these dead, the young men who followed Polydamas and Hector — the greatest part of them, and the bravest, the ones most bent on breaking the wall and burning the ships — were still halted at the ditch, in doubt. For a sign from heaven had stopped them just as they made to cross: an eagle, riding high along the left of their host, with a great blood-red snake in its talons, alive and still fighting.
