The snake had not given up; it twisted back and struck the bird that held it, on the neck, by the breast, and the eagle in its pain let go and dropped it into the middle of the host, then wheeled away down the wind with a sharp cry. The Trojans shuddered when they saw the writhing snake lying among them, the sign of Zeus who bears the storm-shield. And Polydamas came up to fearless Hector and said, "Hector, in our councils you are always quick to rebuke me, even when my counsel is good — because it suits no one, you think, for a man of the people to cross you, in the field or at the council. Still I will say what I judge is best. Let us not march on now to fight the Greeks at their ships. I think I know how this will end, if it was truly an omen for us, this eagle that crossed high on the left of our host as we made to cross the trench, with the living blood-red snake in its grip. It did not hold its prey; it never carried it home to the chicks in its nest. And so it will be with us: even if by some great effort we break through the gates and the wall, and the Greeks give way, we will not come back the same road in good order — we will leave many a Trojan behind us, cut down by the Greeks defending their ships. That is how a seer would read it, a man who truly knew such signs and whom the people trusted."

Hector glared at him and said, "Polydamas, I have had enough of this. You can do better than this if you try. But if you mean it in earnest, then the gods themselves have taken your wits. You would have me forget the will of Zeus, the promise he made me and sealed with a nod of his head, and steer instead by the wings of birds — which way they fly, toward the dawn or toward the dark, to my right hand or my left. What is that to me? Let us trust the will of great Zeus, who is lord of all mortals and all the gods. One omen is best: to fight for your country. Why are you so afraid of the war? Even if the rest of us are killed at the Greek ships, you need not fear dying yourself — you have no stomach for a stand, no heart for the fight. But if you hang back from the battle now, or talk another man out of it, my spear will find you on the spot, and the life will go out of you."

With that he led the way, and the others came after him with a roar that split the air. And Zeus, lord of thunder, sent down a blast of wind from the mountains of Ida that drove the dust straight at the ships; he dulled the Greeks' resolve and handed the glory to Hector and the Trojans, who trusted his signs and their own strength and threw themselves at the great wall. They wrenched the breastworks off the ramparts and toppled the battlements; they pried up the buttress-beams the Greeks had set in the ground to brace the wall, and as these gave way they were sure of breaking through. But still the Greeks did not yield. They fenced the battlements with their ox-hide shields and struck down at every man who came under the wall.

The two Ajaxes ranged everywhere along the walls, rousing the Greeks, fair words for one man, hard words for any they saw flagging. "Friends," they cried, "Greeks, every one of you — the best, the middling, and the worst, for no two men were ever equal in a fight — there is work here for all of you now, as you well know. Let no man turn back toward the ships because the enemy is shouting. Press forward, hold one another up, and Olympian Zeus, the lord of lightning, may yet let us beat back this attack and drive them home to their city."

So the two went on shouting, calling the Greeks to the fight. And as snowflakes fall thick on a winter day, when Zeus the counselor stirs himself to snow and to show men his arrows — he stills the winds and pours it down hour after hour until he has covered the high mountain peaks and the jutting headlands and the clover meadows and the rich tilled fields of men, and it lies deep over the harbors and shores of the gray sea, only the breaking wave holding it off, while everything else is wrapped under it, weighed down from the sky — so thick flew the stones from both sides, some hurled at the Trojans, some by the Trojans at the Greeks, and the whole length of the wall was an uproar.

Even so, the Trojans and bright Hector would not yet have broken through the gates and the great bar, had not Zeus driven his own son Sarpedon at the Greeks, like a lion on a herd of horned cattle. He held before him his round shield of hammered bronze, beaten smooth by the smith and lined inside with layers of ox-hide stitched with golden rivets all around the rim. Holding it before him and shaking two spears, he came on like a mountain lion long starved for meat, whose proud heart drives him even into a close-fenced fold to try for the sheep. He may find the shepherds there, keeping watch over the flock with dogs and spears — but he will not be turned away without one charge at it; he will leap in and seize a sheep, or take a spear from a strong hand and fall. So Sarpedon's spirit drove him to rush the wall and tear down its battlements. And he said to Glaucus, son of Hippolochus, "Glaucus, why is it that the two of us are held in such honor back in Lycia — the seats of honor, the choice cuts of meat, the cups kept full — and men look on us as gods? Why do we hold a great estate along the banks of the Xanthus, fine land of orchard and wheat? It is so that now we may take our stand at the front of the Lycians and meet the fire of the battle head-on, and one of them may say, 'These are no idle lords who rule us in Lycia, who eat the fat sheep and drink the best of the honeyed wine — their strength is great, for they fight in the front of the Lycians.' My friend, if escaping this war we could be sure of living forever, ageless and undying, I would not fight in the front line myself, nor send you into the battle where men win glory. But as it is, the fates of death stand over us in their thousands, and no man can run from them or escape — so let us go forward, and give the glory to another, or another give it to us."

Glaucus heard him and did not turn aside, and the two led on the host of the Lycians. Menestheus, son of Peteos, saw them coming and was filled with dread, for it was his stretch of the wall they came at, bringing ruin with them. He looked along the rampart for some captain who could shore up his men, and saw the two Ajaxes, never weary of the fight, and Teucer just come from his hut, standing nearby — but he could not make his voice carry to them, so loud was the din: the crash of shields and helmets, the gates hammered, the whole tumult of it climbing to the sky. For all the gates were shut, and the Trojans stood pounding at them to force a way through. So Menestheus sent Thootes running to Ajax with a message: "Run, Thootes — call Ajax, or better, the two of them, for it will soon be over with us here. The Lycian captains are on us, men who have always fought like fury. But if they have too much on their hands to come, then at least send Ajax, son of Telamon, and let Teucer the great archer come with him."

The messenger heard and obeyed, and set off along the Greek wall, and when he reached the Ajaxes he said, "You two, lords of the Greeks — the son of brave Peteos asks you to come and bear a share of the fighting with him, both of you if you can, for it will soon be over with him; the Lycian captains are on him, men who have always fought like fury. But if you have too much on your hands here, then let Ajax, son of Telamon, come at least, and Teucer the great archer with him."

Great Ajax, son of Telamon, heard and answered the son of Oileus at once: "Ajax — you and brave Lycomedes stay here and keep the Greeks fighting hard. I will go over there and take my part in the battle, and come straight back when I have given them the help they need." With that, Ajax son of Telamon set out, and his brother Teucer went with him, and Pandion to carry Teucer's bow.

They went along inside the wall, and when they came to the tower where Menestheus was — and they found him hard pressed indeed — the brave captains and leaders of the Lycians were already storming the parapet like a dark, dense storm-cloud, fighting at close quarters, the war cry rising. Ajax, son of Telamon, was the first to kill — Epicles, a comrade of Sarpedon — striking him with a jagged stone that lay among the rubble at the very top of the wall. No man as men are now, not even one in the bloom of youth, could lift it easily with both hands; but Ajax raised it high and flung it down, and it smashed the four-ridged helmet and crushed the bones of the head together, and Epicles dropped from the high wall like a diver, the life gone out of him. Then Teucer hit Glaucus, the brave son of Hippolochus, as he climbed at the wall: he caught his arm bare and shot an arrow into it, and Glaucus broke off the attack. He sprang back down out of sight, so that no Greek would see he was hit and taunt him. Sarpedon felt the pang when he saw Glaucus go, but he did not give up the fight. He drove his spear at Alcmaon, son of Thestor, struck home, and as he wrenched the spear back Alcmaon came down headlong after it, his bronze armor clanging around him. Then Sarpedon caught the parapet in his strong hands and hauled, and the whole length of it gave way at once, leaving the wall stripped bare on top and a path open for many to cross.

Ajax and Teucer both turned on him at once. Teucer hit the strap across his chest that held the great shield, but Zeus turned death away from his son, that he might not fall there at the sterns of the ships. And Ajax leapt at him and drove his spear into the shield; it did not punch clean through, but it checked him in mid-charge, and he fell back a little from the parapet — not all the way, for his heart was still set on winning glory. He wheeled and shouted to the Lycians, "Lycians, why are you failing me? Strong as I am, I cannot break through alone and open the road to the ships. Come with me, all of you — the more hands, the better the work."

Stung by their king's rebuke, the Lycians pressed closer around the man who led them and counseled them. And the Greeks, on their side, drew up their ranks tight inside the wall, and there was deadly work between them. The Lycians could not break through and force a road to the ships, and the Greeks could not drive the Lycians off the wall once they had a hold on it. As two men with measuring rods in hand will quarrel over the boundary in a field they share, each fighting for his rights in a narrow strip of ground, so the two sides fought across the battlements, hacking at each other's round shields over a wall's-breadth of contested space. Many a man took the pitiless bronze in his body — some struck in the back as they turned and left it bare, many run clean through the shield. And the wall and the parapets ran everywhere with the blood of Trojans and Greeks alike. Even so, the Trojans could not break the Greeks, who held their line; and as an honest working woman holds the balance with the wool and the weight, leveling the two until they hang true, to earn some poor wage for her children, so the fight hung even between them — until Zeus lifted the greater glory to Hector, son of Priam, who was the first to leap inside the Greek wall. In a piercing voice he cried to the Trojans, "Up, Trojans, breakers of horses — break through the Greek wall and throw blazing fire on their ships."

So he spurred them on, and they all heard it, and rushed straight at the wall in one body and went swarming over the parapets, the sharp spears in their hands. And Hector laid hold of a stone that lay before the gates, broad at the base and tapered to a point — no two of the strongest men in a town, as men are now, could easily lever it off the ground onto a wagon, but Hector hefted it alone and with ease, for the son of crooked-minded Cronus made it light for him. As a shepherd lifts a ram's fleece in one hand and barely feels the weight, so easily Hector raised the great stone and carried it against the doors that closed the gates, doors set strong and high, two leaves fastened by two cross-bars with a single bolt holding them. He came up close, set his feet wide for the full force of the blow, and struck them square in the middle, throwing all his weight behind it. He broke both hinges, and the stone crashed through under its own great weight. The gateway boomed with the sound, the bars gave, the doors flew apart under the blow, one leaf this way and one that. And bright Hector leaped inside, his face dark as the falling night. The bronze blazed terribly about his body, and he held two spears in his hands. No one could have stood against him as he sprang through the gate, no one but a god, and his eyes glared like fire. He wheeled to the Trojans and called them on to climb the wall, and they did as he said — some scaling the rampart, others pouring through the open gates. And the Greeks fled in panic toward their ships, and the whole place was an uproar without end.
books.title: The Storming of the Wall

books.label: Book XIII
paragraphs: Now that Zeus had brought Hector and the Trojans up to the ships, he left them there to their endless toil and trouble and turned his bright eyes away, gazing off into the distance — toward the horse-breeding Thracians, the Mysians who fight hand to hand, the proud Hippemolgi who milk their mares, and the Abians, the justest men alive, who live on milk and shed no blood. He no longer turned so much as a glance toward Troy, for it never crossed his mind that any of the immortals would go down to help the Trojans or the Greeks.

But lord Poseidon had not been keeping a blind watch. He sat marveling at the battle from the highest wooded crest of Samothrace, and from there he could see the whole of Ida, and Priam's city, and the Greek ships. He had come up out of the sea and taken his seat there, for he pitied the Greeks as the Trojans beat them down, and his anger at Zeus burned in him.

Down he came at once from the mountaintop, striding hard, and the high hills and the forest shook under the tread of his immortal feet. Three strides he took, and with the fourth he reached his goal — Aegae, where his glittering golden palace stands, deep in the sea, imperishable. There he yoked his swift bronze-hoofed horses, their golden manes streaming, and clothed himself in gold, and took up his golden whip, well made, and mounted his chariot. He drove out over the waves, and the sea-creatures came gamboling up around him from every hollow of the deep, for they knew their lord; and the sea parted in gladness to open a path before him. The horses flew so lightly that the bronze axle below was never wetted, and his bounding team carried him on to the ships of the Greeks.

There is a great cave in the depths of the sea, midway between Tenedos and rocky Imbros. There Poseidon, shaker of the earth, halted his horses and unyoked them, and set ambrosial fodder before them. He hobbled their feet with golden hobbles, which none could loose or break, so they would wait for their lord until he came back. Then he went his way to the Greek host.

Meanwhile the Trojans came on after Hector, son of Priam, in a packed mass, like a storm-cloud or a sheet of flame, raising the war cry, fighting with all their might — sure that they would take the Greek ships now and kill the best of the men there beside them. But Poseidon, who holds the earth and shakes it, came up out of the sea to rouse the Greeks, taking on the form and the voice of Calchas.

He spoke first to the two Ajaxes, who were already straining at the work: "You two, you Ajaxes, you can be the saving of the Greeks if you put your whole strength into it and don't give way to fear. Anywhere else along the wall I'm not afraid the Trojans will break us, even though they've come over it in force — the Greeks will hold all the rest of them. But here is where I dread some ruin — here, where furious Hector leads them on like a pillar of fire, Hector who boasts he is the son of mighty Zeus. So may some god put it in your hearts to stand firm here yourselves and to steady the others. If you do, you can drive him back from the fast ships, however hard Zeus himself urges him on."

As he spoke, the lord who shakes the earth touched both of them with his staff and filled them with daring strength, and made their limbs light — their feet, their hands above them. Then, like a swift hawk that lifts from a sheer high rock and stoops to chase a bird across the plain, the earth-shaker rose into the air and flew from them. Swift Ajax, son of Oileus, was the first of the two to know him, and he said to Ajax, son of Telamon: "Ajax, that was one of the gods who hold Olympus, taking the shape of the prophet and telling us to fight by our ships. That was not Calchas, the seer who reads the birds — I knew him as he turned to go, by the look of his feet and his legs from behind. The gods are easy to recognize. And now my own heart in me burns harder for battle, and my hands and feet below are itching for the fight."

Ajax, son of Telamon, answered: "My hands too — they grip the spear-shaft tighter now, my strength is rising in me, and my feet feel quick beneath me. I long to meet furious Hector, son of Priam, even alone, one against one."

So the two of them talked, glad of the lust for battle the god had put in them. But the earth-shaker, behind them, was rousing the rest of the Greeks, who were standing back by the fast ships, resting, worn out at once with the hard fighting and with grief at the sight of the Trojans over the wall in force. They watched, and the tears welled in their eyes, for they did not think they would come out of it alive. But the shaker of the earth went lightly among them and set their ranks in motion toward the front.

First he came to Teucer and Leitus, to the hero Peneleos, to Thoas and Deipyrus, and to Meriones and Antilochus, brave men in the war cry — to all of these he called sharp words: "Shame on you, young men of Greece! It was on your fighting that I counted to save our ships. If you flinch from the hard work of war, the day has come that sees us beaten by the Trojans. This is a sight I never thought to see — a great and terrible thing — the Trojans at our very ships. Until now they were like frightened does, drifting through the woods with no fight in them, prey for jackals and leopards and wolves, good for nothing but running. Until now the Trojans never once dared to stand and face the Greeks. But now they have come far from their city and are fighting among our ships, all through our leader's failure and the slackness of the men, who in their grudge against him will not fight to save the ships, but are cut down beside them. Yes, the fault may lie with the hero Agamemnon, son of Atreus, who dishonored the swift-footed son of Peleus — but that is no excuse for us to drop out of the fighting. Heal it, and quickly; the hearts of good men mend fast. You do wrong to let your courage go cold, you, the best soldiers in the whole army. I would not pick a quarrel with a man who hung back from the war because he was weak — but you, I am furious with. Friends, this slackness will soon make a worse thing of it. Let each of you take to heart his own honor, his own good name; the struggle now is at its sharpest. Great Hector is fighting at the ships, full-voiced; he has burst the gates and the long bolt that held them."

So the earth-encircler called to the Greeks and drove them on. Around the two Ajaxes the ranks closed up, strong companies that not even Ares could have faulted, going among them, nor Athena who marshals armies — for these were the picked men, waiting for Hector and the Trojans. They made a living wall, spear braced to spear, shield to shield, edge to overlapping edge, helmet to helmet, man to man. The horsehair crests on the gleaming helmet-ridges brushed together as the heads bent forward, so close they stood; the spears, brandished in bold hands, crossed and locked; and their hearts were set straight ahead, on battle.

The Trojans came on in a dense body, with Hector at their head, driving straight in — like a boulder that crashes down a mountainside, torn from the brow of a cliff by a winter flood that has eaten away the rock that held it: it leaps and bounds, and the forest roars beneath it, and on it goes, swerving for nothing, until it hits the level ground, and there for all its fury it rolls no farther. So Hector, for a while, threatened to cut his way clear through the Greek huts and ships to the sea, killing as he came — until he ran up against the close-packed ranks, and there he stopped short. The sons of the Greeks stood and met him, stabbing with swords and double-pointed spears, and thrust him back so that he reeled and gave ground. Then he raised his voice and shouted to the Trojans: "Trojans! Lycians! Dardanians who fight hand to hand! Hold your ground! The Greeks won't keep me off for long, packed against me like a wall though they are. They'll fall back before my spear, if the greatest of the gods has truly set me on — Hera's loud-thundering husband."

With that he put fresh heart and fire into every man. And Deiphobus, son of Priam, strode out among them, high in his own daring, his round shield held before him, moving light and quick behind its cover. Meriones took aim at him and let his bright spear fly, and did not miss — he struck the broad orb of bull's hide — but the bronze did not break through; the long shaft snapped clean in two before it could, for Deiphobus had seen it coming and held the shield well out from his body. Furious — at losing both the kill and his spear — Meriones drew back under cover of his own men, and went off toward the huts and the ships to fetch another spear, one he had left behind.

The rest fought on, and the war cry rose to the sky. Teucer, son of Telamon, was the first to kill his man — the spearman Imbrius, son of Mentor, rich in horses. He had lived in Pedaeum before the Greeks came, and had married Medesicaste, a daughter of Priam's, born out of wedlock; but when the curved ships of the Greeks arrived, he came back to Ilios, and he was a great man among the Trojans, and lived close to Priam, who honored him like one of his own sons. The son of Telamon struck him below the ear with the long spear, then wrenched it free, and Imbrius fell — like an ash tree on the crown of a high hill, seen far off, cut down by the bronze, that brings its soft green leaves to the ground. So he fell, and his armor of bright bronze rang harshly around him. Teucer sprang forward to strip it, but as he came on, Hector cast his bright spear at him. Teucer saw it and just managed to dodge aside, and the spear caught Amphimachus instead — son of Cteatus, the son of Actor — full in the chest as he came into the fighting, and he crashed down, and his armor clattered around him. Hector rushed in to tear the close-fitting helmet from the temples of great-hearted Amphimachus, but Ajax lunged with his shining spear at Hector — though he could not reach the flesh, sheathed as it was in fearsome bronze; he struck the boss of the shield and shoved him back by main force from the two bodies, and the Greeks dragged them out. Stichius and Menestheus, captains of the Athenians, carried Amphimachus back to the Greek host; and the two Ajaxes, hot for the fight, took up Imbrius. As two lions snatch a goat from sharp-toothed hounds and carry it off through the thick brush, holding it high in their jaws above the ground, so the two armed Ajaxes held Imbrius high and stripped his armor. And the son of Oileus, in anger for the death of Amphimachus, hacked the head from the soft neck and sent it spinning through the crowd like a ball, and it rolled in the dust to fall at Hector's feet.

Then Poseidon's heart blazed with anger that his grandson had fallen in the cruel fighting, and he went off among the huts and ships of the Greeks to spur the men on still more, and to set trouble brewing for the Trojans. Idomeneus met him, coming away from a comrade who had just left the fighting, struck behind the knee by the sharp bronze; his men had carried him in, and Idomeneus, after giving orders to the healers, had gone on toward his own hut, for he was still hungry for war. The mighty shaker of the earth spoke to him, taking on the voice of Thoas, son of Andraemon — who ruled the Aetolians in all Pleuron and steep Calydon, and was honored among his people like a god: "Idomeneus, lawgiver of the Cretans — what has become now of the threats the sons of the Greeks once made against the Trojans?"

Idomeneus, lord of the Cretans, answered him: "Thoas, no one is at fault, so far as I can see — we all know how to fight. No man is gripped by helpless fear, and no man hangs back out of slackness. It must be the will of almighty Zeus himself, that the Greeks should die here without glory, far from Argos. But you, Thoas, were always one to stand firm, and to rally any man you saw giving way. Don't let up now. Call on every man to do his utmost."

Poseidon, the shaker of the earth, answered: "Idomeneus — may the man never come home from Troy, but stay here to feast the dogs, who willingly holds back from the fight this day. Come, take up your armor and go. We must hurry, the two of us together, in case we can do some good, even though we are only two. Courage comes even to cowards when they stand together, and you and I know how to fight beside the best." With that the god went back into the toil of men. And Idomeneus, when he reached his well-built hut, pulled on his fine armor, took up two spears, and went out — like the lightning the son of Cronus catches up from gleaming Olympus to show a sign to mortals, and the flash leaps far and bright. So the bronze blazed about his chest as he ran. And Meriones, his sturdy aide, met him still close to the hut — he was going for the bronze spear he meant to fetch — and mighty Idomeneus said to him:

"Meriones, swift son of Molus, dearest of my companions — why have you come away from the war and the fighting? Are you hurt? Is a spear-point's pain bearing down on you? Or have you come with some message for me? I have no wish to sit in my hut; I would far rather fight."

Meriones, the cool-headed, answered: "Idomeneus, lawgiver of the bronze-armored Cretans — I am coming for a spear, if there is one left in your hut to take. I broke the one I had, throwing it against the shield of arrogant Deiphobus."

Idomeneus, lord of the Cretans, answered: "You will find spears, if you want them — one, or twenty — standing against the bright wall inside my hut. I took them from Trojans I have killed; I am not a man to fight my enemies from a distance. So I have spears, and bossed shields, and helmets, and breastplates polished to a shine."

Then Meriones, the cool-headed, said: "In my own hut and by my ship I too have plenty of Trojan spoils, but they are not close to hand. I tell you, I am not one to forget my courage. I stand in the front ranks, where men win glory, whenever the fighting of war breaks out. Some other Greek may not know how I fight — but you, you know it well enough."

Idomeneus, lord of the Cretans, answered: "I know what you are worth. You needn't say it. If the best of us were being picked now, beside the ships, for an ambush — and there is no better test of what a man is made of, the place where the brave man and the coward both stand revealed — the coward's color keeps changing, this way and that; his heart will not let him sit still, but he keeps shifting his weight from one foot to the other; his heart pounds in his chest as he broods on death, and his teeth chatter in his head. But the brave man's color does not change, and once he has settled into the ambush, he is not afraid; he only prays for the moment to plunge into the bitter work. In a place like that, no one could find fault with your courage or your hands. And if you were hit, in the toil of war, by a thrown spear or a thrust at close quarters, it would not strike you from behind, in the neck or the back — it would catch you full in the chest or the belly, as you pressed in among the foremost fighters. But come, let's not stand here talking like children — someone might take it the wrong way. Go to the hut and get yourself a strong spear."

At that, Meriones, the equal of swift Ares, went and quickly took a bronze spear from the hut, and went after Idomeneus, his whole mind set on war — like Ares himself, the bane of men, going out to battle, with Terror at his side, his own dear son, strong and fearless, who frightens even the steadfast warrior: the two of them arm and stride out of Thrace to the Ephyrians, or to the great-hearted Phlegyans, and they will not hear the prayers of both sides at once, but give the glory to one. So Meriones and Idomeneus, leaders of men, went out to the fighting in their gleaming bronze. And Meriones spoke first: "Son of Deucalion, where would you have us go into the fighting? On the right of the whole host? In the center? Or to the left? — for nowhere, I think, are the long-haired Greeks so hard pressed as there."

Idomeneus, lord of the Cretans, answered: "There are others to hold the center — the two Ajaxes, and Teucer, who is the finest archer of all the Greeks, and good as well in close fighting. They will give Hector enough of a fight, hungry for it as he is. He'll find it hard work, however he strains for the killing, to break their unbeatable hands and their fury and set the ships afire — unless the son of Cronus himself drops a blazing brand on the fast ships with his own hand. Great Ajax, son of Telamon, will give way to no man who is mortal and eats the grain of Demeter, no man bronze and great stones can break. He would not even step back before Achilles, who shatters the ranks — not in standing fight; in speed of foot there's no matching Achilles. So steer us to the left of the army, and let's find out, and soon, whether we win glory from another, or another from us."

So Meriones, the equal of swift Ares, led the way to the part of the host that Idomeneus had named. And when the Trojans saw Idomeneus coming on like a flame, him and his aide in their finely worked armor, they raised the cry and made for him in one body, and a furious fight broke out at the ships' sterns, all together. As gusting winds shriek across the land on a day when the dust lies thick on the roads, and they whip it up into a great cloud — so the battle joined and clashed together, and every man's heart was set on killing his enemy in the press. The field of slaughter bristled with the long flesh-tearing spears they held, and the eyes ached with the glare of bronze from the bright helmets, the new-burnished breastplates, the shining shields, as the men closed in. Hard-hearted indeed would the man be who could look on that struggle and feel joy and no dread.

So the two mighty sons of Cronus, set against each other, were forging hard fortune for the heroes of men. Zeus willed victory for the Trojans and for Hector, to glorify swift-footed Achilles — yet he did not mean to destroy the Greek host utterly before Troy; he only wanted to lift up Thetis and her strong-hearted son. Poseidon, for his part, slipped up secretly out of the gray sea and went among the Greeks to drive them on, grieved that the Trojans were beating them, and his anger at Zeus burning. The two of them were of one stock and one fathering, but Zeus was the elder-born and knew the more. So Poseidon held back from helping the Greeks in the open, and instead, always in the likeness of a man, kept stirring them through the host. So the two of them stretched taut over both armies the rope of fierce strife and the leveling war — a knot none could break or loose, that buckled the knees of many men.

And now Idomeneus, though his hair was already shot with gray, called to the Greeks and leapt in among the Trojans and sent them scattering in fear. He killed Othryoneus, a man from Cabesus who had been living among them, who had only lately come for the war's sake. He had asked for the loveliest of Priam's daughters, Cassandra — and offered no gifts for her, but a great promise: he would drive the sons of the Greeks out of Troy whether they liked it or not. Old Priam had agreed and pledged her to him, and so the man fought on, trusting that promise. Idomeneus took aim with his bright spear and struck him as he came striding on, and the bronze corselet he wore did not hold; the spear stood fixed in his belly, and he crashed down. And Idomeneus boasted over him: "Othryoneus — I'll honor you above all men in the world, if you really mean to do everything you promised Priam, son of Dardanus, who pledged you his daughter. Come, we'll make you a promise too, and keep it: we'll give you the loveliest of the daughters of the son of Atreus, and bring her here from Argos for you to wed — if only you'll join us in sacking the strong city of Ilios. Come along, then, to the seafaring ships, and let's settle the marriage. You'll find us no hard bargainers over the bride-gifts." And with that the hero Idomeneus began dragging him by the foot through the thick of the fighting.

But Asius came up to defend the body, on foot, in front of his horses, which his charioteer drove so close behind that their breath was forever on his shoulders. His heart was set on striking Idomeneus down — but Idomeneus was quicker, and stabbed him with the spear in the throat, under the chin, and drove the bronze straight through. He fell as an oak falls, or a poplar, or a tall pine that carpenters fell on the mountains with their whetted axes to make ship-timber: so he lay there, full length, before his horses and his chariot, groaning, clutching at the bloody dust. The charioteer lost his wits and had not the nerve to wheel the horses round and escape, and steadfast Antilochus caught him full in the body with a spear; the bronze corselet he wore did not hold, and the spear stood fixed in his belly. He fell gasping from the well-built chariot, and Antilochus, son of great-hearted Nestor, drove the horses off, out of the Trojans, and in among the Greeks.

Then Deiphobus came in close on Idomeneus, grieving for Asius, and let his bright spear fly. But Idomeneus saw it and dodged the bronze, ducking under his round shield — the one he always carried, made of bull's hide and gleaming bronze, fitted with two arm-rods on the inside. He crouched low behind it all, and the spear flew over him, but the shield rang dryly as it grazed past; and still it did not leave the heavy hand of Deiphobus for nothing — it struck Hypsenor, son of Hippasus, shepherd of his people, in the liver below the midriff, and at once his knees gave under him. And Deiphobus boasted terribly over him, in a great voice: "There — Asius does not lie unavenged after all. Even on his way down to the strong gatekeeper, Hades, his heart will be glad: I have given him an escort." So he boasted, and the grief of it stung the Greeks — and most of all it stirred the heart of warlike Antilochus. Yet for all his grief he did not forget his comrade, but ran and stood astride him and covered him with his shield, while two trusted friends, Mecisteus, son of Echius, and noble Alastor, stooped under and bore him away, groaning heavily, to the hollow ships.

But Idomeneus did not slack his fury. He kept straining, always, either to shroud some Trojan in the dark of death or to go down himself, holding ruin off from the Greeks. And next there fell Alcathous, the son of lordly Aesyetes — he was son-in-law to Anchises, having married his eldest daughter, Hippodameia, whom her father and her honored mother loved beyond all the children in the house, for she surpassed everyone her age in beauty, in skill, and in good sense; and so the best man in all wide Troy had taken her to wife. Now Poseidon brought him low under the hand of Idomeneus, casting a fog over his bright eyes and binding fast his shining limbs, so that he could not run back, nor swerve aside, but stood stock-still as a pillar or a high-crowned tree — and Idomeneus drove the spear straight into the middle of his chest, and split the bronze plate of the corselet that until then had warded death from his body. It rang harshly now, torn through by the spear. He fell with a crash, and the spear stood fixed in his heart, which still beat on, so that the butt of the spear quivered with it — until at last mighty Ares stilled its force. And Idomeneus boasted over him, terribly, in a great voice: "Deiphobus — are we even now, would you say, three men killed for your one? You did your share of boasting. Strange man, come stand and face me yourself, and learn what kind of son of Zeus I am, come here against you. Zeus first fathered Minos, the warden of Crete; and Minos fathered a son, the blameless Deucalion; and Deucalion fathered me, to be lord over many men in broad Crete; and now my ships have carried me here, to be a curse to you, and to your father, and to all the Trojans."

So he spoke, and Deiphobus was torn two ways — whether to draw back and bring up some other great-hearted Trojan as a partner, or to try it alone. As he weighed it, this seemed the better course: to go for Aeneas. He found him standing at the very rear of the fighting, for Aeneas was forever angry with noble Priam, who gave him no honor among the men, for all his courage. Deiphobus stood close and spoke winged words: "Aeneas, counselor of the Trojans — now is the time, if any tie of kin can touch you, to come defend your sister's husband. Follow me, and let us protect Alcathous, who was your sister's husband, and who raised you when you were small in his halls. Now Idomeneus, the famous spearman, has killed him."

So he spoke, and stirred the heart in Aeneas's chest. He went for Idomeneus, his whole mind set on war. But Idomeneus did not take to his heels like a frightened boy; he stood his ground, like a boar in the mountains, sure of his own strength, that waits for a great crowd of men coming on against him in a lonely place: the bristles rise along his back, his eyes blaze with fire, and he whets his tusks, raging to fight off the dogs and the men. So Idomeneus, the famous spearman, stood and did not give way as Aeneas came on. But he called to his companions — to Ascalaphus, Aphareus, Deipyrus, Meriones, and Antilochus, all of them masters of the war cry — and urged them on with winged words: "Here, friends! Stand by me — I'm alone, and badly afraid of swift-footed Aeneas, bearing down on me, who is a great killer of men in battle, and in the very flower of his youth, when a man's strength is at its height. If we were the same age, with the spirit I have now, soon he or I would carry off the great prize."

So he spoke, and they all, as one, came and stood near him, shields tilted to their shoulders. And on the other side Aeneas called to his own — to Deiphobus, to Paris, and to noble Agenor, who were leaders of the Trojans with him; and the people followed them, as sheep follow the ram out of the pasture down to their drinking, and the shepherd's heart is glad. So the heart of Aeneas was glad in his chest when he saw the people streaming after him.

Then they fell on one another in close fight around Alcathous, with their long spears, and the bronze rang fearfully on their bodies as they aimed at each other in the press. And two warriors beyond all the rest, Aeneas and Idomeneus, both the equals of Ares, strained to tear each other's flesh with the pitiless bronze. Aeneas threw first at Idomeneus, but Idomeneus saw it coming and dodged the bronze, and the spear of Aeneas drove on past and stood quivering in the ground, flung for nothing from that strong hand. But Idomeneus struck Oenomaus full in the belly, and broke the plate of the corselet, and the bronze let the guts spill out, and he fell in the dust and clawed the earth in his hands. Idomeneus pulled the long spear from the body, but could not strip the fine armor from his shoulders — the missiles were raining too thick. And his legs no longer had the spring in them, after the strain, to dart after his own cast spear or to swerve from another's. So while he still fought off the pitiless day at close quarters, his feet would no longer carry him swiftly out of the fighting. As he drew slowly back, Deiphobus cast at him again — for he kept his hard hatred for the man — and missed him again, but hit Ascalaphus, the son of Ares; the heavy spear went through his shoulder, and he fell in the dust and clawed the earth in his hands.

And mighty loud-voiced Ares did not yet know that his son had fallen in the hard fighting; he was sitting up on the heights of Olympus, under the golden clouds, held back by the will of Zeus, where the other immortal gods were also held from the war. Around the body the men fought on, hand to hand. Deiphobus tore the bright helmet off Ascalaphus, but Meriones, the equal of swift Ares, sprang in and struck his arm with a spear, so that the crested helmet dropped ringing from his grip to the ground. Meriones swooped on him again like a vulture, dragged the heavy spear out of the top of his arm, and fell back among his own men. Then Polites, Deiphobus's own brother, threw his arms around his waist and brought him out of the wailing war until he reached his swift horses, which were standing behind the toil of the fight with their charioteer and the gleaming chariot. These carried him toward the city, groaning hard, racked with pain, and the blood ran from his fresh-wounded arm.

The others fought on, and the war cry rose without end. Aeneas lunged at Aphareus, son of Caletor, and struck his throat as he turned toward him with the sharp spear; his head dropped to one side, and his shield came down with him, and his helmet, and death that breaks the spirit poured around him. Antilochus watched Thoon turn, and rushed him, and slashed him as he wheeled, cutting clean through the vein that runs all the way up the back to the neck. He severed it entire, and Thoon went down on his back in the dust, stretching both hands out to his dear companions. Antilochus sprang on him and stripped the armor from his shoulders, glancing about him as he did — and the Trojans came at him from every side and struck his broad bright shield, but could not lay open his tender flesh with the pitiless bronze, for Poseidon, the shaker of the earth, guarded Nestor's son even in the storm of spears. He was never clear of the enemy but kept turning among them; his spear was never still, but always shaking, always poised, his mind set on hurling it at some man far off or rushing him hand to hand.

But as he aimed across the press, Adamas, the son of Asius, did not miss him; he closed in and struck the middle of his shield with the sharp bronze. But Poseidon, the dark-haired god, robbed the spear of its force, grudging him the life of Antilochus. Half the shaft stuck fast in Antilochus's shield, like a fire-hardened stake, and half lay on the ground. Adamas drew back among his own men to escape his doom, but Meriones came after him and threw, and caught him with the spear midway between the navel and the groin, where wounding is most cruel for wretched mortals at war. There the spear went home, and Adamas convulsed about it as a bull twists when the herdsmen in the hills have bound it with cords against its will and drag it off. So he writhed when he was struck — but not for long, only until the hero Meriones came up and pulled the spear from his flesh, and the darkness closed over his eyes.

Then Helenus came in close and struck Deipyrus on the temple with a great Thracian sword, and tore the helmet off, and it fell to the ground, and one of the Greeks fighting there caught it up as it rolled between his feet. And the dark of death closed over the eyes of Deipyrus. Grief seized Menelaus, good at the war cry, and he made for the warrior Helenus, brandishing his sharp spear with a threat; and Helenus drew his bow. The two came on together — the one to hurl the long spear, the other to loose an arrow from the string. The son of Priam hit the breastplate of Menelaus on the chest, but the bitter arrow glanced off. As black beans or chickpeas leap from a broad winnowing-shovel on the great threshing floor, driven by the whistling wind and the heave of the winnower, so the bitter arrow glanced far off the breastplate of glorious Menelaus. But Menelaus, good at the war cry, struck the hand that held the polished bow, and the bronze spear drove on through the hand and into the bow itself. Helenus shrank back among his own men to escape his doom, his hand hanging at his side, dragging the ashwood spear along with it — until great-hearted Agenor drew the spear out of his hand and bound the hand up in a twist of well-spun wool, a sling the aide of that shepherd of the people carried.

Then Pisander came straight at glorious Menelaus — his evil fate leading him on toward death's end, to be beaten down by you, Menelaus, in the dread crash of war. When the two had come up close against each other, the son of Atreus missed his throw, the spear turning aside; and Pisander struck the shield of glorious Menelaus, but could not drive the bronze clean through, for the broad shield checked it, and the shaft snapped at the socket. Yet his heart leapt, and he hoped for the kill. But the son of Atreus drew his silver-studded sword and sprang on him. And Pisander, from behind his shield, took up a fine axe of good bronze on a long, smooth handle of olive wood, and the two came together. Pisander struck the ridge of the crest on Menelaus's helmet, just under the plume itself; and Menelaus struck Pisander on the forehead as he came on, above the nose, and the bones cracked, and the two eyes, dripping blood, dropped in the dust at his feet. He doubled over and fell, and Menelaus set his heel on his chest, stripped the armor, and boasted over him: "This is how you will leave the ships of the fast-horsed Greeks at last — you arrogant Trojans, who can never get your fill of the dread war cry. Nor will you go without the rest of the shame and the outrage you heaped on me, you cowardly dogs, who felt no fear in your hearts of the hard anger of Zeus, who thunders on high, the lord of host and guest — Zeus, who will one day bring your steep city down in ruin. You carried off my wedded wife, and a heap of treasure with her, for nothing, when she had made you welcome. And now you are mad to fling deadly fire on the seafaring ships and kill the Greek heroes. But you will be stopped from war, however hungry you are for it. Father Zeus — they say you surpass all others, gods and men alike, in wisdom, and all this flows from you — how can you favor men like these, lawless men, the Trojans, whose fury never tires, who can never get their fill of the leveling war? A man can take his fill of all things — of sleep, of love, of sweet song and the faultless dance, things a man would sooner take his fill of than of war. But the Trojans are insatiable for battle."

So saying, noble Menelaus stripped the bloody armor from the body and handed it to his men, and went back himself to mix among the foremost fighters. There Harpalion, the son of King Pylaemenes, came at him — he had followed his dear father to the war at Troy, and he never went home again. He struck the middle of Menelaus's shield from close in with his spear, but could not drive the bronze through, and drew back among his own men to escape his doom, glancing about on every side in case the bronze should graze him. But Meriones loosed a bronze-tipped arrow after him as he went, and hit him in the right buttock; the arrow pierced clean through, under the bone, and on into the bladder. He sat down where he was, in the arms of his dear companions, breathing his life out, stretched on the earth like a worm; and the dark blood ran out and soaked the ground. The great-hearted Paphlagonians tended him, lifted him into the chariot, and bore him, grieving, to holy Ilios; and his father went with them, weeping — but there was no blood-price that could pay for his dead son.

Paris's heart was bitter at the death of Harpalion, for he had been his host among the many Paphlagonians. In his anger for him he let an arrow fly. Now there was a man named Euchenor, son of Polyidus the seer, a rich man and a brave one, who had his home in Corinth. He had taken ship for Troy knowing well his own ruin, for his good old father Polyidus had told him again and again that he must either die in his own halls of a wretched sickness, or be killed by the Trojans among the ships of the Greeks. So he chose to avoid both the Greeks' heavy fine for staying home and the hateful pain of disease. Paris struck him below the jaw, under the ear, and the life fled fast from his limbs, and the hateful dark took him.

So they fought on, like blazing fire. But Hector, beloved of Zeus, had not yet heard, and did not know, that off to the left of the ships his own men were being cut down by the Greeks — for the glory was very nearly turning to the Greeks, so hard did the earth-encircler urge them on, and lend them his own strength besides. No, Hector held on where he had first burst through the gates and the wall, breaking the close ranks of the Greek shield-bearers. There, where the ships of Ajax and of Protesilaus were drawn up on the gray sea's shore, the wall was built lowest, and there the fighting of men and horses raged at its fiercest. The Boeotians and the long-robed Ionians, the Locrians, the men of Phthia, and the bright Epeians could barely hold Hector off from the ships, and could not drive him back, blazing as he was like fire. The picked men of the Athenians held the front, led by Menestheus, son of Peteos, and with him Pheidas, Stichius, and brave Bias; Meges, son of Phyleus, with Amphion and Dracius, led the Epeians; and Medon and steadfast Podarces led the men of Phthia. Medon was a bastard son of noble Oileus and a brother of Ajax, but he lived in Phylace, far from his own land, for he had killed a kinsman of his stepmother Eriopis, the wife of Oileus; and Podarces was the son of Iphiclus, son of Phylacus. These two stood armed in the front of the great-hearted men of Phthia, fighting beside the Boeotians to defend the ships.

And swift Ajax, son of Oileus, would not leave the side of Ajax, son of Telamon — not for a moment. As two dark-coated oxen strain with one heart to draw the jointed plow through a fallow field, and the sweat wells up at the roots of their horns, and only the polished yoke holds them apart as they break the furrow down to the field's edge — so the two stood close, shoulder to shoulder. Many good companions followed the son of Telamon, ready to take his great shield from him whenever the toil and the sweat reached his knees. But the Locrians did not follow the great-hearted son of Oileus, for their hearts were no good for standing close in the fight: they had no bronze helmets crested with horsehair, no round shields, no ashwood spears. They had come to Ilios trusting in their bows and in slings of well-twisted wool, and with these they shot fast and broke the Trojan ranks. So while the men in front, in their heavy armor, bore the brunt against the Trojans and against bronze-helmeted Hector, the Locrians shot from behind, under cover, unseen; and the Trojans began to lose all heart for the fight, for the arrows threw them into confusion.

Then the Trojans would have been driven, in misery, back from the ships and the huts to windy Ilios, had not Polydamas come and stood by bold Hector and said: "Hector, you are an impossible man to win over with reason. Because a god has made you supreme in the work of war, you think you must therefore outdo everyone in counsel too. But you cannot take everything for yourself at once. To one man a god gives the work of war; to another, dancing; to another, the lyre and song; and in the heart of yet another, far-seeing Zeus sets a good mind, and many men reap the good of it, and many are saved by it, and the man himself knows it best of all. So I'll say what seems best to me. The ring of war blazes around you everywhere. Our own great-hearted Trojans, now they are over the wall, some are standing apart in their armor, and the rest are fighting scattered, few against many, strung out among the ships. Draw back, then, and call all our best leaders here, and let us take counsel together on the whole matter — whether to fall on the many-benched ships, in the hope that a god will hand us the victory, or to pull back from the ships unharmed while we still can. For I am badly afraid the Greeks will pay back yesterday's debt in full. There is a man waiting beside their ships, insatiable for war, and I think he will not hold off from the fighting much longer."

So Polydamas spoke, and his safe counsel pleased Hector. At once he leapt to the ground from his chariot in his armor and spoke winged words: "Polydamas, keep all the best men here with you; I will go over there into the fighting, and come straight back once I have given them their orders." So he spoke, and away he went, towering like a snowy mountain, shouting, and flew through the Trojans and their allies. And they all hurried toward kind Polydamas, son of Panthous, when they heard Hector's voice. But Hector kept on through the foremost fighters, hunting for Deiphobus and for the strong prince Helenus, for Adamas, son of Asius, and Asius, son of Hyrtacus — to find them, if he could, alive and unhurt. But he could not. Some were lying dead at the sterns of the Greek ships, struck down by Greek hands; and others were back inside the wall, wounded, hit by arrow or by spear. But on the left of the wailing battle he found one — Alexandros, the husband of lovely-haired Helen — heartening his companions and rousing them to fight. He came up to him and reproached him with shaming words: "Paris, you misery, fine to look at, woman-mad, smooth talker — where are Deiphobus and the strong prince Helenus, and Adamas, son of Asius, and Asius, son of Hyrtacus? Where is Othryoneus? Now all steep Ilios is falling from its height — now is your own headlong ruin sure."

Godlike Alexandros answered him: "Hector, since your heart is set on blaming a man who deserves no blame — there may be other days when I hold back from the fighting, but not today: my mother bore me no coward. From the moment you set our companions on around the ships, we have stood here and never let up against the Greeks. The friends you ask after are dead. Only Deiphobus and the strong prince Helenus have left the field, both struck through the hand by the long spears — and the son of Cronus warded off their death. Now lead on, wherever your heart and spirit command, and we will follow you eagerly. I tell you, you will not find us short of courage, as far as our strength holds out — and no man can fight beyond his strength, however willing he is."

So the hero spoke, and turned his brother's heart. They went to where the war and the slaughter were thickest — to Cebriones and faultless Polydamas, to Phalces and Orthaeus and godlike Polyphetes, to Palmys and Ascanius and Morys, son of Hippotion, who had come the day before, in turn, from deep-soiled Ascania, as a relief; and now Zeus stirred them to the fight. They came on like a blast of furious winds that strikes the earth under the thunder of Father Zeus, and dives into the salt sea with a roar, and many are the seething waves all along the sounding water, arching, white with foam, one after another in front of the rest. So the Trojans drew up rank behind rank, gleaming with bronze, and followed their leaders. And Hector, son of Priam, led them, the equal of Ares, the bane of men, his round shield before him, packed thick with hides and beaten bronze, and the bright helmet shaking on his temples. He kept testing the ranks on every side, stepping out from behind his shield to see whether they would give way before him — but he could not break the steady heart in the Greeks' chests. And Ajax, striding far ahead, was the first to challenge him: "You strange man, come closer. Why try to frighten the Greeks for nothing? We are not unskilled in war — it is only the cruel lash of Zeus that has beaten us down. Your heart is set, I'm sure, on burning our ships. But we too have hands ready to defend them — and your own well-built city will fall, taken and sacked by our hands, far sooner than that. The day is near, I tell you, when you yourself will be running, and praying to Father Zeus and the rest of the immortals that your fine-maned horses be swifter than hawks, as they raise the dust and carry you back to the city."

As he spoke, a bird flew past him on the right, an eagle, high up; and the host of the Greeks shouted, heartened by the omen. But glorious Hector answered: "Ajax, you blundering boaster — what nonsense you talk. I wish I were as sure of being, all my days, the son of Zeus who carries the storm-shield, born of lady Hera, and held in honor like Athena and Apollo, as I am that this day brings ruin to the Greeks — to all of them — and you among them, if you have the nerve to stand against my long spear. It will tear your lily-soft skin, and you will glut the dogs and birds of Troy with your fat and your flesh, struck down beside the Greek ships."

So he spoke and led the way, and they followed him with an unearthly cry, and the whole host roared behind them. And the Greeks raised their own shout in answer; they did not forget their courage, but stood and waited for the best of the Trojans charging in. And the roar of the two went up together, into the high clear air and the brightness of Zeus.
books.title: Poseidon at the Ships

books.label: Book XIV
paragraphs: Nestor was sitting over his wine, but the cry of battle did not pass him by. He turned to the son of Asclepius and said: “Tell me, noble Machaon, what does all this mean? The shouting of men fighting by the ships keeps growing louder. Stay here, sit, and drink your wine, while lovely Hecamede heats a bath and washes the clotted blood off you. I’ll go up to the lookout and see for myself.”

He took up the gleaming bronze shield of his son Thrasymedes, who had gone off with his father’s, gripped a stout bronze-tipped spear, and stepped outside — and saw the ruin laid bare: the Greeks in headlong rout, their wall thrown down, the Trojans driving them before it. As when the open sea heaves with a heavy, silent swell, holding its breath for the shrieking winds that may come, but going neither this way nor that until one of them sweeps down from Zeus to settle it — so the old man stood torn, whether to make for the crowd of the Greeks or go straight to Agamemnon. In the end he judged it best to go to the son of Atreus. And all the while men were killing one another, the hard bronze ringing on their bodies as they thrust with swords and double-edged spears.

The wounded kings met him on the way — Diomedes, Odysseus, and Agamemnon, son of Atreus — coming up from their ships. Their ships were drawn up far from the fighting, on the shore itself, for they had been beached first, and the wall built behind the last of them. Wide as the beach was, it could not hold the whole fleet, and the army was cramped for room; so they had hauled the ships up in rows, one behind another, filling the long mouth of the bay between its two headlands. The kings came leaning on their spears to look out over the fight, sick at heart. The sight of old Nestor filled them with dread. Agamemnon, lord of men, called to him: “Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Greeks — why have you left the battle and come here? I’m afraid the words of fierce Hector are coming true. He boasted to the Trojans that he’d never go back to Troy until he had burned our ships and slaughtered us all. That’s what he said — and look, it’s happening. The rest of the Greeks must be nursing the same anger Achilles does, if they won’t fight for the ships.”

Nestor the horseman answered: “It’s true, all of it, and happening now — not even Zeus who thunders on high could turn it back. The wall is down, the wall we trusted to be an unbreakable shield for us and the fleet. The Trojans are fighting at the ships without let or pause; look where you will, you can’t make out from which side the rout is coming — the men are dying in a confused mass, and the war cry climbs to heaven. Let’s think what to do, if thinking can still help. But I don’t advise us to go into the fight ourselves: a wounded man can’t fight.”

Agamemnon, lord of men, answered: “Nestor, if the Trojans are really fighting at the sterns of our ships, and neither the wall nor the trench has saved us — the trench the Greeks broke their backs to dig, sure it would be an unbreakable shield for us and the fleet — then it must be the will of Zeus that the Greeks die here without glory, far from Argos. I knew it when he was willing to defend us; I know it now, when he lifts the Trojans up like the blessed gods and ties our hands. So do as I say. Let’s drag the ships nearest the water down into the sea and ride them at anchor a little way out, until the holy night comes on — if even night will make the Trojans break off — and then we can launch the rest. There’s no shame in running from ruin, even by night. Better to run and be saved than be caught and killed.”

Odysseus glared at him and said: “Son of Atreus, what is this you’re saying? You should be giving orders to some other army, some lesser one — not ruling over us, men Zeus has set to wind the bitter skein of war from youth to old age, until we die to the last man. So this is how you’d walk away from Troy, the wide-streeted city we’ve suffered so much to take? Be quiet, before another Greek overhears the kind of thing no man with sense in his head, no king with this great an army under his command, should ever let past his lips. I have no respect left for your judgment, none, after what you’ve just said. With the battle raging, you want us to haul the ships into the sea — to hand the triumphant Trojans the one thing more they want, and drop the doom on our own heads? Once the men see the ships being launched, the Greeks won’t go on fighting; they’ll keep glancing back at them and slacken off. Your plan, commander, would destroy us.”

Agamemnon, lord of men, answered: “Odysseus, you’ve cut me to the heart with your rebuke, and it was deserved. No — I’m not ordering the Greeks to drag the ships down against their will. Let someone speak who has a better plan, young or old; I’d be glad to hear it.”

Then Diomedes, master of the war cry, spoke up: “The man is here — you need not look far — if you’ll listen and not take it ill that I’m the youngest of you. I too come of a noble father, Tydeus, who lies buried at Thebes. Portheus had three good sons, who lived in Pleuron and steep Calydon — Agrius, Melas, and the horseman Oeneus, my father’s father, the bravest of the three. Oeneus stayed in his own land, but my father wandered to Argos — so Zeus and the gods willed it. He married into the house of Adrastus and lived in plenty, with broad fields of wheat and orchards all around and many flocks, and no Greek could match him with a spear. You must have heard all this is true. So when I give good counsel, don’t despise it as if I were a coward or low-born. I say this: let’s go back to the fighting, wounded as we are — we must. But once there, let’s keep clear of the throw of the spears, out of range, so we take no fresh wounds on the old ones. We can still drive the others on — the men who have been standing back, indulging their grudges, holding off from the fight.”
They heard him gladly and did as he said, and went off, with Agamemnon, lord of men, leading the way.

Poseidon, the great Earth-Shaker, had kept no idle watch. He came to them in the likeness of an old man, took Agamemnon’s right hand in his own, and spoke winged words: “Son of Atreus, I’d guess Achilles is glad in his heart now, watching the Greeks routed and dying — there’s no feeling left in him, not a grain. May he rot for it, may the gods bring him low. But with you the blessed gods are not so bitterly angry yet. The day will come when the captains and counselors of the Trojans go raising dust across the wide plain, and you’ll see them flying from the ships and the tents, back toward the city.”

With that he gave a great cry and sped off across the plain. Loud as the shout of nine thousand men, ten thousand, joining battle in the thick of the fighting — such was the voice that broke from the lord Earth-Shaker’s chest, and he poured fresh strength into every Greek heart to wage the war without pause.

Hera of the golden throne stood on a peak of Olympus and looked down, and her heart leaped to see him — her own brother and brother by marriage — hard at work, ranging through the battle where men win glory. Then she turned her eyes to Zeus, where he sat on the highest crest of Ida of the many springs, and she hated the sight of him. And the ox-eyed lady Hera began to plot how she might cheat the mind of Zeus who wields the storm-shield. The best way, she decided, was this: to make herself beautiful and go down to Ida, in the hope that he would burn to lie with her — and that, while he did, she might pour a warm and trusting sleep over his eyes and his cunning mind.

So she went to her chamber, the room her dear son Hephaestus had built for her, with a secret bolt on the doors that no other god could open. She went in and closed the gleaming doors. First she cleansed every stain from her lovely body with ambrosia, then rubbed herself with rich oil, sweet, divine, scented for her alone — stir it but once in the bronze-floored house of Zeus, and the fragrance would breathe out across all heaven and earth. With this she anointed her soft skin, and combed out her hair, and with her own hands plaited the bright, shining braids — immortal, beautiful — that streamed from her undying head. She put on the wondrous robe that Athena had worked for her with all her art, sewn over with many a figure, and pinned it across her breast with brooches of gold; she belted herself with a girdle hung with a hundred tassels, fixed the earrings in her pierced ears — three drops to a cluster, glinting with grace — and over it all a fresh veil, fair as the new sun. On her shining feet she bound her lovely sandals. And when she had dressed herself in all her finery, she left the room and called Aphrodite aside, away from the other gods, and said to her: “Will you do something for me, dear child — or will you refuse, because I take the side of the Greeks while you stand with the Trojans?”
Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus, answered: “Hera, honored goddess, daughter of mighty Cronus — say what you want. My heart bids me do it, if I can, and if it can be done at all.”

And Hera, scheming, told her a lie: “Give me the love and the longing with which you yourself bring the whole world to its knees, gods and mortal men alike. I am going to the ends of the earth, to visit Ocean, the source of all the gods, and mother Tethys — they took me in and raised me in their own house, when Zeus thrust Cronus down beneath the earth and the barren sea. I must go and see them and end their quarrel. They’ve been at odds so long that they’ve held back from each other’s bed in their anger. If I can win them round with words and bring them back into each other’s arms, they’ll love me and call me dear forever.”
Aphrodite, who loves laughter, said: “I cannot refuse you, and I should not — you sleep in the arms of Zeus, the greatest of us all.”

And she loosed from her breast the embroidered band, the band into which all her powers had been worked: in it was love, in it was longing, in it was the soft, coaxing talk of lovers — the whispered word that steals the wits even of the wise. She put it into Hera’s hands and said: “Here — take this band and lay it in the fold of your robe. Everything is wrought into it, and I promise you won’t come back with your errand undone, whatever your heart is set on.”
At that the ox-eyed lady Hera smiled, and still smiling she laid the band in the fold of her robe.

Aphrodite went back into the house of Zeus, and Hera darted down from the peak of Olympus. She passed over Pieria and lovely Emathia, on over the snowy mountains of the Thracian horsemen, skimming the highest crests, her feet never touching the ground. From Athos she crossed the swelling sea and came to Lemnos, the city of godlike Thoas. There she found Sleep, the brother of Death, and caught him by the hand, and called him by name: “Sleep, lord over all gods and all men — if you ever heard a prayer of mine before, do this for me now, and I’ll be grateful all my days. Lull the bright eyes of Zeus to sleep under his brows the moment I lie down in his arms. And I’ll give you a beautiful throne for it, gold, that will never break — my own son, the lame smith Hephaestus, will make it and fit it with a footstool, where you can rest your shining feet when you sit at the feast.”

Sleep answered her: “Hera, honored goddess, daughter of mighty Cronus — any other of the everlasting gods I would gladly put to sleep, even the streams of Ocean, the source of them all. But Zeus, son of Cronus, I will not go near; I will not lull him, unless he tells me to himself. A command of yours taught me that once before — the day his great-hearted son Heracles sailed from Troy, after he had sacked the city. That day I poured myself sweet and soft over the mind of Zeus who wields the storm-shield and laid him to rest, while you plotted ruin against Heracles and stirred the angry winds across the sea, and drove him off to Cos, far from all his friends. Zeus woke in a fury and flung the gods about his house, hunting for me above all — he’d have hurled me out of the sky into the sea, lost forever, if Night had not saved me, Night who masters gods and men alike. I ran to her, and Zeus, angry as he was, held back, for he would not do anything to offend swift Night. And now you’re asking me for something else I dare not do.”

The ox-eyed lady Hera said: “Sleep, why take such fears to heart? Do you think Zeus will defend the Trojans the way he raged for his own son Heracles? Come — I’ll give you one of the younger Graces to marry, to be your own. Pasithea — the one you’ve longed for all your days.”

Sleep was glad to hear it, and answered: “Then swear it to me — by the dread water of the Styx. Lay one hand on the nourishing earth, the other on the shining sea, so that all the gods below with Cronus may be our witnesses, that you truly will give me one of the younger Graces — Pasithea, whom I have longed for all my days.”

Hera, white-armed goddess, did as he asked. She swore it, and named to witness all the gods below, the Titans, as they are called. When she had sworn the oath in full, the two of them wrapped themselves in mist and went lightly on their way, leaving Lemnos and Imbros behind. They came to Ida of the many springs, mother of wild beasts, to Lecton, where they left the sea and went on by land, and the tops of the forest trees stirred and whispered under their feet. There Sleep halted, before the eyes of Zeus could find him, and climbed a tall pine — the highest that had grown on Ida, reaching up through the air to heaven. He hid himself in the thick branches, in the likeness of the shrill mountain bird the gods call chalcis and men call cymindis.

Hera went on to Gargarus, the topmost peak of Ida, and Zeus who herds the clouds saw her. And the moment he saw her, desire wrapped close around his cunning heart — the same as the first time they lay together and crept into each other’s bed, with their dear parents knowing nothing of it. He stood up before her and spoke: “Hera, what brings you down here from Olympus? And with no chariot, no horses to carry you?”

And Hera, scheming, told him a lie: “I am going to the ends of the earth, to visit Ocean, the source of all the gods, and mother Tethys, who took me in and raised me in their house. I must go and see them and end their quarrel. They’ve been at odds so long they hold back from each other’s bed in their anger. My horses are waiting at the foot of Ida of the many springs, to carry me over land and sea. I’ve come here to you from Olympus on purpose — I didn’t want you angry with me afterward, if I slipped away to the house of deep-flowing Ocean without a word.”

Zeus who herds the clouds answered: “Hera, you can go there another time. Come — let us lie down and take our joy in love. Never has desire for goddess or for woman so flooded me and overmastered the heart in my breast — not for the wife of Ixion, who bore me Pirithous, a match for the gods in counsel; not for Danae of the slim ankles, daughter of Acrisius, who bore me Perseus, most renowned of men; not for the far-famed daughter of Phoenix, who bore me Minos and godlike Rhadamanthus; not for Semele, nor for Alcmene in Thebes, who bore my lion-hearted son Heracles, while Semele bore Dionysus, the joy of mortals; not for lady Demeter of the lovely hair, nor for glorious Leto — nor even for you, as I desire you now and sweet longing takes hold of me.”

And Hera, scheming, answered him again: “Most dread son of Cronus, what a thing to say. Lie down with you here, and take our joy on the heights of Ida, where everything is open to view? What if one of the everlasting gods caught sight of us asleep together and went off and told the rest? I could never rise from this bed and go back into your house again — the shame of it. But if this is your wish, if your heart is set on it, there is a chamber my dear son Hephaestus built for me, with strong doors fitted to their posts. Let us go there and lie down, since the bed is what you long for.”

Zeus who herds the clouds answered: “Hera, have no fear that god or man will see. I will hide us in a cloud of gold, so thick that not even Helios could see through it — and his light is the keenest thing there is for looking.”

With that the son of Cronus caught his wife in his arms. And beneath them the holy earth sent up fresh new grass — dewy clover and crocus and hyacinth, soft and thick, that lifted them clear of the ground. There they lay, and a beautiful cloud of gold closed over them, and from it fell glittering drops of dew.

So the father of all slept in peace on the crest of Ida, mastered at once by love and by sleep, his wife in his arms. And Sleep ran lightly to the ships of the Greeks, to bring his word to Poseidon, the Earth-Shaker. He came up close and spoke winged words: “Now, Poseidon, help the Greeks with all your heart, and give them the glory — even if only for a little while, while Zeus is still asleep. I’ve wrapped him in a soft slumber; Hera beguiled him into her bed.”

With that Sleep was gone, off among the tribes of men, and he left Poseidon more eager than ever to help the Greeks. At once the god sprang to the front ranks and shouted: “Greeks — are we going to hand the victory to Hector, son of Priam, and let him take our ships and cover himself with glory? That’s what he says he’ll do, now that Achilles sits sulking by the hollow ships. But we won’t miss him much, if the rest of us spur one another on and stand fast together. Now do as I say. The best, biggest shields in the whole army — let us take them up, put the bright helmets on our heads, grip the longest spears we have, and go. I’ll lead the way, and I tell you, Hector, son of Priam, for all his fury, will not stand against us. Any tough soldier holding a small shield — let him hand it to a lesser man and take a bigger one for himself.”

They heard him and obeyed. The kings themselves marshaled the lines, wounded as they were — Diomedes, Odysseus, and Agamemnon, son of Atreus — going through the ranks and ordering the exchange of armor, the best fighters into the best gear, the worse to the worse. When they had clad themselves in gleaming bronze they marched out, Poseidon, the Earth-Shaker, at their head, a long terrible sword in his strong hand, edged keen and flashing like lightning. No man may close with it in the grim work of battle; dread holds them all back.

And on the other side glorious Hector marshaled the Trojans. Then Poseidon, dark-haired god, and Hector strained the cord of war to its breaking point, the one bracing the Trojans, the other the Greeks. The sea came surging up to the tents and the ships, and the two armies clashed with a roar. Not so loud does the wave thunder on the shore, driven in from the deep by the cruel breath of the North Wind; not so loud does a forest fire roar when it leaps up the mountain glens to burn the woods; not so loud does the gale scream through the high crests of the oaks when it blows its hardest — as the great cry of the Trojans and the Greeks, terrible to hear, as they hurled themselves on one another.

Glorious Hector cast his spear first at Ajax, who was turned straight toward him, and did not miss — but it struck where the two straps crossed his chest, the baldric of his shield and the strap of his silver-studded sword, and they saved his flesh. Hector drew back among his men, raging that the throw had gone for nothing. As he went, Ajax, son of Telamon, caught up one of the many stones that lay rolling under the fighters’ feet — props for the beached ships — and hurled it. It caught Hector over the rim of his shield, high on the chest near the throat, and sent him spinning like a top, reeling round and round. As an oak goes down headlong, torn up by the lightning-stroke of father Zeus, and a terrible reek of brimstone rises from it, and the man who stands near loses his nerve, for the bolt of great Zeus is a fearful thing — so all at once mighty Hector dropped in the dust. The spear fell from his hand; his shield and helmet went down with him; and the bronze armor clashed about his body.

The sons of the Greeks ran at him with a great shout, hoping to drag him off, and showered their spears — but no one could reach him with a thrust or a throw, for the bravest were already around him: Polydamas and Aeneas and Agenor, Sarpedon, lord of the Lycians, and noble Glaucus. None of the rest forgot him either; they held their round shields over him. His comrades lifted him in their arms and carried him out of the fighting, to where his swift horses stood waiting at the rear with their charioteer and the painted car. They bore him toward the city, groaning, in deep pain. When they reached the ford of the fair-flowing Xanthus, the eddying river that immortal Zeus begot, they took him down from the chariot and laid him on the ground and poured water over him. He drew breath again and opened his eyes; he came up on his knees and vomited dark blood — then fell back, and darkness closed over his eyes again, for the stone had stunned him still.

When the Greeks saw Hector carried from the field, they pressed the Trojans harder and threw themselves into the fight with fresh fury. First of all, swift Ajax, son of Oileus, sprang on Satnius and wounded him with his spear — Satnius, whom a flawless naiad nymph had borne to Enops as he herded his cattle by the banks of the Satnioeis. The son of Oileus came up and struck him in the side, and he fell, and a hard fight broke out over his body, Trojans and Greeks together. Polydamas, son of Panthous, came to avenge him, brandishing his spear, and struck Prothoenor, son of Areilycus, on the right shoulder; the heavy spear drove clean through, and he went down clutching the earth in his fist. Polydamas shouted over him in triumph: “This time too, I’d say, the spear has not flown for nothing from the strong hand of the proud son of Panthous.
