A Greek has taken it in his body — it’ll serve him for a staff as he goes down into the house of Hades.”

The Greeks were stung to fury by his boast, and Ajax, son of Telamon, most of all — the man had fallen right beside him. As Polydamas drew back, Ajax let fly at him; Polydamas swerved aside and escaped, but the spear caught Archelochus, son of Antenor — the gods had marked him for death. It struck where the head joins the neck, at the topmost vertebra, and cut through both sinews, so that his head and mouth and nostrils hit the ground before his shins and his knees as he fell. And Ajax shouted to Polydamas: “Think, Polydamas — tell me the truth: was this man not worth killing to pay for Prothoenor? He doesn’t look low-born or of low stock — a brother of Antenor the horseman, maybe, or a son; the family likeness is strong.”

He knew well who it was, and grief seized the Trojans. Then Acamas, standing astride his brother’s body, drove his spear into Promachus the Boeotian, who was trying to drag the corpse away by the feet. Acamas shouted over him in triumph: “You Greeks — archers, big talkers, never sated with threats — it won’t be only we who toil and suffer; you too will die, sooner or later, just like this. Look how your Promachus sleeps now, brought down by my spear. The blood-price for my brother didn’t wait long. That’s why a man prays to leave a kinsman behind in his house, to avenge his fall.”

His boast cut the Greeks to the quick, and Peneleos most of all. He charged Acamas, who would not stand to meet him, and instead Peneleos struck Ilioneus, the only son of Phorbas, rich in flocks, whom Hermes had loved above all the Trojans and given great wealth. He struck him in the eye, beneath the brow, and the spearhead drove the eyeball out and on through the socket into the nape of the neck, and Ilioneus sank down, both arms thrown wide. Then Peneleos drew his sharp sword and hewed through the neck, and the head with its helmet dropped to the ground, the heavy spear still fixed in the eye. He held it up like the head of a poppy and showed it to the Trojans, crying in triumph: “Trojans — go tell the father and mother of proud Ilioneus to weep for him in their halls; for the wife of Promachus, son of Alegenor, will never gladden her eyes with her husband’s coming, when we Greeks sail home from Troy.”

Fear ran cold through them at his words, and every man looked around for some way out of sheer destruction. Tell me now, Muses who hold the homes of Olympus — who was the first of the Greeks to carry off bloody spoils, once the Earth-Shaker had turned the tide of battle? Ajax, son of Telamon, was first; he wounded Hyrtius, son of Gyrtius, captain of the stout-hearted Mysians. Antilochus killed Phalces and Mermerus; Meriones brought down Morys and Hippotion; Teucer killed Prothoon and Periphetes. And the son of Atreus struck Hyperenor, shepherd of his people, in the side, and the bronze tore through his bowels and ripped them out, and his life rushed from the wound, and darkness closed over his eyes. But Ajax, swift son of Oileus, killed the most by far — no man was as fast as he to run down a fleeing enemy, once Zeus had loosed the panic among them.
books.title: The Deception of Zeus

books.label: Book XV
paragraphs: When their flight had carried them back past the trench and the row of stakes, and many had gone down under Greek hands, the Trojans halted by their chariots, pale and shaking. And on the heights of Ida Zeus woke, where he had lain beside golden-throned Hera, and he sprang to his feet and looked out and saw the Trojans and the Greeks — the one side scattered in rout, the other driving them headlong with lord Poseidon in their midst. He saw Hector lying on the plain, his comrades crouched around him, struggling for breath, his mind wandering, vomiting blood; for the man who had struck him was not the weakest of the Greeks.

The father of gods and men pitied him, and turned a terrible look on Hera. “This is your work, Hera — your scheming, your treachery. You crippled Hector and routed his army. I have half a mind to be the first to make you taste what your cunning earns: I will lash you for it. Have you forgotten the time I hung you out of heaven, with two anvils chained to your feet and your wrists bound in a band of gold that nothing could break? You swung there in the high air among the clouds. The gods on Olympus raged at the sight, but they could not reach you to set you free — and any one of them I caught, I seized and flung from the threshold of the sky, and down he came half-dead to the earth. Even that did not ease the grief that gnawed at me over godlike Heracles, my son, when you and the North Wind had whipped up a storm and driven him over the barren sea to Cos, out of pure spite. I rescued him from there and brought him back to Argos, for all the labors he had borne. I remind you of this so you will stop your deceiving, and learn how little you stand to gain from the bed you came down from Olympus to lure me into and trick me.”

Hera shuddered at his words, and answered: “Let Earth be my witness, and the wide Heaven above, and the down-flowing water of the Styx — the most binding oath the blessed gods can swear — and your own sacred head, and the bed we share as man and wife, which I would never swear by falsely: it is no doing of mine that Poseidon is breaking Hector and the Trojans and helping the Greeks. He acts on his own, driven by his own heart, because he was grieved to see the Greeks crushed against their ships. If it were up to me, I would tell him to go wherever you, lord of the storm-cloud, lead.”

The father of gods and men smiled at that, and answered: “If only you would always think with me, Hera, when we sit in council, then Poseidon, however much he might wish otherwise, would soon bend his mind to yours and mine. But if you mean what you say and speak the truth, then go among the gods and send me Iris and Apollo, lord of the bow. Iris will go down to the Greek army and tell Poseidon to break off the fighting and come home to his own halls. And Apollo will send Hector back into battle and breathe fresh strength into him, so he forgets the pain that wracks him now, and drives the Greeks back in headlong panic until they fall among the ships of Achilles, son of Peleus. Then Achilles will rouse his comrade Patroclus into the fighting, and bright Hector will kill him in front of Troy, after Patroclus has cut down many strong men — among them my own son, noble Sarpedon. And in fury for Patroclus, brilliant Achilles will kill Hector. From that hour on I will turn the tide and drive the Trojans steadily back from the ships, on and on, until the Greeks take steep Troy through the counsels of Athena. But until then I will not let my anger rest, and I will let no other god help the Greeks, not until the desire of the son of Peleus is fulfilled — as I promised him, bowing my head, on the day Thetis clasped my knees and begged me to give honor to Achilles, sacker of cities.”

Hera did not disobey. She went from the peaks of Ida to high Olympus. Swift as the mind of a man who has traveled over much of the world and thinks, “I wish I were there, or there” — and in a flash his thought has flown across it all — so swiftly did queenly Hera dart upward, until she came to steep Olympus and entered among the immortal gods gathered in the house of Zeus. When they saw her they all rose and lifted their cups toward her in welcome. She passed the others by, but took the cup from lovely Themis, who had run to her first, and who spoke to her with care: “Hera, why have you come? You look stricken. Has the son of Cronus, your husband, been frightening you?”

White-armed Hera answered: “Don't ask me, Themis. You know yourself how arrogant and hard his temper is. Take your place at the feast among the gods, and you will hear, with all the immortals, what evil things Zeus is announcing. I tell you, this will not gladden every heart, mortal or divine, however cheerfully some of them are feasting now.”

She sat down, and through the house of Zeus the gods were troubled. Her lips were smiling, but above her dark brows her forehead was not, and she spoke out in anger to them all: “Fools that we are, to rage against Zeus like children. We keep wanting to go up to him and stop him, by force or by words — and he sits apart and cares nothing for us, because he knows he is far the strongest of all the immortals. So each of you make the best of whatever grief he chooses to send you. Ares, I think, has already had his share: his son Ascalaphus is dead, fallen in the fighting — the man Ares loved best of all, the man he calls his own.”

When Ares heard this he struck both his sturdy thighs with the flat of his hands and cried out in grief: “Don't blame me, you gods who live on Olympus, if I go down to the Greek ships to avenge my son's death — even if I am fated to be struck by the bolt of Zeus and to lie there among the corpses in blood and dust.”

And he gave the order to yoke his horses, Terror and Rout, and he began to put on his armor. Then Zeus would have been roused to an anger against the immortals greater and more bitter than ever — but Athena, fearing for all the gods, sprang from her seat and ran out through the doorway. She tore the helmet from Ares' head and the shield from his shoulders, took the bronze spear from his strong hand and set it aside, and rounded on furious Ares: “Madman — you've lost your mind, you're ruined. You have ears but you cannot hear; your judgment and your sense are gone. Did you not hear what white-armed Hera said, who came to us straight from the side of Olympian Zeus? Do you want to drink your fill of sorrow and be dragged back to Olympus sick and beaten, with disaster sown for the rest of us? At once Zeus would leave off with the Trojans and the Greeks and come up here to drive us all before him, seizing us one after another, guilty or not. So let go of this rage over your son. Better men than he have been killed already, or will be yet. It is not possible to keep every man's whole line alive.”

With that she sat raging Ares back in his seat. And Hera called Apollo out of the hall, and Iris with him, the messenger of the gods, and said to them: “Zeus orders you to come to him on Ida at once. When you have seen him, do whatever he commands.”

Queenly Hera went back in and took her seat, and the two of them sped off. They reached Ida, the mother of wild beasts, with its many springs, and found the wide-seeing son of Cronus seated on the highest crest of Gargarus, a fragrant cloud wreathed around him like a crown. They came and stood before him, and he was pleased that they had been so quick to obey his wife's word.

He spoke to Iris first: “Go, swift Iris. Tell lord Poseidon all this — and tell it true. Order him to break off the fighting and join the company of the gods, or go down into the sea. And if he will not listen, if he disobeys me, then let him think hard whether he is strong enough to hold his ground against me when I come for him. I am the elder, and far the stronger — and yet he does not shrink from setting himself up as my equal, the one whom all the other gods fear.”

Iris, swift as the storm-wind, did not disobey. Down she swept from the heights of Ida to holy Troy, fast as the snow or the cold hail that flies from the clouds before the blast of the North Wind, until she came up close to the great Earthshaker and spoke: “I have come, dark-haired lord who holds the earth in your embrace, to bring you word from Zeus. He orders you to break off the fighting and join the company of the gods, or go down into the sea. And if you will not listen, if you disobey, he threatens to come here himself and fight you — and he warns you to keep clear of his hands, for he is the elder, and far the stronger; and yet you do not shrink from setting yourself up as his equal, the one whom all the other gods fear.”

Poseidon, deeply angered, answered: “No — for all his strength, this is too much, if he would force me down by threats, when I am of equal honor with him. We are three brothers, sons of Cronus by Rhea: Zeus, and myself, and Hades, who is lord of the dead below. The whole world was split three ways, and each of us drew his share. The lot gave me the gray sea to live in forever; Hades drew the misty dark; Zeus drew the wide sky among the clouds and the bright upper air. But the earth and high Olympus are still common to us all. So I will not live by the will of Zeus. Strong as he is, let him stay content with his own third, and not try to frighten me as if I were some nobody. Let him save his bullying for the sons and daughters he fathered — they have no choice but to obey him.”

Iris, swift as the wind, answered: “Dark-haired lord who holds the earth, am I truly to carry this hard and unbending answer back to Zeus? Or will you give a little? The minds of good men can be turned. And you know the Furies always stand with the elder-born.”

Poseidon, who holds the earth, replied: “Iris, you speak well, and in season. It is a fine thing when a messenger has good sense. But it galls me to the heart that he would scold an equal, one who shares his rank, in such angry words. Still — for now, and against my will, I'll give way. But I tell you this, and I mean it: if, against my wish and Athena's and Hera's, against Hermes and lord Hephaestus, Zeus spares steep Troy and will not let the Greeks have the great triumph of sacking it — let him know there will be a wound between us that nothing will ever heal.”

With that the Earthshaker left the field and went down into the sea, and the Greeks felt his loss keenly. Then Zeus who gathers the clouds said to Apollo: “Go now, dear Phoebus, to Hector of the bronze helmet. Poseidon who holds the earth has gone down into the sea, out of reach of my anger — and well for both of us that he did, for it would have cost us a hard struggle, and the gods below with Cronus would have heard the noise of it. Take up the tasselled aegis, and shake it hard, and put the Greek champions to flight. And take great Hector into your own care, far-shooter, and rouse his strength again, until the Greeks are driven back in panic to their ships and to the Hellespont. From there I will see to it myself, how the Greeks may have some relief from their trouble.”

Apollo did not disobey his father. Down he came from the crests of Ida like a falcon, the swift killer of doves, the fastest thing that flies. He found Hector no longer lying on the ground but sitting up, just coming back to himself, knowing the men around him; the sweat and the hard breathing had passed, now that the will of Zeus had revived him. Apollo stood beside him and said: “Hector, son of Priam — why are you sitting here, faint and apart from the rest? Has some trouble come over you?”

Faintly Hector answered: “Which of the gods are you, kind one, who ask me this? Don't you know that at the Greek ships, while I was killing his comrades, Ajax struck me in the chest with a boulder and took the fight out of me? I was sure this was the day I would breathe my last and go down to the house of the dead.”

Then lord Apollo who strikes from afar said: “Take heart. The son of Cronus has sent you a powerful helper down from Ida, to stand by you and guard you — Phoebus Apollo of the golden sword, who has watched over you and your high city all this time. Up now — order your charioteers to drive their teams hard against the hollow ships. I will go before you and smooth the whole way for the horses, and turn the Greek champions in flight.”

And he breathed great strength into the shepherd of his people. As a stalled horse, full-fed at the manger, snaps his halter and gallops thundering over the plain, headed for his bathing place in the sweet-running river — head high, mane streaming over his shoulders, sure of his own splendor, his legs carrying him to the haunts and the pastures of the mares — so Hector, when he heard the god's voice, moved his feet fast and called on his charioteers. And the Greeks — as when hunters and their hounds press a horned stag or a wild goat, but it has taken cover under a rock or in dark woods, for it was not their fate to catch it, and then their shouting raises a great bearded lion in their path, and at once they lose all heart for the chase — so the Greeks for a while kept pressing on in a body, thrusting with swords and double-edged spears; but when they saw Hector going up and down the ranks, their courage drained into their feet.

Then Thoas spoke out, son of Andraemon, the best of the Aetolians — a fine spear-thrower, steady in close fighting, and few of the Greeks could beat him in debate when the young men argued out a plan. With good will he spoke: “What is this I'm seeing? It can't be — is that Hector, back on his feet and alive? Every one of us was sure Ajax, son of Telamon, had killed him. Some god has snatched him up and saved him again. He has killed many of us already, and he'll kill more — the hand of Zeus is plainly behind him, or he would never stand so far out in front. Listen to me, all of you. Let's order the main body of the army to fall back on the ships. But those of us who claim to be the best, let us stand our ground here, and try whether we can hold him off when he comes near, meeting him with leveled spears. I think that even he, for all his fury, will think twice before he plunges into the press of the Greeks.”

They heard him and did as he said. The men around Ajax and lord Idomeneus, with Teucer and Meriones and Meges, who matched Ares in war, called all their best fighters together and made a wall against Hector and the Trojans, while behind them the main body fell back on the ships.

The Trojans came on packed close together, Hector striding huge at their head; and before him went Phoebus Apollo, his shoulders wrapped in cloud, holding the terrible aegis, shaggy and bright at the fringe, which Hephaestus the smith had given to Zeus to carry terror into men. With this in his hands he led the Trojans on.

The Greeks held together and stood their ground. The war cry rose sharp from both sides, and arrows leapt from the bowstrings; and many a spear from a strong hand drove home in the bodies of fighting men, while many fell short in the ground between, hungry for flesh they never tasted. As long as Apollo held the aegis steady in his hands, the missiles of both sides struck home and men kept falling. But when he looked the Greeks full in the face and shook it, and let loose his own great war cry, their hearts melted in their chests and they forgot how to fight. As two wild beasts in the dead of night will stampede a herd of cattle or a great flock of sheep, falling on them suddenly while the herdsman is away — so the Greeks were thrown into helpless rout, for Apollo had loosed panic on them and given the glory to Hector and the Trojans.

Now the fighting broke up, and man killed man wherever he could. Hector killed Stichius and Arcesilaus — the one a leader of the Boeotians, the other the loyal friend of Menestheus. Aeneas killed Medon and Iasus: Medon was the bastard son of Oileus and Ajax's brother, but he lived far from his own country at Phylace, having killed a man, a kinsman of his stepmother Eriopis, Oileus' wife; and Iasus was a captain of the Athenians, son of Sphelus, the son of Boucolus. Polydamas cut down Mecisteus, and Polites killed Echius in the front rank, and Agenor killed Clonius. And Paris struck Deiochus from behind, low at the base of the shoulder, as he fled among the foremost, and drove the bronze clean through him.

While the Trojans were stripping the armor from these dead, the Greeks went stumbling back into the trench and the line of stakes, fleeing this way and that, and were forced back behind their wall. And Hector shouted to the Trojans in a great voice: “On to the ships — leave the bloody spoils. If I see any man hanging back from the ships, anywhere along this wall, I'll have him killed on the spot. His own kin, men and women alike, will give him no funeral fire; the dogs will tear him in front of our city.”

With that he laid the lash across his horses' shoulders and called to the Trojans up and down the ranks; and they all shouted together with a cry that split the air and drove their teams beside his own. And out in front Phoebus Apollo kicked down the banks of the deep trench with his feet, tumbling the earth into the middle to make a long broad causeway, as wide as the cast of a spear when a man throws to test his strength. Over it the Trojan companies poured in a flood, and Apollo led the way before them with the terrible aegis, and threw down the Greek wall as easily as a child at the seashore who builds his sand into toys and then, in play, kicks them flat again with his feet and hands. So you, Apollo, the far-shooter, scattered the long toil and labor of the Greeks, and loosed panic and confusion on them.

So the Greeks were penned in among their ships, calling out to one another, and lifting their hands to all the gods, each man praying aloud. Above them all old Nestor, the Greeks' tower of strength, lifted his hands to the starry sky and prayed: “Father Zeus — if ever any man in wheat-rich Argos burned for you the fat thighs of a sheep or an ox and prayed to come safely home, and you bowed your head and promised it — remember it now, Olympian, and turn this pitiless day from us. Don't let the Trojans break the Greeks like this.”

So he prayed, and Zeus of the counsels thundered loud, hearing the prayer of the old son of Neleus. But the Trojans, when they heard the thunder of Zeus, only flung themselves harder at the Greeks, mad for battle. As a great wave of the open sea breaks over a ship's rail when the wind is high — for the wind is what builds the wave to its full height — so the Trojans came over the wall with a roar and drove their chariots in among the ships, and fought hand to hand with their double-edged spears: the Trojans from their chariots, the Greeks climbing high onto the black ships' decks and fighting down with the long pikes that lay aboard, jointed and tipped with bronze, kept ready for fighting at sea.

Now Patroclus, all the while the Greeks and Trojans had been fighting around the wall, away from the swift ships, had stayed in the hut of good Eurypylus, keeping him company and laying soothing herbs on his wound to ease its pain. But when he saw the Trojans pouring over the wall and the Greeks crying out in panic and breaking, he groaned aloud and struck both his thighs with the flat of his hands, and said in his grief: “Eurypylus — I can't stay with you any longer, badly as you need me. The fighting has come to its worst. Let one of your men tend you now; I have to run to Achilles and try to move him to fight. Who knows — with a god's help I may yet sway his heart. A man does well to listen to a friend who loves him.”

And with that he was gone, running. The Greeks held firm against the Trojans' attack, and though the Trojans were the fewer, they could not drive the Greeks back from the ships; and the Trojans could not break the Greek line and force their way in among the huts and the ships. As a chalk-line draws a ship's timber straight and true in the hands of a skilled carpenter, a man Athena has taught the whole of his craft — so even and taut was the strain of the fighting between them, as they fought it out, this group around one ship and that around another.

But Hector went straight for glorious Ajax, and the two of them fought hard over the same ship. Hector could not force Ajax back and set fire to it, and Ajax could not drive Hector off, now that a god had brought him to that spot.

Then Ajax speared Caletor, son of Clytius, in the chest as he was bringing fire to the ship; he crashed down, and the torch fell from his hand. When Hector saw his own cousin fallen there before the ship, he shouted to the Trojans and Lycians: “Trojans, Lycians, Dardanians who fight at close quarters — don't give an inch here in the thick of it. Save the son of Clytius before the Greeks can strip his armor where he's fallen by the ships.”

And he cast his spear at Ajax. He missed him, but hit Lycophron, Ajax's man, the son of Mastor from Cythera, who had come to live with Ajax after killing a man at home, and was honored in the household like one of his own parents. The bronze struck him on the head above the ear, and he toppled headlong from the ship's stern to the ground, with the life gone out of him. Ajax shuddered, and called to his brother: “Teucer, our trusted friend is dead — the son of Mastor, whom we honored in our house like one of our own. Hector has just killed him. Where are your deadly arrows now, where is the bow Phoebus Apollo gave you?”

Teucer heard him and ran to his side with his bow and his quiver, and at once began raining arrows on the Trojans. He hit Cleitus, son of Pisenor, Polydamas' comrade, as he held the reins in his hands — he was in the thick of the fighting, doing good service to Hector and the Trojans, but in an instant the evil came on him that none who wished it could turn aside, for the arrow struck him in the back of the neck. He fell from the chariot, and the horses swerved, rattling the empty car. Polydamas saw it at once and was first to the team; he gave it over to Astynous, son of Protiaon, ordering him to keep the horses close at hand, and went back into the front ranks.

Then Teucer aimed another arrow at Hector — and there would have been an end to the fighting at the ships, if he had hit him and brought him down. But Zeus, who was watching over Hector, did not miss it; he robbed Teucer of his triumph and snapped the well-twisted bowstring just as he drew it to take aim. The arrow flew wild, and the bow dropped from his hands. Teucer shuddered, and said to his brother: “This is no use — a god is cutting the ground from under everything we try. He has snapped my bowstring out of my hand, and broken the fresh-corded bow I strung only this morning to carry all the arrows I would loose.”

Great Ajax, son of Telamon, answered: “Then let your bow and your arrows lie, since a god, set against the Greeks, has made them useless. Take a long spear in your hands, sling a shield on your shoulder, and fight the Trojans yourself, and call on the others to do the same. Let them not take the ships without a hard fight, even if they break through. Let us think only of the work in front of us.”

Teucer set the bow down in his hut, slung a four-layered shield on his shoulders, set a well-made helmet on his strong head, the horsehair crest nodding above it, took up a stout spear shod with bronze, and went and stood at Ajax's side.

When Hector saw that Teucer's arrows were useless to him, he called out to the Trojans and Lycians: “Trojans, Lycians, Dardanians who fight at close quarters — be men, my friends; remember your courage here at the hollow ships. I have seen with my own eyes how Zeus has crippled the weapon of one of their best. It is easy to know when Zeus is helping men — and easy to know whom he leaves behind to ruin. Now he is bringing the Greeks low and standing with us. So close on the ships, all of you, and fight. And if any man among you meets his death by spear or arrow, let him die. There is no shame in dying for your country. His wife will be safe behind him, and his children, his house and his lands unharmed — if only the Greeks can be driven back to the land they came from, in their ships.”

So he put strength into them all. And Ajax on the other side called out to his men: “Shame on you, Greeks. Now it is win or die. Do you think, if Hector takes the ships, that you'll go home on foot? Can't you hear him cheering his whole army on to burn the fleet? He isn't calling them to a dance — he's calling them to a fight. There's nothing for us now but to throw our hands and our whole strength into it. Better to settle it once, life or death, than to be ground down slowly, pinned against the ships by lesser men.”

So he too put strength into them all. Then Hector killed Schedius, son of Perimedes, a leader of the Phocians, and Ajax killed Laodamas, captain of foot soldiers, son of Antenor. Polydamas killed Otus of Cyllene, comrade of the son of Phyleus and a chief of the proud Epeians. Meges saw it and lunged at him, but Polydamas ducked aside — Apollo would not let the son of Panthous fall — and the spear caught Croesmus full in the chest, and Meges stripped his armor. As he did, Dolops sprang at him — Dolops son of Lampus, son of Laomedon, a hard fighter who knew every trick of war. He drove his spear into the center of Meges' shield at close range, but the close-set plates of his breastplate saved him, the corslet Phyleus had brought from Ephyra, from the river Selleis, a guest-gift from King Euphetes to wear in battle; and now it saved his son's life. Then Meges thrust at the crest of Dolops' bronze helmet and sheared off the plume, newly dyed scarlet, and it fell in the dust. And while Dolops still fought on, sure of victory, Menelaus came up to help, and got beside him unseen, and speared him from behind in the shoulder; the point drove through into his chest, and he pitched forward on his face. The two ran in to strip his armor — but Hector called on all his brothers, and rounded most of all on Melanippus, son of Hicetaon, who once had grazed his cattle in Percote before the war, but when the Greek ships came had gone back to Troy and won a high name among the Trojans, living near Priam, who treated him like a son. Now Hector rebuked him: “Are we going to slacken now, Melanippus? Does it move you nothing that your kinsman is dead, and that they're stripping Dolops' armor? Come with me. There's no more killing the Greeks from a distance — we close with them now, until either we cut them down or they storm the high towers of Troy and slaughter her people.”

He led on, and Melanippus followed. And Ajax, son of Telamon, was urging the Greeks: “Be men, my friends. Set honor in your hearts; let each fear the shame of looking weak to the rest. When men hold to each other's good opinion, more come through alive than die. But in flight there is no safety and no glory.”

They needed no telling — they were already set on driving the Trojans back — and they took his words to heart, and fenced the ships about with a wall of bronze, while Zeus drove the Trojans on against them. Then Menelaus of the great war cry called to Antilochus: “Antilochus — there's no Greek younger than you, none faster on his feet or braver. Spring out and bring down a Trojan.”

And he was gone again, having spurred Antilochus on. Out from the front rank he darted, glanced around, and threw; and the Trojans gave way as the spear flew, and it did not leave his hand for nothing, for it struck Melanippus, the proud son of Hicetaon, in the chest by the nipple as he came on, and he crashed down, and his armor rang about him. Antilochus sprang at him like a hound on a fawn that a hunter has struck as it broke from cover — so Antilochus leapt on you, Melanippus, to strip your armor. But noble Hector saw it and came running through the press, and Antilochus, brave as he was, would not stand to face him, but bolted like a wild thing that has done some harm — killed a dog, or a herdsman among his cattle — and runs before the men can gather against it. So the son of Nestor fled, and the Trojans and Hector after him, with a roar that split the air, showering their weapons. Only when he reached his own comrades did he turn and stand.

And the Trojans, fierce as lions, came storming on toward the ships, fulfilling the will of Zeus, who kept rousing them to new daring while he deadened the hearts of the Greeks and stole away their glory and gave it to the Trojans. For he meant to give the great glory to Hector, son of Priam — to let him hurl ravening fire on the curved ships, and so fulfill the cruel prayer of Thetis. Zeus, the lord of counsel, was only waiting to see with his own eyes the glare of a single burning ship; for from that hour he meant to turn the Trojans back from the ships and give the glory to the Greeks. With this in mind he drove Hector, mad for battle already, against the hollow ships. Hector raged like the war-god Ares with his spear, or like a fire that rages through the thick brush on the mountains; he foamed at the mouth, his eyes blazed under his terrible brows, and the helmet shook fearfully about his temples as he fought. For Zeus himself, out of heaven, was on his side, and gave glory and honor to him alone among so many men — because his life was to be short, and even now Pallas Athena was driving on the day of his death at the hands of the son of Peleus. He kept trying to break the Greek line wherever he saw it thickest and best-armed — but he could not break it, for all his fury; they held like a tower, square and solid, like a great sheer cliff above the gray sea that stands against the screaming wind and the waves that thunder up against it. So the Greeks stood firm against the Trojans and did not run. But Hector, all ablaze, hurled himself on them from every side, and fell upon them as a wave reared mountain-high by the wind and storm comes crashing down on a swift ship and buries it in foam, while the wind howls in the sail and the sailors' hearts shake in their chests, barely saved from death by a hair — so the hearts of the Greeks were torn within them. And he came at them like a savage lion falling on a herd of cattle grazing by the thousand in the wet meadows of a wide shore, with a herdsman among them who does not yet know how to fight a beast for his cattle, and the lion springs into the midst of the herd and pulls one down, and the rest scatter in terror — so the Greeks were thrown into godlike panic by Hector and father Zeus. Yet Hector killed only one of them, Periphetes of Mycenae, the son of Copreus — the man who used to carry King Eurystheus' orders to mighty Heracles. From that poor father came a far better son, swift of foot and brave in battle, and among the wisest men in Mycenae. He it was who handed Hector this triumph: turning back, he tripped on the rim of his own shield, the great shield that reached to his feet and warded off the spears; he stumbled over it and fell on his back, and the helmet rang loud about his head as he went down. Hector saw it and ran in, and drove a spear into his chest, and killed him there among his own companions — who, for all their grief, could not help him, in their own terror of Hector.

Now they were back among the ships, with the sterns of the foremost line all around them, and the Trojans came pouring on. The Greeks were forced back from the first row of ships, but they made a stand by the huts, not scattered, holding together; shame and fear held them. And they kept calling out to one another, and most of all old Nestor, the Greeks' tower of strength, begged each man by his own parents to stand firm: “Be men, my friends. Set the shame of others' eyes in your hearts. Think, each of you, of your children, your wives, your goods, your parents, whether they are still living or dead. For their sake — though they are not here — I beg you: hold your ground. Do not turn and run.”

So he put strength into them all. And Athena lifted the thick cloud of darkness from their eyes, and the light poured down on them, on the side of the ships and on the side where the battle still raged; and they could see Hector of the great war cry and all his men — both those behind, out of the fighting, and those at the swift ships.

But Ajax could not bear to fall back with the rest. He went striding from deck to deck along the ships, swinging in his hands a great sea-pike, twenty-two cubits long, jointed together with rings. As a man who has mastered horses harnesses four of them together and comes galloping full speed from the country toward a great town along the public road, and the men and women crowd to watch and marvel as he leaps surely from one horse to the next, never missing his footing, while the team runs flat out — so Ajax went striding from one ship's deck to another, and his voice went up into the sky as he shouted, over and over, to the Greeks to defend their ships and their huts. And Hector, too, would not stay back in the mass of the Trojans, but as a tawny eagle stoops on a flock of birds feeding by a river — geese, or cranes, or long-necked swans — so Hector hurled himself straight at a dark-prowed ship, charging full at it, for Zeus thrust him on from behind with his mighty hand, and roused the army to come after him.

And the battle blazed up again around the ships. You would have thought these were fresh, untired men, so fiercely did they fall on each other — and this was the mind of each side: the Greeks no longer believed they would escape ruin, but thought themselves doomed; while there was not a Trojan whose heart did not beat high with the hope of firing the ships and killing the Greek champions. With this in their hearts they faced each other.

Then Hector laid hold of the stern of a fine ship — the swift seagoing ship that had brought Protesilaus to Troy, and never carried him home again. Around that ship the Greeks and Trojans fought hand to hand, butchering each other. No more standing off with bows and javelins now: they stood close and cut at one another with one rage in them, with sharp axes and hatchets, with great swords and double-edged spears. Many a good blade, dark-hilted and heavy, fell to the ground, struck from a man's hand or sheared from his shoulder as he fought, and the earth ran black with blood. And Hector, once he had hold of the stern, would not let go; he gripped the curved sternpost and shouted to the Trojans: “Bring fire — and all together, raise the war cry. Now Zeus has given us the day that pays for everything: to take the ships that came here against the will of heaven and brought us so much grief, through the cowardice of our elders, who held me back when I would have fought at the ships, and would not let the army follow. But if Zeus, the wide-seeing, blunted our wits then, now he himself is driving us on and urging us forward.”

At his words the Trojans flung themselves still harder on the Greeks. And Ajax could no longer hold his ground; he was beaten back by the storm of missiles, and gave himself up for dead. He left the high deck at the stern and stepped down onto the seven-foot rowing bench, and stood there, watching, holding off with his spear every Trojan who came to the ships with fire, and shouting all the while in a terrible voice to the Greeks: “Friends — Greek champions, fighters of Ares — be men, and remember your fighting strength. Do you think there are reinforcements somewhere behind us, or a stronger wall than this to keep off ruin? There is no walled city near where we might fall back and bring up fresh men. We are out on the plain of the Trojans and their bronze, with the sea at our backs, far from our own land. Our deliverance is in our hands and in hard fighting — not in slacking off.”

So he spoke, and drove on with his spear in a still greater fury; and whenever a Trojan came at the hollow ships with blazing fire, hoping to please Hector, Ajax was watching for him, and ran him through with the long spear. Twelve men he killed that way, hand to hand, in front of the ships.
books.title: The Battle at the Ships

books.label: Book XVI
paragraphs: So they fought on around the ship of Protesilaus. And Patroclus came to Achilles, shepherd of the people, the tears running hot down his face like a dark spring that spills its water down the face of a cliff. Achilles, swift of foot, saw him and pitied him, and spoke: “Why are you crying, Patroclus, like a little girl who runs beside her mother and begs to be picked up, clutching at her dress, holding her back though she's in a hurry, and looks up at her in tears until she lifts her? Those are the tears you're shedding now. Have you something to tell the Myrmidons, or me? Some news from Phthia that only you have heard? They say Menoetius, son of Actor, is still alive, and Peleus, son of Aeacus, still lives among the Myrmidons — we'd grieve hard for either of them. Or is it the Greeks you're weeping for, the way they're dying at the hollow ships, paying for their own arrogance? Don't hide it. Tell me, so we both can know.”

With a heavy groan you answered him, Patroclus, master of horses: “Achilles, son of Peleus, far the bravest of the Greeks — don't be angry. The Greeks are in too much pain. The best of them, all the men who were our shield, are lying among the ships, hit by spear or sword. Diomedes, Tydeus's strong son, is wounded; Odysseus is speared, and Agamemnon too; Eurypylus has an arrow in his thigh, and the healers are crowded around them with their drugs, tending their wounds. But you — there's no reaching you, Achilles. God keep me from a rage like the one you nurse, you with your ruinous courage. What use will you be to anyone in the years to come, if you won't save the Greeks from this shameful ruin now? You have no pity in you. Peleus was never your father, nor Thetis your mother — the gray sea bore you, and the sheer cliffs, your heart is so hard. But if some prophecy holds you back, something your mother brought you from Zeus, then at least send me out, and the rest of the Myrmidons with me, and maybe I'll be a light to the Greeks. And give me your armor to wear on my shoulders — the Trojans might take me for you and pull back from the fight, and the worn-out sons of the Greeks could breathe again. There's little enough breathing room in war. We're fresh; we could easily drive tired men back from our ships and tents to their own city.”

So he begged, the fool — for what he was begging for was his own death, his own black end. Achilles, deeply troubled, answered him: “What are you saying, Patroclus, prince that you are? No prophecy is holding me back, none that I know of; my mother has brought me nothing from Zeus. It's only this — a terrible grief comes over my heart and spirit when a man wants to rob one who is his equal and tear away the prize, just because he holds more power. After all I've been through, that is more than I can bear. The girl the sons of the Greeks chose out for me, that I won with my own spear when I sacked a walled city — King Agamemnon snatched her back out of my hands, as if I were some nobody with no honor at all. But let it go; what's done is done. I never meant to keep my anger forever. I said I wouldn't let it rest until the war cry reached my own ships. So now — put my famous armor on your shoulders and lead the war-loving Myrmidons out, since the dark cloud of the Trojans has broken over the ships, and the Greeks are penned against the lip of the sea with only a thin strip of ground left to them, and the whole city of Troy has come boldly out against them. They no longer see the gleam of my helmet flash before their eyes. If only King Agamemnon had treated me right, they'd have filled the ditches with their own dead as they ran. As it is, the Trojans are fighting around our camp, and the spear of Diomedes no longer rages in his hands to keep death from the Greeks, and I've not heard the voice of the son of Atreus shouting from his hateful head — only murderous Hector's, ringing out everywhere as he calls the Trojans on, and they hold the whole plain with their cry, beating the Greeks down. Even so, Patroclus, fall on them hard and save the ships, before they burn them and cut off our way home. But do exactly as I tell you, so you win me great honor and glory from all the Greeks, and they hand the girl back to me with splendid gifts besides. Once you've driven them from the ships, come back. Even if Hera's loud-thundering husband puts the chance of triumph in your hands, don't go fighting the Trojans on your own, with me away — you'll only strip me of my honor. And don't, in the joy of slaughter, keep killing your way toward Troy and lead the Greeks up to the city — some god from Olympus may come down against you. Apollo, who strikes from afar, loves the Trojans dearly. Turn back the moment you've saved the ships, and let the rest of them fight it out on the plain. By Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo — if only not one of all the Trojans could escape death, and not one of the Greeks, and the two of us alone could be left to tear away the holy veil from the brow of Troy.”

So they spoke to each other. But Ajax could hold his ground no longer; the storm of missiles was beating him down. The will of Zeus and the spears of the proud Trojans were too much for him. The bright helmet around his temples rang with the constant clatter of weapons striking the well-made cheek-pieces, and his left shoulder ached from holding the broad gleaming shield so long; yet for all they hurled at him, they could not shake him from his place. His breath came hard, the sweat poured from every limb, and there was no rest anywhere — only danger heaped on danger.

Tell me now, you Muses who hold your homes on Olympus, how fire first fell on the ships of the Greeks. Hector came in close and struck Ajax's ashen spear with his great sword, just behind the head where the point joins the shaft, and sheared it clean through. Ajax was left brandishing a headless pole, while the bronze point flew off and rang on the ground far away. He knew the work of the gods in this, and his heart shuddered: Zeus, who thunders on high, had cut his fighting short and willed the victory for the Trojans. So he gave way, and they threw tireless fire on the ship, and the flame poured over it in an instant and would not be quenched.

The fire was already licking around the stern when Achilles struck both his thighs with his hands and cried out to Patroclus: “Up now, prince Patroclus, master of horses — I see the glare of the enemy's fire at the ships. Don't let them take our ships and leave us no way home. Get into your armor, fast — I'll call the men together.”

And Patroclus armed himself in gleaming bronze. First he fastened the greaves around his shins, fine ones, fitted with silver ankle-clasps. Around his chest he buckled the breastplate of the swift-footed son of Aeacus, starry and richly worked. Over his shoulders he slung the bronze sword with its silver studs, and then the great strong shield. On his proud head he set the well-made helmet with its horsehair crest, and the plume nodded down terribly above it. He took up two stout spears that fit his grip — but not the spear of Achilles himself, heavy and huge and strong, for no other Greek could wield it; Achilles alone could swing it, that Pelian ash that Cheiron had cut on a mountaintop and given to his father, to deal out death to heroes. He told Automedon to yoke the horses quickly — the man he honored most after Achilles, the one he trusted most to stand by him in the crush of battle. So Automedon yoked the swift horses Xanthus and Balius, who flew like the wind; the storm-mare Podarge had borne them to the West Wind as she grazed in a meadow by the stream of Ocean. And in the side-trace he set the matchless horse Pedasus, that Achilles had brought back when he sacked Eetion's city — a mortal horse, but he kept pace with the immortal pair.

Meanwhile Achilles went through the huts and ordered all the Myrmidons to arm. Like ravening wolves with the fury still in their hearts, that have brought down a great antlered stag in the hills and are tearing at it, their jaws all red — and then they go in a pack to lap the dark water from a spring with their thin tongues, belching blood and slaughter, the heart in their chests unflinching, their bellies full — so the leaders and captains of the Myrmidons swarmed around the brave companion of the swift-footed son of Aeacus, and among them stood Achilles himself, urging on the horses and the men with their shields.

Fifty fast ships Achilles had brought to Troy, and in each there were fifty men at the oars. Over them he set five captains he could trust, while he commanded them all. Menesthius of the glittering breastplate led the first company, son of the heaven-fed river Spercheius; lovely Polydora, Peleus's daughter, bore him to the tireless river, a woman lying with a god, though in name he was the son of Borus, son of Perieres, who married her openly and gave a great bride-price. The second was led by warlike Eudorus, son of an unwed girl: Polymele, Phylas's daughter, lovely in the dance, bore him — the strong slayer of Argus, Hermes, had desired her when he saw her among the singing girls at a dance for Artemis of the golden arrows, and went up with her into an upper room and lay with her in secret, and she bore him a brilliant son, swift on his feet and fierce in battle. When Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth's pains, had brought him into the light and he saw the rays of the sun, mighty Echecles, Actor's son, took the mother home for a great price, but old Phylas raised the boy and cherished him as if he were his own. The third company was led by warlike Peisander, Maemalus's son, the finest spearman among all the Myrmidons after Achilles' own companion. The old horseman Phoenix led the fourth, and Alcimedon, Laerces's noble son, the fifth.

When Achilles had ranked them all in good order behind their captains, he gave them a hard charge: “Myrmidons — don't forget the threats you flung at the Trojans down by the ships through all the time of my anger, and how you blamed me. ‘Cruel son of Peleus,’ you'd say, ‘your mother nursed you on bile, you're so merciless — you hold us here at the ships against our will. If you're so set on your rage, we'd be better off sailing home.’ You said such things, gathered in your groups. Well, here it is — the great work of war you've been aching for all along. So let every man fight the Trojans with the heart he has in him.”

With those words he fired the spirit in every one of them, and the ranks pulled tighter when they heard their king. As a man fits stone to stone in the wall of a high house, to keep out the force of the winds, so close were the helmets and the bossed shields packed — shield leaning on shield, helmet on helmet, man on man, the horsehair plumes on the bright ridges touching as the heads bent together.

Out in front of them all, two men armed with a single mind to lead the Myrmidons — Patroclus and Automedon. Then Achilles went into his hut and opened the lid of a beautiful, well-wrought chest that silver-footed Thetis had set on his ship for him to take, filled with tunics and cloaks against the wind and thick warm rugs. In it lay a cup of rare make; no other man drank wine from it, and he poured a libation from it to no god but Father Zeus. He took it out, cleansed it with sulphur, rinsed it in clear running water, washed his own hands, and drew the bright wine. Then he stood in the middle of the yard and prayed, his eyes lifted to the sky, pouring out the wine — and Zeus, who delights in the thunder, did not fail to see him. “Lord Zeus of Dodona, Pelasgian, you who dwell far off and rule over wintry Dodona, where your interpreters the Selloi live around you, men with unwashed feet who sleep on the ground — you heard me once before when I prayed, and you honored me and struck the Greeks hard. Grant me this too, now. I will stay here where the ships are gathered, but I'm sending my companion out to fight with the Myrmidons in their numbers. Send glory out with him, far-seeing Zeus; put courage in his heart, so Hector may learn whether my companion knows how to fight alone, or whether his hands only rage so unstoppably when I myself go into the storm of war. And when he has driven the battle and the war cry from the ships, then let him come back to me unharmed, with his armor and all his close-fighting men.”

So he prayed, and Zeus, the lord of counsel, heard him. The Father granted him one half and refused the other. He granted that Patroclus would beat back the battle and the fighting from the ships — but he refused to let him come safe out of the fight.

When he had poured the libation and made his prayer, Achilles went back into his hut and put the cup away in the chest. Then he came out again and stood there, for his heart still longed to watch the terrible struggle of Trojans and Greeks.

And the men around brave Patroclus marched out and fell on the Trojans full of fight. They came pouring forth like wasps along the road that thoughtless boys love to torment, stirring them up where they nest by the way — the silly fools, and they make trouble for many a passerby, for if some traveler brushes them by accident, every wasp comes flying out with a fierce heart to defend its young. So the Myrmidons came swarming from the ships with hearts and courage like theirs, and their war cry rose to heaven. Patroclus shouted to his men with all his voice: “Myrmidons, companions of Achilles, son of Peleus — be men, my friends, remember your fighting strength, so we win glory for the son of Peleus, far the best of the men at the ships of the Greeks, he and his close-fighting men — and so the son of Atreus, wide-ruling Agamemnon, learns his blindness, that he gave no honor to the best of the Greeks.”

With those words he fired the spirit in every one of them, and they fell on the Trojans in one mass, and the ships rang terribly around them with the shout of the Greeks. When the Trojans saw the brave son of Menoetius and his companion blazing in their armor, their hearts shook and the ranks broke into confusion — they thought the swift-footed son of Peleus had thrown off his anger by the ships and made his peace, and every man looked around for some way to escape sheer death.

Patroclus was the first to throw, straight into the thick of the crowd where they were jammed most densely, by the stern of brave Protesilaus's ship. He hit Pyraechmes, who had led his Paeonian horsemen from Amydon by the broad waters of the Axius; the spear caught him in the right shoulder, and he fell back in the dust with a groan, and his men scattered around him, for Patroclus had killed their leader, the best of them all, and struck the fight out of them. So he drove them off the ships and quenched the blazing fire, leaving the half-burned ship to lie there. The Trojans fled with a deafening cry, and the Greeks poured out after them among the hollow ships, and the noise never stopped. As when Zeus, who gathers the lightning, lifts a thick cloud off the peak of a high mountain, and all the lookout points and jutting headlands and forest glades stand out, and the boundless air breaks open from the sky — so the Greeks, having beaten the deadly fire back from the ships, caught their breath a little. But the fight was not yet over: the Trojans were not yet turned in headlong rout, but still gave way only because they had to, fighting all the while.

Then the battle scattered, leader hunting leader, and the killing began. First the brave son of Menoetius drove his spear into the thigh of Areilycus as he turned away; the bronze went clean through and broke the bone, and he pitched forward on his face. Menelaus, dear to Ares, struck Thoas in the chest where it showed above the shield's rim, and his limbs gave way beneath him. Phyleus's son saw Amphiclus coming for him and got in first, hitting him high on the leg where a man's muscle is thickest; the spearpoint tore through the sinews, and darkness covered his eyes. Of Nestor's sons, Antilochus speared Atymnius through the flank, and he fell forward; and Maris, in fury over his brother, lunged at Antilochus across the body, but brilliant Thrasymedes was too quick and struck before he could — caught him square in the shoulder, and the spearpoint sheared the muscle from the arm and tore it down to the bone, and he fell with a crash and darkness took his eyes. So those two brothers, comrades of Sarpedon, went down into the dark, the warrior sons of Amisodarus, the man who reared the raging Chimaera, the ruin of many. And Ajax, son of Oileus, rushed Cleobulus and took him alive, tangled in the press, then loosed his strength on the spot with a sword-stroke to the neck; the whole blade ran warm with blood, and dark death and strong fate closed over his eyes.

Peneleos and Lycon ran together, for they had both missed with their spears, and now they drew their swords. Lycon struck the ridge of the other's plumed helmet, and his blade snapped at the hilt; but Peneleos caught him in the neck under the ear, and the sword sank in so deep that the head hung by nothing but a fold of skin, and the life went out of him. Meriones chased Acamas down on foot and caught him just as he was climbing to his chariot, and ran a spear through his right shoulder; he tumbled from the car, and the mist closed over his eyes. Idomeneus speared Erymas through the mouth; the pitiless bronze drove straight on under the brain, splitting the white bones, and his teeth were shaken loose, and both his eyes filled with blood, and the blood came spurting up through his mouth and nostrils as the black cloud of death wrapped him round.

So these leaders of the Greeks each killed his man. As ravening wolves fall on lambs or kids, snatching them from under the flock when a careless shepherd has let them stray on the hills, and the wolves take them at once because they have no fight in them — so the Greeks fell on the Trojans, who turned to shameful flight and forgot their fighting strength.

And all this while great Ajax kept trying to hurl his spear at bronze-helmeted Hector, but Hector knew his craft of war: he kept his broad shoulders covered behind his bull's-hide shield, watching for the hiss of arrows and the thud of spears. Well he knew the day's tide had turned, but even so he held his ground and tried to save his trusted men.

As when a cloud climbs from Olympus into the bright sky after fair weather, when Zeus stretches out the storm — so the Trojans broke from the ships now in panic and rout, and there was no order in their going. Hector's swift horses carried him out of the fight, armor and all, and he left the Trojan army trapped behind them, pinned against the trench they could not cross. Many a chariot's pole snapped in the trench, and the horses tore loose, leaving their masters' cars behind. Patroclus came on hard after them, shouting to the Greeks, his heart full of death for the Trojans, who filled all the ground between with their cries as they fled, broken; the dust rose in a cloud to the sky, and the horses strained at full stretch back toward the city, away from the ships and the tents.

Wherever Patroclus saw the men most jammed in their panic, he drove his horses straight at them, shouting all the while; under his wheels men kept pitching headlong from their cars, and the chariots crashed and overturned. Straight across the trench at a single bound went his immortal horses, the splendid gift the gods had given to Peleus, for he was set on reaching Hector — he was wild to spear him — but Hector's swift horses were already carrying him away. As the whole black earth groans under a storm in the autumn, when Zeus pours the hardest rain in his anger at men who give crooked judgments in the assembly and drive justice out, with no regard for the watching gods — and all the rivers run in flood and the torrents cut new channels down the hillsides, roaring headlong to the dark sea, and the works of men are ruined — so loud the Trojan horses groaned and labored in their flight.

Patroclus cut off the front of their broken ranks and drove them back toward the ships; he would not let them reach the city they were straining for, but pressed them in the space between the ships and the river and the high wall, and there he killed and killed and made them pay for the dead. First he hit Pronous in the chest where it showed beside the shield's rim, and his limbs gave way; then he sprang on Thestor, son of Enops, who sat huddled in his polished chariot, out of his wits, the reins gone from his hands. Patroclus came up and drove the spear into his right jaw and through his teeth, and hauled him by it over the rail of the car — the way a man on a jutting rock pulls a great fish from the sea on his line and bright hook — so he dragged him gaping from his chariot, and threw him down on his face, and the life left him as he fell. Next, as Erylaus charged him, he caught him full on the head with a stone, and the whole head split inside the heavy helmet, and he dropped face-down on the ground, and death that breaks the spirit poured over him. Then one after another he laid low Erymas, Amphoterus, Epaltes, Tlepolemus, Echius and Pyris, Ipheus and Euippus and Polymelus, son of Argeas — heaped them all on the nourishing earth.

But when Sarpedon saw his comrades going down under the hands of Patroclus, the son of Menoetius, he called out to the godlike Lycians and rebuked them: “Shame, Lycians — where are you running? Stand and fight. I'll face this man myself and find out who it is who rules the field here and has done the Trojans so much harm, cutting the knees out from under so many brave men.”

He sprang from his chariot in his armor, and on the other side Patroclus saw him and leapt down too. They flew at each other crying aloud, like hook-clawed, hook-beaked vultures that scream and tear on a high rock. And the son of crooked-counseling Cronus looked down and pitied them, and said to Hera, his sister and his wife: “This is bitter — that Sarpedon, the man I love most, is fated to die at the hands of Patroclus, the son of Menoetius. My heart is torn two ways. Shall I snatch him up out of the tears of battle, alive, and set him down in the rich land of Lycia? Or shall I let him fall now under Patroclus's hands?”

And ox-eyed lady Hera answered: “Dread son of Cronus, what a thing to say. A mortal man, marked for death long ago by his fate — and you want to free him from death and all its sorrow? Do it, if you must, but the rest of us gods won't praise you for it. And I tell you this, and lay it to your heart: if you send Sarpedon home alive, then think — some other god will want to carry his own son out of the hard fight too, for there are many sons of gods battling around Priam's great city, and you'll set bitter envy among them. No. If you love him, if your heart grieves for him, then let him fall in the strong battle under Patroclus's hands; but when the life and the spirit have left him, send Death and gentle Sleep to carry him away, until they bring him to the broad land of Lycia, where his brothers and his kin will bury him with mound and pillar — for that is the honor owed the dead.”

So she spoke, and the father of gods and men agreed. And he rained drops of blood down on the earth, in honor of his dear son, whom Patroclus was about to kill on the deep soil of Troy, far from his own home.

When the two had come up close to each other, Patroclus struck the famous Thrasymelus, the brave companion of lord Sarpedon, in the lower belly, and brought him down. Then Sarpedon cast and missed Patroclus, but his spear caught the horse Pedasus in the right shoulder; the horse screamed as the life went out of him, then fell in the dust with a groan, and his spirit flew away. The other two reared apart, the yoke creaked, the reins tangled where the trace-horse had gone down in the dust. But Automedon, famous spearman, found the cure: he drew the long sword from his sturdy thigh, leapt in, and cut the trace-horse loose, and the other two settled and pulled straight in the reins again. And the two men closed once more in the heart-eating struggle.

Again Sarpedon cast, and again he missed; the spearpoint passed over Patroclus's left shoulder and did not touch him. Then Patroclus drove home in his turn, and the bronze did not fly from his hand in vain: he caught Sarpedon where the midriff guards the beating heart. He fell as an oak falls, or a white poplar, or a tall slender pine that shipwrights cut down in the mountains with their sharp axes for ship-timber — so he lay stretched out before his horses and his chariot, groaning, clutching at the bloody dust. As a lion goes in among a herd and kills a bull, a great tawny high-hearted bull among the shambling cattle, and it bellows and dies under the lion's jaws — so under Patroclus the leader of the Lycian shield-bearers struggled, dying, and called his dear companion by name: “Glaucus, dear friend, fighter among fighters — now is the time to be a spearman, a man of nerve. Now, if ever, let this evil war be your heart's desire. First go through all the Lycian captains and rouse them to fight for Sarpedon, and then fight for me yourself, over my body, with the bronze. I'll be your shame, your reproach, all your days forever, if the Greeks strip the armor from me here, fallen among the ships. Hold hard, and call all the men to me.” As he spoke, the end that is death closed over his eyes and nostrils. And Patroclus set his heel on his chest and pulled the spear from the flesh, and the midriff came with it — he drew out the spearpoint and Sarpedon's life in a single motion. And close by, the Myrmidons held the snorting horses, wild to bolt now that they had left their masters' chariot.

Terrible grief came over Glaucus when he heard Sarpedon's voice, and it tore his heart that he could not save him. He gripped his own arm and held it, for it pained him — the wound that Teucer's arrow had dealt him from the wall, defending his men, when Glaucus had come against it. So he prayed to Apollo, who strikes from afar: “Hear me, lord, wherever you are — in the rich land of Lycia, or here in Troy — for you can hear a man in distress everywhere, and distress is on me now. I have this cruel wound; sharp pains shoot all through my arm, the blood won't stop, my shoulder is heavy with it, and I cannot hold a spear steady or go and fight the enemy. And the best of men is dead, Sarpedon, son of Zeus — and Zeus did not even defend his own son. But you, lord — heal this cruel wound of mine, lull the pains, give me strength, so I can call the Lycians to the fight and do battle myself over the body of the dead.”

So he prayed, and Phoebus Apollo heard him. At once he stilled the pains, staunched the dark blood in the cruel wound, and put strength into his heart. Glaucus knew it, and rejoiced that the great god had heard his prayer so quickly. He went among the Lycian captains and roused them to fight for Sarpedon; then he strode off into the Trojans, to Polydamas, son of Panthous, and to brilliant Agenor, and to Aeneas and bronze-helmeted Hector, and stood beside them and let his words fly: “Hector — you have utterly forgotten your allies, the men wasting their lives for you, far from their friends and their own land, and you will not lift a hand to save them. Sarpedon lies dead, the leader of the Lycian shield-bearers, who held Lycia safe by his judgment and his strength — brazen Ares has brought him down under the spear of Patroclus. Stand by him, friends, and let your hearts burn with shame, in case the Myrmidons strip his armor and shame his body, in revenge for all the Greeks we have killed by the ships.”

So he spoke, and a grief past bearing and past control swept through the Trojans, for Sarpedon, though a foreigner, had been a great pillar of their city; he had brought many men, and was the best of them all. Led by Hector, raging now over the fall of Sarpedon, they came straight at the Greeks with all their fury. And the unflinching heart of Patroclus, son of Menoetius, drove the Greeks on. He spoke first to the two Ajaxes, men who needed no urging: “Ajaxes — now let it please you to fight as you have always fought, or better. The man who was first to break over the wall of the Greeks lies dead — Sarpedon. Now let us take him, and shame his body, and strip the armor from his shoulders, and cut down with the bronze any of his comrades who try to save him.”

But they were already burning for it. And both sides braced their ranks — Trojans and Lycians, Myrmidons and Greeks — and joined in the fight over the dead man with a fearful shout, and the clash of their armor was huge. And Zeus stretched a deadly night over the bitter struggle, so the toil over his dear son would be all the worse.

At first the Trojans drove the bright-eyed Greeks back, for a man was killed who was no worst among the Myrmidons, brave Epeigeus, son of great-hearted Agacles, who had once been king in well-built Budeum, but had killed a noble kinsman and fled for refuge to Peleus and silver-footed Thetis, and they had sent him with Achilles, breaker of men, to Troy of the fine horses, to fight the Trojans. As he laid hold of the corpse, glorious Hector struck him on the head with a stone, and the whole head split inside the heavy helmet, and he fell face-down across the body, and death that breaks the heart poured over him. And grief for his dead companion seized Patroclus, and he charged through the front ranks like a swift hawk that scatters jackdaws and starlings — straight at the Lycians, Patroclus, master of horses, and at the Trojans, your heart enraged for your friend. He caught Sthenelaus, the dear son of Ithaemenes, on the neck with a stone, and tore the tendons from the bone. And Hector gave ground, and the front ranks with him — as far as a long javelin flies when a man hurls it, trying his strength in a contest or in war, so far did the Trojans give way before the Greeks. Then Glaucus, leader of the Lycian shield-bearers, was the first to turn, and he killed great-hearted Bathycles, the dear son of Chalcon, who had lived in Hellas, the richest of the Myrmidons. Glaucus wheeled suddenly and speared him through the middle of the chest just as he closed to overtake him, and he fell with a crash. The Greeks felt the loss of a brave man hard, and the Trojans rejoiced and crowded around him, but the Greeks did not forget their fighting strength, and bore straight down on them.

Then Meriones killed an armed warrior of the Trojans, Laogonus, the brave son of Onetor, priest of Zeus of Ida, honored by his people like a god. Meriones struck him under the jaw and ear, and the life rushed out of his limbs and the hateful dark took him. Then Aeneas cast at Meriones, hoping to catch him under the shield as he came on, but Meriones, watching, ducked the bronze, leaning forward, and the long spear stuck quivering in the ground behind him, until raging Ares drained the force from it. And Aeneas, his heart hot, called out: “Meriones — you may be a fine dancer, but my spear would have stopped your dancing for good if I'd hit you.” And Meriones, famous spearman, answered: “Aeneas, strong as you are, you can hardly quench the fight in every man who comes against you. You are mortal too. If I caught you square with the bronze, then for all your strength and the trust in your own hands, you would give me the glory, and your life to Hades of the famous horses.” But the brave son of Menoetius rebuked him: “Meriones, why talk like this, brave as you are? My friend, the Trojans won't draw off from the body for hard words — the earth will hold many a man first. War is settled with the hands; counsel with words. No more talk now — fight.”

And he led the way, and the godlike man went with him. As the din of woodcutters rises from a mountain glade, and the sound of it carries far, so a clamor rose from the wide earth — the clash of bronze and good ox-hide shields, as the swords and double-edged spears struck home. By now no man, however keen his eyes, could have known noble Sarpedon, for he was buried from head to foot in weapons and blood and dust. And still they thronged around the body, like flies that buzz in a sheepfold around the brimming milk-pails in the season of spring, when the milk overflows. So they swarmed around the corpse. And Zeus never turned his shining eyes from the fierce fight, but watched it all the while, his mind working over the death of Patroclus, weighing whether glorious Hector should kill him then and there, in the struggle over godlike Sarpedon, and strip the armor from his shoulders, or whether he should let him bring still more men to ruin first. And in the end he judged it better that the brave companion of Achilles, son of Peleus, should drive the Trojans and bronze-helmeted Hector back toward the city once more, and tear the life from many. So first he made Hector's heart turn weak; he mounted his chariot and fled, and called the rest of the Trojans to flee, for he saw that the sacred scales of Zeus had turned. And then not even the strong Lycians stood; they all gave way when they saw their king lying with a spear through his heart, in the heap of the dead — for many had fallen over him when the son of Cronus drew the hard fight tight. So the Greeks stripped the gleaming armor from Sarpedon's shoulders, and the brave son of Menoetius gave it to his men to carry to the hollow ships. Then Zeus, who gathers the clouds, said to Apollo: “Up now, dear Phoebus — go, lift Sarpedon out of range of the weapons, wipe the dark blood from him, and carry him far off and wash him in a running river, and anoint him with ambrosia, and wrap him in immortal clothing. Then give him to the swift escorts to carry, Sleep and Death, the twin brothers, who will set him down quickly in the rich land of Lycia, where his brothers and his kin will bury him with mound and pillar — for that is the honor owed the dead.”

So he spoke, and Apollo did not fail to hear his father. He came down from the hills of Ida into the dread struggle, and lifted godlike Sarpedon clear of the weapons, and carried him far off and washed him in a running river, anointed him with ambrosia, and wrapped him in immortal clothing. Then he gave him to the swift escorts to carry, Sleep and Death, the twin brothers, who set him down quickly in the rich land of Lycia.

But Patroclus, shouting to his horses and to Automedon, drove on after the Trojans and Lycians — the great blindness on him, the fool. Had he kept the word of the son of Peleus, he would have escaped the black fate of death. But the mind of Zeus is always stronger than a man's; he frightens even a brave man and snatches the victory from him, and at other times drives a man to fight — as now he put the fury in Patroclus's heart. Who then was the first you killed, Patroclus, and who the last, when the gods had called you to your death? Adrestus first, then Autonous, and Echeclus, and Perimus, son of Megas, and Epistor, and Melanippus; and after them Elasus, and Mulius, and Pylartes. Those he killed; the rest were glad to run.

And now the sons of the Greeks would have taken high-gated Troy by the hands of Patroclus, so wild was his spear in every direction — had not Phoebus Apollo taken his stand on the strong-built tower, with deadly intent toward him and help for the Trojans. Three times Patroclus charged the angle of the high wall, and three times Apollo flung him back, beating his bright shield with his immortal hands. But when he came on a fourth time, like something more than human, Apollo cried out to him in a terrible voice: “Back, prince Patroclus. It is not your fate to sack the city of the proud Trojans with your spear — no, nor Achilles's, who is far the better man than you.” At that Patroclus drew well back, dreading the anger of Apollo, who strikes from afar.

Hector was holding his horses at the Scaean gates, in two minds: should he drive back into the rout and go on fighting, or call the army inside the walls? While he wavered, Phoebus Apollo came up beside him in the shape of a young strong man, Asius, who was Hector's own uncle, full brother to Hecuba and son of Dymas, who lived in Phrygia by the streams of the Sangarius. In his likeness Apollo, son of Zeus, said to him: “Hector — why have you left off fighting? You should not. If only I were as much stronger than you as I am weaker, you'd soon be sorry you hung back. Come — drive your horses straight at Patroclus, and see if Apollo grants you the kill and the glory.”

With that the god went back into the toil of men. And glorious Hector told Cebriones to whip the horses into the fight. And Apollo went in among them and struck panic into the Greeks, and gave the glory to the Trojans and to Hector. Hector let the other Greeks be and killed none of them; straight at Patroclus he drove his horses. And Patroclus, on the other side, leapt from his chariot to the ground, a spear in his left hand, and in his right a jagged stone, all his hand could hold. He braced and threw it — and it did not travel far without finding a man, nor was the cast wasted: it struck Cebriones, Hector's charioteer, a bastard son of glorious Priam, full on the forehead as he held the reins, and the stone crushed both his brows together and the bone gave way, and his eyes dropped at his feet into the dust, and he plunged from the well-wrought car like a diver, and the life left his bones. And you mocked him then, Patroclus, master of horses: “Well now — there's a nimble man, the way he dives. If he were out at sea, this fellow would feed a whole crew, diving for oysters, going over the side in any weather, the way he's just dived from his chariot onto the plain. So — there are divers among the Trojans too.”

And he sprang at the body of Cebriones with the spring of a lion that, ravaging a fold, takes a spear in the chest, and his own courage destroys him — so you leapt, Patroclus, on Cebriones. Hector, on the other side, leapt down from his chariot, and the two fought over Cebriones like two lions on a mountain height, fighting over a fallen deer, both starved, both high of heart — so over Cebriones the two masters of the war cry, Patroclus, son of Menoetius, and glorious Hector, strained to cut each other with the pitiless bronze. Hector had hold of the head and would not let go; Patroclus gripped the feet; and around them the rest of the Trojans and Greeks joined in the hard struggle. As the east wind and the south wind strive against each other in a mountain glen to shake a deep wood — oak and ash and smooth-barked cornel, and the long boughs lash one another with a great roar, and the snapping of the broken branches carries far — so the Trojans and the Greeks fell on each other, hacking, and neither side thought of ruinous flight. Many sharp spears stood fast in the ground around Cebriones, and many winged arrows sprang from the strings, and many great stones beat on the shields of the men fighting around him — and there in the whirl of dust he lay, mighty in his might, his horsemanship forgotten.

While the sun stood astride mid-heaven, the weapons of both sides reached their mark and the men fell on both sides alike. But when the sun came round to the hour when the oxen are unyoked, then the Greeks proved the stronger, beyond all fate; they dragged the hero Cebriones out from under the weapons and the Trojan shouting, and stripped the armor from his shoulders. And Patroclus charged the Trojans with murder in his heart. Three times he charged, fast as the war god Ares, with a terrible cry, and three times he killed nine men. But when he came on a fourth time, like something more than human — then, Patroclus, the end of your life appeared. For Phoebus met you in the hard fight, terrible now. Patroclus did not see him coming through the rout, for the god came against him wrapped in thick mist. He stood behind him and struck his back and his broad shoulders with the flat of his hand, and Patroclus's eyes spun. And Phoebus Apollo knocked the helmet from his head, and it rolled clattering away under the horses' feet, and the plumes were fouled with blood and dust — that helmet which the gods had never let be soiled before, that had guarded the head and noble brow of godlike Achilles.
