But now Zeus gave it to Hector to wear on his own head, and his own death was near. And the long heavy spear, bronze-tipped, broke in Patroclus's hands, and the great fringed shield with its strap fell from his shoulders, and lord Apollo, son of Zeus, loosed his breastplate.

Blindness took his mind, and his shining limbs gave way beneath him, and he stood there stunned. Then from close behind a Dardanian struck him in the back with a sharp spear, between the shoulders — Euphorbus, son of Panthous, who outdid all the young men of his age with the spear and the horses and his running feet; already he had brought twenty men down from their chariots, the first time he came out to learn the war. He was the first to hit you with a spear, Patroclus, master of horses, but he did not bring you down. He pulled the ashen spear out of the wound and ran back into the crowd; he would not stand and face Patroclus, naked of armor though he was, in the open fight. And Patroclus, broken by the god's blow and the spear, drew back into the company of his men, away from death. But Hector, when he saw great-hearted Patroclus giving ground, wounded by the sharp bronze, came at him through the ranks and struck him with a spear, low in the belly, and drove the bronze clean through, and he fell with a crash, and a great anguish took hold of the Greeks. As a lion overpowers a tireless boar in a fight, when the two of them battle with high hearts on a mountain ridge over a little spring where they both want to drink, and the lion's strength masters the panting boar — so Hector, son of Priam, came up close and tore the life from the brave son of Menoetius, who had killed so many. And he stood over him and let his words fly: “Patroclus — so you thought you would sack our city, and rob the Trojan women of the day of their freedom, and carry them off in your ships to your own land. You fool. In front of all that, Hector's swift horses go out to fight; and I, of all the war-loving Trojans, am the best spear to keep the day of slavery from them. As for you, the vultures will eat you here. Poor wretch — Achilles, for all his courage, was no help to you. I'm sure he charged you sternly, staying behind while you went out: ‘Don't come back to me, Patroclus, master of horses, at the hollow ships, until you've torn the bloody shirt on murderous Hector's chest.’ That, I think, is what he told you, and your foolish heart said yes.”

Then, with the life going out of you, you answered, Patroclus, master of horses: “Boast loud now, Hector. Zeus, the son of Cronus, and Apollo gave you the victory, and they beat me — it was easy for them; they stripped the armor from my shoulders themselves. If twenty men like you had come against me, all of them would have died here under my spear. No — it was deadly fate and the son of Leto who killed me, and of men, Euphorbus; you are only the third to take my armor. And I'll tell you one thing more; lay it to your heart. You yourself won't live long now. Already death and strong fate are standing close at your side, and you will go down under the hands of blameless Achilles, the son of Aeacus.”

As he spoke, the end that is death closed over him, and his spirit flew from his limbs and went down to the house of Hades, mourning its fate, leaving manhood and youth behind. And though he was dead, glorious Hector still answered him: “Patroclus, why do you foretell my death? Who knows whether Achilles, the son of fair-haired Thetis, may not lose his own life first, struck down by my spear?” And as he spoke he set his heel on the body, drew the bronze spear from the wound, and shoved him off it onto his back. Then he went straight for Automedon, the godlike companion of the swift-footed son of Aeacus, eager to spear him too — but the immortal horses bore him away, the swift, splendid horses the gods had given to Peleus.
books.title: The Death of Patroclus

books.label: Book XVII
paragraphs: Menelaus, son of Atreus, dear to Ares, did not fail to see that Patroclus had gone down under the Trojans in the fighting. He came forward through the front ranks in his gleaming bronze and took his stand astride the body — the way a cow stands over her first calf, lowing low and tender, a young mother who has never known birth before. So yellow-haired Menelaus stood over Patroclus, holding his spear and his round shield out in front of him, set to kill any man who dared come near.

But the son of Panthous, Euphorbus of the good ash spear, had marked the body too. He came up to Menelaus and said: “Menelaus, son of Atreus, lord — pull back. Leave the body, leave the bloody spoils. I was first of the Trojans and their famous allies to drive my spear into Patroclus in the hard fighting. Let me win the glory I'm owed among the Trojans — or I'll take aim and kill you.”

Yellow-haired Menelaus answered him in anger: “Father Zeus, there's an ugly thing — a man who boasts. The leopard has no such pride, nor the lion, nor the wild boar, whose heart is fiercest of all — and yet the sons of Panthous in their high spirits outdo them all. But the strength of Hyperenor, breaker of horses, did him no good when he made light of me, when he stood and faced me and called me the worst of fighters among the Greeks. He never walked home on his own feet to gladden his wife and his honored parents. So I'll break you too, if you stand against me. Get back into the crowd; don't face me, before something worse happens. Even a fool learns once it's done.”

Euphorbus would not listen. “Now, Menelaus,” he said, “now you'll pay for my brother — the one you killed and then crowed over, the one whose wife you widowed in her new bridal chamber, leaving his parents in grief beyond all words. I'll bring some comfort to those poor people if I carry your head and your armor and lay them in the hands of Panthous and lovely Phrontis. Enough delay — let's fight it out and see which way it falls.”

With that he struck Menelaus full on the shield. But the bronze did not break through; the point bent back against the strong shield. Then Menelaus came on in his turn, praying to father Zeus, and as Euphorbus drew back he struck him at the base of the throat and threw his whole weight behind the spear, trusting his heavy hand. The point drove clean through the soft neck. He fell with a crash, and his armor rang around him. His hair, lovely as the hair of the Graces, his locks braided tight with gold and silver, were soaked now with blood. As a man raises a strong young olive shoot in a lonely place where the water runs clear — a fine thing, full of promise, swaying in the breath of every wind, breaking into white blossom — and then a sudden storm comes screaming out of nowhere and tears it from its trench and lays it flat on the earth: so Menelaus, son of Atreus, killed the son of Panthous, Euphorbus of the good ash spear, and began to strip his armor.

As a lion bred in the mountains, sure of his own strength, snatches the best cow out of a grazing herd — first he breaks her neck in his strong jaws, then tears her open and gulps the blood and the inward parts, while around him the dogs and the herdsmen raise a great noise but hang back, not one with the nerve to come close, for pale fear has them — so not one of the Trojans had the heart to go up against glorious Menelaus. And the son of Atreus would have carried off the splendid armor of the son of Panthous easily, if Phoebus Apollo had not begrudged it him. Apollo roused Hector against him, swift as Ares, taking the shape of Mentes, lord of the Cicones, and said: “Hector, you're chasing what can't be caught — the horses of the proud son of Aeacus. They're hard for any mortal man to master or to drive, for any but Achilles, whose mother is a goddess. Meanwhile Menelaus, son of Atreus, stands astride Patroclus and has killed the best of the Trojans, Euphorbus son of Panthous — he's stopped his fighting for good.”

Then the god went back into the toil and the killing, but a black cloud of grief came down over Hector's heart. He looked along the ranks and saw the one man stripping the bright armor and the other lying on the ground, the blood still running from the wound. He went forward through the front, blazing in his bronze, with a sharp cry like a flame that nothing puts out. The son of Atreus heard it, and spoke to his own great heart in dismay: “What now? If I leave this splendid armor and Patroclus, who fell here fighting for my honor, then any Greek who sees it will cry shame on me. But if for very shame I take on Hector and the Trojans alone, they'll surround me — one man against many, for Hector is bringing them all up. And yet — why is my heart even debating this? When a man fights against the god's own will, against a man a god is backing, the ruin comes down on him fast. No Greek will blame me for giving way to Hector, since Hector fights with heaven behind him. If only I could find Ajax, good at the war cry — the two of us together might remember our fighting strength even against the god, and bring the body off for Achilles. That, of these bad choices, would be the least bad.”

While he turned it over in his mind, the Trojans came on with Hector at their head. Menelaus drew back and left the body — turning his head as he went, like a bearded lion that men and dogs are driving from a farmyard with spears and shouting, until his proud heart freezes inside him and he slinks off, sore against his will. So Menelaus, son of Atreus, gave up Patroclus. He reached his own men and turned to look for huge Ajax, son of Telamon, and found him quickly on the far left of the fighting, steadying his men and urging them on, for Phoebus Apollo had thrown a great panic into them. He ran to him and said: “Ajax — here, friend, this way, fast. We have to fight for dead Patroclus. We may at least bring the body back to Achilles, the bare body — Hector has the armor already.”

The words stirred the heart of warlike Ajax, and he strode out through the front ranks with Menelaus beside him. Hector, having stripped Patroclus of his glorious armor, was hauling him away to hack the head from the shoulders with his bronze and throw the trunk to the dogs of Troy. But Ajax came up close with his shield like a tower in front of him, and Hector fell back into the press of his own men and leaped onto his chariot. He handed the beautiful armor to the Trojans to carry into the city, a great glory for himself. And Ajax spread his broad shield over the son of Menoetius and stood astride him — like a lion over its cubs, when hunters meet it in the woods as it leads its young, and it draws itself up tall in its strength, dragging its brows down low till they curtain its eyes. So Ajax stood over the warrior Patroclus, and beside him stood Menelaus, son of Atreus, his heart swelling with grief.

Then Glaucus, son of Hippolochus, captain of the Lycians, gave Hector a black look and rebuked him hard: “Hector — fine to look at, but you fall short in a fight. That great name of yours is wasted; you're a runner. Now think how you'll save your city and your stronghold with only your own people, the ones born in Ilium — for not one Lycian will go out to fight the Greeks for your city, when there's never been any thanks in it, fighting your enemies day in, day out, without rest. How are you going to save a lesser man in the crush, you ungrateful man, when you let Sarpedon — your own guest, your own comrade in arms — be left as spoil and prey to the Greeks? While he lived he did your city and you good service, and now you hadn't the stomach even to keep the dogs off his body. So if the Lycians will hear me, we're going home, and the steep ruin of Troy can come. If the Trojans had the daring, the fearless heart, that fills men who fight and labor for their own land, we'd have dragged Patroclus inside Ilium by now. If we could get this dead man into the great city of Priam, hauled out of the fighting, the Greeks would hand back Sarpedon's armor at once, and we'd carry his body home as well. For the man whose squire was just killed is the finest fighter at the ships of the Greeks — he and his close-fighting men. But you — you hadn't the heart to stand and face great-hearted Ajax, to look him in the eye in the battle's roar, because he's the better man.”

Hector of the flashing helm scowled at him and said: “Glaucus — that you, of all men, should talk so out of turn. I'd thought you the wisest head in Lycia, the whole of it; but now I think nothing of you, saying I won't stand and face huge Ajax. I don't shrink from the fight or the thunder of horses. It's the mind of Zeus who wields the storm-shield that's stronger always — Zeus, who makes even a brave man run and strips the win from him, then turns and drives him on to fight. Come here, then, friend; stand by me and watch the whole day through, and see whether I'm the coward you call me, or whether I won't bring more than one of these high-spirited Greeks to a stop, for all his eagerness, here over the body of dead Patroclus.”

So he spoke, and called aloud to the Trojans: “Trojans, Lycians, Dardanians who fight up close — be men, my friends, remember your wild fighting strength, while I put on the splendid armor of brilliant Achilles, the armor I stripped from Patroclus when I killed him.”

With that Hector of the flashing helm left the bitter fighting and ran full speed after his men, who were carrying the famous armor of the son of Peleus toward the city; they had not gone far. He caught them, and standing apart from the war and its tears he changed his armor. His own he gave to the warlike Trojans to carry to sacred Ilium, and he put on the immortal armor of Achilles, son of Peleus — the armor the gods of heaven had given to his father Peleus, and Peleus when he was old had given to his son. But the son did not grow old in his father's armor.

Zeus, who herds the clouds, saw him from far off, arming himself in the armor of the godlike son of Peleus, and he shook his head and said to his own heart: “Poor man — death is nowhere in your thoughts, and it's already standing close to you. You put on the immortal armor of the best of men, the man other men shake before. You've killed his comrade, gentle and strong, and stripped the armor wrongly from his head and shoulders. Well — for now I'll grant you great power, in payment for this: that you will never come home out of the fighting, and Andromache will never take the splendid armor of the son of Peleus from your hands.” And the son of Cronus bowed his head, his dark brows, in confirmation.

Zeus fitted the armor to Hector's body, and dread Ares entered into him, and his limbs filled with strength and fighting fury. He went in among the famous allies with a great shout, and to all of them he flashed in the armor of the great-hearted son of Peleus, until they took him for Achilles himself. Going from man to man he roused them — Mesthles and Glaucus, Medon and Thersilochus, Asteropaeus, Deisenor and Hippothous, Phorcys, Chromius, and Ennomus the bird-reader. To all of them he called out, his words flying: “Hear me, you countless tribes of allies from the lands around — it was not to swell a crowd that I called you here, each from your own city. I called you to guard the wives and little children of the Trojans, with all your heart, from the war-loving Greeks. That is why I wear out my own people with the food and the gifts that keep your spirit high. So turn now, straight at the enemy, and live or die — that is the game of war. Whoever drags Patroclus, dead as he is, into the hands of the horse-breaking Trojans, and makes Ajax give ground before him, I'll give half the spoils and keep half myself; and his glory will be equal to my own.”

At his word they bore down with their full weight on the Greeks, leveling their spears, and the hope ran high in every man that he would haul the body out from under Ajax, son of Telamon. Fools — Ajax was about to take the life out of many of them over that body. Then Ajax spoke to Menelaus, good at the war cry: “My friend, Menelaus — I no longer think the two of us will come out of this fighting alive. It isn't the body of Patroclus that I fear for most — he'll soon be glutting the dogs and birds of Troy — it's my own head, and yours, that I fear may go down. Hector is a thundercloud of war wrapped around everything, and sheer ruin is hanging over us. Call out to the best of the Greeks — see if any can hear.”

Menelaus, good at the war cry, did as he said and shouted across the Greeks in a great voice: “Friends — leaders and counselors of the Greeks, all you who drink the public wine beside Agamemnon and Menelaus, each of you commanding your own men, with honor and glory from Zeus — the fighting is so thick I can't pick any one of you out by sight. So come unbidden, every man, and burn with shame that Patroclus should become a plaything for the dogs of Troy.”

Swift Ajax, son of Oileus, heard him clearly and was first to come, running up through the fighting; and after him Idomeneus and Idomeneus's man Meriones, a match for the man-killing war-god. As for the rest who came after to wake the Greek attack — what man could call them all by name?

The Trojans came on in a body, Hector leading. As at the mouth of a river fed from heaven the great wave roars in against the current, and the headlands on either side bellow as the salt sea breaks and is flung back — with such a roar the Trojans came. But the Greeks stood firm around the son of Menoetius, of one mind, walled in behind their bronze shields. And the son of Cronus poured a thick mist over their shining helmets, for he had borne the son of Menoetius no grudge while he lived and was the squire of the grandson of Aeacus; he hated to see him made a feast for the enemy's dogs, and he stirred his comrades to defend him.

At first the Trojans pushed the bright-eyed Greeks back, and they let the dead man go and gave ground; yet for all their spears the high-hearted Trojans killed none of them — they only began to drag the body off. But the Greeks would not leave it to them long. Ajax turned them fast — Ajax, who in beauty and in deeds outstripped all the other Greeks after the matchless son of Peleus. He drove through the front like a wild boar that scatters dogs and strong young men with one easy turn, wheeling at bay through the mountain glens. So the lordly son of Telamon charged in among the Trojan ranks and scattered those who had crowded over Patroclus, all of them set on dragging him to their city and winning the glory. There Hippothous, lordly son of Pelasgian Lethus, was dragging the body off by the foot through the brutal fighting, a strap looped around the tendon at the ankle, doing a favor for Hector and the Trojans — and the ruin came on him fast, and not one of them who longed to could keep it off. The son of Telamon sprang through the press and struck him hand-to-hand on the bronze-cheeked helmet. The crested helm split open around the spearhead, struck by the great spear and the heavy hand, and the brain ran out along the socket, mixed with blood. The strength went out of him; he let Patroclus's foot drop from his hands and fell forward across the body, dead — far from the rich soil of Larissa, never to pay his dear parents back for raising him; his life was cut short under the spear of great-hearted Ajax.

Hector hurled his bright spear at Ajax, but Ajax saw it coming and just dodged it, and the spear struck Schedius, son of high-hearted Iphitus, the best of the Phocians, who lived in famous Panopeus and ruled many men. It hit him under the collarbone, and the bronze point ran straight through and out at the base of the shoulder. He fell with a crash, and his armor rang around him. Then Ajax struck warlike Phorcys, son of Phaenops, full in the belly as he stood astride Hippothous, and broke the plate of his corselet, and the bronze tore through his guts; he clutched the dust in his fist as he went down. Hector and the front-fighters gave ground, and the Greeks raised a great cry and hauled off the bodies of Phorcys and Hippothous and began stripping the armor from their shoulders.

And now the Trojans, beaten by the war-loving Greeks, would have been driven back up into Ilium, worn down by their own weakness, and the Greeks would have won glory even against the will of Zeus, by their own force and fighting heart — if Apollo himself had not roused Aeneas, taking the shape of the herald Periphas, son of Epytus, who had grown old serving Aeneas's aged father, a man Aeneas loved. In that shape Apollo said: “Aeneas — how would you ever hold high Ilium if a god were against you? I've seen men do it on their own daring, their own strength, their own numbers, with Zeus against them. But Zeus wants the victory for us, far more than for the Greeks — and you, all of you, are afraid to fight.”

Aeneas looked him in the face and knew Apollo who strikes from afar, and called aloud to Hector: “Hector, and you other captains of the Trojans and the allies — shame on us, if we're driven back up into Ilium, beaten by the war-loving Greeks through our own weakness. Just now a god stood at my side and told me that Zeus, the highest counselor, is fighting for us. Straight at the Greeks, then — don't let them carry dead Patroclus easily to the ships.”

With that he sprang far out ahead of the front rank, and the rest rallied and wheeled to face the Greeks. There Aeneas speared Leiocritus, son of Arisbas, the brave companion of Lycomedes; and Lycomedes, watching him fall, felt the pity catch in him, and came up close and threw, and struck Apisaon, son of Hippasus, shepherd of his people, in the liver below the midriff, and dropped him on the spot — a man come from rich Paeonia, the best of them after Asteropaeus. Warlike Asteropaeus sprang to defend him and rushed at the Greeks — but it was no use, for they were fenced on every side with shields around Patroclus, their spears leveled out before them. Ajax had gone all along the line with hard orders: no man was to fall back from the body, and no man was to push forward ahead of the rest to fight; they were to hold close around it and fight hand to hand. So huge Ajax commanded, and the earth ran red with dark blood, and the dead fell thick — Trojans and proud allies on one side, Greeks on the other; for the Greeks did not fight a bloodless fight either, though far fewer of them fell, since they remembered always to ward off sheer death from one another in the press.

So they fought on, like a running fire, and you would not have thought the sun was still safe in the sky, or the moon — such a darkness lay over all that part of the field where the best men stood and fought around the dead son of Menoetius. Elsewhere the other Greeks and Trojans fought at their ease under a clear sky, the sharp sunlight all around them, not a cloud on the whole plain or on the mountains; and they would even pause and rest from the painful work, standing well apart, beyond the reach of one another's spears. But the men in the middle suffered from the war and the dark together; the best of them were worn down under the cruel weight of the bronze. Two good men, though — Thrasymedes and Antilochus — had not yet heard that faultless Patroclus was dead. They still thought him alive and fighting the Trojans at the head of the press, and were holding back in reserve against the rout or death of their own comrades, watching from the flank, as Nestor had ordered them when he sent them out from the ships.

So all day long the great struggle of the bitter battle raged; and without rest the sweat ran down the knees and shins and feet, the hands and the eyes of the men who fought over the brave squire of swift-footed Achilles. As when a man gives his people a great bull's hide, soaked through with fat, to stretch — and they take it and stand around it in a ring and pull, until the wet is drawn out of it and the grease soaks in, with so many hands hauling, and the whole hide is stretched out tight — so the two sides hauled the body this way and that in a little space, hearts high with hope: the Trojans set on dragging it into Ilium, the Greeks on getting it back to the hollow ships. And a savage fighting raged about it — Ares who whips men on could not have faulted it, nor Athena, not even in their full fury. Such was the harsh struggle of men and horses that Zeus strung tight that day over Patroclus.

And all this while brilliant Achilles knew nothing of Patroclus's death. The fighting was far off, under the wall of Troy, a long way from the ships, and it never crossed his mind that Patroclus had fallen. He thought he would come back alive once he had reached the gates and turned away; for Achilles knew he was not fated to sack the city, not with Patroclus's help and not without it. His mother had told him so, again and again, when he sat alone with her — telling him the mind of great Zeus. But this time she had not told him of the great evil that had come on him: that the dearest of all his comrades was dead.

Around the body the others kept driving in with their sharp spears, killing one another. And a man among the bronze-clad Greeks would say: “Friends — there's no glory for us in going back to the hollow ships now. Better the black earth opened under all of us, here on the spot, than that we let the horse-breaking Trojans drag this man off to their city and win the glory.” And on their side a high-hearted Trojan would say: “Friends — even if it's fated that every one of us die beside this man, let no one fall back from the fighting.” So they spoke, and stirred each other's hearts. They fought, and the iron din rose up through the empty air to the bronze sky.

But the horses of the grandson of Aeacus stood apart from the fighting and wept, once they learned that their charioteer had fallen in the dust under man-killing Hector. Automedon, brave son of Diores, beat them hard, again and again, with the lash; he coaxed them with soft words, again and again he cursed them; but they would not go back to the ships at the wide Hellespont, and they would not go forward into the fighting. As a gravestone stands fixed over the mound of a dead man or a dead woman, so they stood, fixed, holding the beautiful chariot still, their heads bowed to the ground. Hot tears ran from their eyes and fell to the earth as they grieved, longing for their charioteer; and their thick manes spilled down, fouled with dust, on either side of the yoke-pad, drooping from under the yoke.

The son of Cronus saw them weeping and was moved with pity, and he shook his head and said to his own heart: “Poor things — why did we give you to lord Peleus, a mortal man, when you have no age and no death? Was it so you could grieve among unhappy men? For of all things that breathe and move upon the earth, there is nothing more wretched than a man. But Hector, son of Priam, will not ride behind you in your patterned chariot — that I will not allow. Isn't it enough that he holds the armor, and brags of it so emptily? No — I'll put strength into your knees and your hearts, to carry Automedon safely out of the fighting to the ships. For I mean to give the Trojans glory still, and let them go on killing until they reach the well-benched ships, until the sun goes down and the holy darkness comes on.”

With that he breathed great strength into the horses. They shook the dust from their manes and ran lightly, carrying the swift chariot into the fighting between the Trojans and the Greeks. Behind them Automedon fought, grieving for his comrade — swooping in his chariot like a vulture among geese, easily out of the Trojans' way as he fled, easily charging back through the thick of the press. But for all his rush he killed no man, since he could not, alone in the sacred car, both drive at them with the spear and hold the swift horses. At last a comrade saw him — Alcimedon, son of Laerces, son of Haemon — and came up behind the chariot and called: “Automedon — what god has put this empty plan in your chest and stolen your good sense? You're fighting the Trojans in the front rank, alone, with your comrade dead, and Hector glorying in the armor of Achilles on his own shoulders.”

Automedon, son of Diores, answered him: “Alcimedon — what other Greek is your equal at handling and holding these immortal horses, except only Patroclus, a match for the gods in counsel, while he lived? But now death and fate have him. Here — take the whip and the shining reins, and I'll get down from the car and fight.” Alcimedon leaped onto the war-chariot and took up the whip and reins, and Automedon jumped down.

Hector saw it and at once said to Aeneas, who was close by: “Aeneas, counselor of the bronze-clad Trojans — I see the horses of swift-footed Achilles coming into the fighting with feeble drivers. I think the two of us could take them, if your heart is willing; they wouldn't dare hold their ground and face us in a fight.” The brave son of Anchises agreed, and the two went straight on, their shoulders hidden under shields of tough oxhide overlaid with thick bronze. With them went Chromius and godlike Aretus, both together, and their hearts were high with the hope of killing the men and driving off the strong-necked horses. Fools — they were not to come back from Automedon without blood. He prayed to father Zeus, and his dark heart filled with strength and courage, and he said to Alcimedon, his trusted comrade: “Alcimedon, hold the horses close — keep them breathing right at my back. For I don't think Hector, son of Priam, will check his fury until he's killed the two of us and climbed behind the lovely-maned horses of Achilles, and scattered the ranks of the Greeks — or gone down himself among the front-fighters.”

With that he called to the two Ajaxes and to Menelaus: “Ajaxes, captains of the Greeks, and you, Menelaus — leave the dead man to the best men you have to stand over him and hold the ranks off, and come keep death from us, the living. For here, where the fighting breaks like a wave, Hector and Aeneas are bearing down on us — the two best of the Trojans. Well — these things lie in the lap of the gods. I'll make my throw, and leave the rest to Zeus.” He balanced his long-shadowed spear and threw, and struck the round shield of Aretus. The shield did not hold it; the bronze drove on through, through the belt and into the lower belly. As a strong young man with a sharp axe strikes a field-ox behind the horns and cuts straight through the tendon, so that the beast leaps forward and drops — so Aretus leaped forward and fell on his back, and the keen spear stood quivering in his guts and unstrung him. Hector hurled his bright spear at Automedon, but he saw it coming and ducked low under it; the long spear flew over and stuck in the ground behind him, the butt-end shivering, until the war-god drained its force. They would have closed and fought with swords, but the two Ajaxes forced their way through the crowd at their comrade's call and broke them apart — and Hector and Aeneas and godlike Chromius drew back in fear, leaving Aretus lying there with his heart cut through. And Automedon, a match for swift Ares, stripped the armor and cried over him: “There — I've eased my heart a little for the death of the son of Menoetius, though the man I killed was the lesser man.” With that he gathered up the bloody spoils and laid them in the chariot, and climbed up himself, his hands and feet running with blood, like a lion that has fed on a bull.

And once more over Patroclus the grim fight raged, heavy with tears, for Athena came down from heaven and woke it; far-seeing Zeus had sent her to put heart into the Greeks, for his mind had turned. As Zeus stretches a glowing rainbow out of the sky to mortals, a sign of war, or of a cold storm that stops men's work in the fields and troubles the flocks — so Athena wrapped herself in a glowing cloud and went down among the Greek ranks and roused each man. First she came to the son of Atreus, to strong Menelaus, who was near her, and taking the shape and the tireless voice of Phoenix she said: “Menelaus — it will be your shame and your disgrace, if the dogs drag the brave comrade of glorious Achilles under the wall of Troy. So hold fast, and drive on all your people.”

Menelaus, good at the war cry, answered her: “Phoenix, old friend, father — if only Athena would give me strength and keep the storm of spears off me. Then I'd gladly stand over Patroclus and defend him; his death has gone deep into my heart. But Hector rages like a fire that nothing puts out, and never stops killing, for Zeus is granting him the glory now.” It pleased the goddess, gray-eyed Athena, that of all the gods he had named her first. She put strength into his shoulders and his knees, and into his chest she set the brashness of a fly — the fly a man keeps brushing off his skin, and back it comes to bite, so sweet to it is human blood. With that boldness she filled his dark heart, and he stood over Patroclus and let his bright spear fly. There was among the Trojans a man named Podes, son of Eetion, rich and brave; of all the Trojans Hector honored him most, for he was a dear companion at the feast. Yellow-haired Menelaus struck him on the belt as he turned to run, and drove the bronze clean through; he fell with a crash, and Menelaus, son of Atreus, dragged the body out from the Trojans into the ranks of his own people.

Then Apollo came and stood by Hector and stirred him on, in the shape of Phaenops, son of Asius, who lived in Abydos and was the dearest of all Hector's guest-friends. In his shape Apollo who strikes from afar said: “Hector — what other Greek will fear you now, when you've shrunk back from Menelaus, who used to be a soft spearman? Yet he's come and carried a dead man off from the Trojans single-handed, and killed your own true comrade, a brave man among the front-fighters — Podes, son of Eetion.” A black cloud of grief came down over Hector, and he went forward through the front-fighters, armed in his blazing bronze. And then the son of Cronus took up his bright tasseled storm-shield, and shrouded Ida in cloud, and lightened and thundered hard, and shook the shield — and gave the victory to the Trojans and routed the Greeks.

Peneleos the Boeotian was the first to break and run. He had been hit on the upper shoulder, a grazing wound to the surface of the bone, by the spear of Polydamas, who had come up close and thrown. Then Hector wounded Leitus, son of great-hearted Alectryon, on the hand at the wrist, and ended his fighting; Leitus shrank back, looking about him, for his heart no longer believed he could hold a spear and battle the Trojans. And as Hector went after Leitus, Idomeneus struck him on the corselet, on the chest beside the nipple — but the long spear snapped at the socket, and the Trojans gave a great shout. Then Hector threw at Idomeneus, son of Deucalion, as he stood on the chariot, and only just missed him; but the spear struck Coeranus, the companion and driver of Meriones, who had come with him from well-built Lyctus. Idomeneus had come on foot from the ships and would have handed the Trojans a great triumph, if Coeranus had not driven up fast and saved him — bringing him life and rescue, but losing his own to man-killing Hector. For Hector struck him below the ear, on the jaw, and the spearhead drove the teeth out and split the tongue in two; he tumbled from the chariot and let the reins spill to the ground. Meriones stooped and gathered them up in his own hands and said to Idomeneus: “Lay on with the whip now, till you reach the fast ships. You can see for yourself the day is no longer ours.” So Idomeneus lashed the lovely-maned horses back toward the hollow ships, for fear had fallen on his heart.

Great-hearted Ajax and Menelaus did not fail to see that Zeus had turned the tide of the fight to the Trojans. And huge Ajax, son of Telamon, was the first to speak: “Look — by now even a fool, a child, would know that father Zeus himself is backing the Trojans. Every weapon of theirs strikes home, whether a brave man throws it or a coward — Zeus speeds them all alike; and ours fall to the ground and do nothing. Come, then — let's think how to do two things at once: bring off the body, and get home ourselves to gladden our friends, who must be grieving as they look this way, sure that nothing will hold off the murdering hands of Hector now, that he'll fall on the black ships. If only there were a man to carry the word to the son of Peleus, fast — for I don't think he's so much as heard the bitter news, that his dearest comrade is dead. But I can't see such a man anywhere among the Greeks: the men and their horses alike are wrapped in the dark. Father Zeus — lift this mist off the sons of the Greeks, make the sky clear, give us back our eyes; and if it's your will to destroy us, then destroy us — but in the light.”

So he spoke, with the tears running, and the Father pitied him, and at once scattered the mist and pushed the darkness back. The sun blazed out, and the whole battle lay open. Then Ajax said to Menelaus, good at the war cry: “Look now, Menelaus, prince — if Antilochus, son of great-hearted Nestor, is still alive, get him to run to brilliant Achilles with the word that the dearest by far of all his comrades is dead.”

Menelaus, good at the war cry, did as he said, and turned to go — like a lion turning from a farmyard, worn out at last with baiting the men and the dogs, who keep watch the whole night through and will not let him take the fat of the herd; in his hunger for meat he charges in, but it comes to nothing, for thick spears fly to meet him from bold hands, and blazing torches, and he flinches from them for all his fury, and at dawn he slinks off, sore at heart. So Menelaus turned, sore against his will, from Patroclus — afraid the Greeks in a terrible rout might leave the body to the enemy. He gave hard orders to Meriones and the two Ajaxes: “Ajaxes — captains of the Greeks — and Meriones — now, every one of you, remember poor Patroclus, how gentle he was while he lived. He had a kind heart for all men. Now death and fate have caught him.” With that yellow-haired Menelaus went off, glancing round on every side like an eagle — the sharpest-eyed, they say, of all the birds under heaven; high as he is, the swift hare crouching under a leafy bush does not escape him; he stoops on it and snatches its life away. So your bright eyes, Menelaus, prince, ranged everywhere over the crowd of your many companions, to find if Nestor's son were still alive. He saw him quickly, on the far left of the fighting, heartening his comrades and driving them on, and he came up close and said: “Antilochus — come here, prince, and hear bad news, the kind I wish had never been. You can see for yourself, I think, that the god is rolling disaster down on the Greeks and the victory to the Trojans. Patroclus has fallen, the best of the Greeks, and a great loss to us all. Run, fast, to the ships and tell Achilles, in the hope he can save the bare body for the ships — for the armor, Hector of the flashing helm has it already.”

Antilochus shuddered at the words. For a long time he could not speak; his eyes filled with tears and his strong voice was choked. But even so he did what Menelaus asked. He set off running, after handing his armor to a faultless comrade, Laodocus, who was wheeling his horses close by. So he ran from the field in tears, to carry the terrible news to Achilles, son of Peleus.

And you, Menelaus, prince, had no heart to defend the hard-pressed Pylians when Antilochus left them — and they missed him sorely. But Menelaus sent them godlike Thrasymedes, and himself went back again to the warrior Patroclus. He came running up to the two Ajaxes and said: “I've sent Antilochus off to the ships, to brilliant Achilles. But I don't think he'll come now, for all his terrible rage at Hector — he can't fight the Trojans without armor. So let's think for ourselves how to do the best we can — both to bring off the dead man, and to get clear of death and the war cry of the Trojans ourselves.” Great Ajax, son of Telamon, answered him: “Well said, glorious Menelaus. Quick, then — you and Meriones, stoop down and take the body up and carry it out of the fighting; the two of us behind you will hold off the Trojans and Hector — we two of one heart and one name, who have stood our ground side by side in the hard fighting many times before.”

So Menelaus and Meriones gathered the dead man up in their arms and lifted him high, with a great heave; and the Trojan host behind them raised a great cry the moment they saw the Greeks lifting the body, and rushed after them like hounds that fly at a wounded boar ahead of the young hunters — for a while they tear in as if to rip him apart, but every so often he wheels on them in his strength, and they scatter and bolt in all directions. So the Trojans pressed on after them in a body, stabbing with swords and double-edged spears; but every time the two Ajaxes turned and stood to face them, the color drained from the Trojans, and not a man dared spring forward and fight over the dead.

So with all their strength the two carried the body off the field toward the hollow ships. And behind them the battle stretched out savage as fire — fire that breaks out and races over a city until the houses fall in the great glare of it, and the rush of the wind makes it roar — such was the unending roar of men and horses that came after them as they bore Patroclus along. And as a team of mules puts out all its strength to drag a beam or a great ship's timber down a rough mountain track, panting and pouring sweat — so Menelaus and Meriones strained and sweated, carrying the body. Behind them the two Ajaxes held the line — as a wooded ridge thrown across a plain holds back even a great river, turning aside the cruel current of strong streams and sending them out across the flat, and not one of them, for all its force, can break the ridge through. So the two Ajaxes held back the Trojans behind them. But the Trojans kept pressing on, two of them above all — Aeneas, son of Anchises, and glorious Hector. And as a cloud of starlings or jackdaws bursts into screaming flight when it sees a hawk coming on, the killer of small birds — so before Aeneas and Hector the young Greeks ran screaming, all their old fighting heart forgotten. Much fine armor of the fleeing Greeks fell about the ditch and on either side of it, and there was no rest from the fighting.
books.title: The Fight over Patroclus

books.label: Book XVIII
paragraphs: So they fought on like a blaze of fire. Meanwhile the fast runner Antilochus reached Achilles, where he sat by his tall ships, already sensing what had truly come to pass. Heavy at heart, he said to himself: “Why are the Greeks streaming back over the plain to the ships again, driven in panic? I'm afraid the gods are about to bring on me the grief my mother once warned of — that while I still lived, the bravest of the Myrmidons would fall to the Trojans and leave the light of the sun. It must be true: the brave son of Menoetius is dead. The fool — I told him to beat the fire off the ships and come straight back, and not to fight Hector head-on.”

While he was turning this over, the son of Nestor came up to him in tears and told him the bitter news: “Son of brave Peleus, I bring you terrible word — I wish it weren't so. Patroclus is dead. They are fighting over his naked body. Hector has his armor.”

A black cloud of grief closed over Achilles. He scooped up the grimy dust in both hands and poured it over his head, fouling his handsome face, blackening his clean tunic with ash. He threw his whole great length down in the dirt and lay there, tearing at his hair with his hands. The captive women that he and Patroclus had taken cried out in their grief and ran from the tents to him, beating their breasts, their knees buckling under them. And Antilochus knelt over him, weeping, holding both his hands as he groaned — afraid he might cut his own throat with a blade.

Then Achilles let out a terrible cry, and his honored mother heard him, far down in the sea's depths where she sat beside her aged father. She cried out in answer, and the goddesses gathered to her, all the daughters of Nereus who live at the bottom of the sea — Glauce and Thalia and Cymodoce, Nesaia, Speo, Thoe, and dark-eyed Halie; Cymothoe, Actaea, and Limnorea; Melite, Iaera, Amphithoe, and Agave; Doto and Proto, Pherusa and Dynamene; Dexamene, Amphinome, and Callianeira; Doris and Panope and the famous Galatea; Nemertes, Apseudes, and Callianassa; Clymene, Ianeira, and Ianassa; Maera, Oreithyia, and lovely-haired Amatheia, and all the other Nereids of the deep sea. The shining cave filled with them, and they all beat their breasts while Thetis led the lament.

“Listen, sisters, daughters of Nereus,” she cried, “so you may know the full weight of my sorrow. I am wretched, wretched, the mother of the best of men. I bore him strong and faultless, a hero among heroes, and he shot up like a young tree. I raised him like a plant in a rich garden and sent him out in his ships to Troy to fight the Trojans — and I will never welcome him home to the house of Peleus. As long as he lives and sees the light of the sun, he lives in pain, and I can't help him, though I go to him. Still I will go, to see my dear child and learn what grief has reached him, even now, while he keeps out of the fighting.”

She left the cave, and her sisters followed, weeping, and the waves of the sea parted around them. When they came to the rich plain of Troy, they climbed up out of the water one after another onto the sand, where the Myrmidons' ships were drawn up close around Achilles. His mother came to him as he lay groaning, cradled his head in her hands, and spoke through her tears: “My child, why are you weeping? What grief has reached your heart? Tell me — don't hide it. Zeus has surely given you everything you prayed for, when you lifted your hands and begged that the Greeks be penned against their ships and feel your loss bitterly.”

With a deep groan swift-footed Achilles answered: “Mother, yes — the Olympian has done all that for me. But what good is it to me now, when my dear companion Patroclus is dead, the man I honored above all the rest, as much as my own life? I've lost him. And Hector, who killed him, has stripped that splendid armor, that wonder to look at, which the gods gave Peleus on the day they put you in a mortal man's bed. I wish you had stayed among the immortal sea-nymphs, and Peleus had married a mortal woman. Now you will have endless grief in your heart for a dead son you can never welcome home — because I will not live, I will not walk among men, unless Hector is run through by my spear first and pays for stripping the life from Patroclus, son of Menoetius.”
Thetis answered him, weeping: “Then your own death is near, my child. For your doom comes hard on the heels of Hector's.”

And swift-footed Achilles, in his great grief, said: “Then let me die at once — since I was not there to save my friend when he was killed. He fell far from home, and he needed me, and I was not there to fight for him. I will never go back to the land of my fathers. I was no light at all to Patroclus, or to all the others Hector has killed — I sat by my ships, a useless weight on the earth, though there is no Greek my equal in war, whatever better men there are in council. So let strife vanish from gods and from men — and anger, that drives even a level-headed man to fury, anger that wells up in a man's chest sweeter than dripping honey and spreads through him like smoke. That is how Agamemnon angered me. But let it be — it's done, it's behind us; I'll force my heart to bow to it, hard as it is. I'm going now, to find the man who killed the one I loved — to find Hector. And I will take my death whenever Zeus and the other gods choose to send it. Not even Heracles, the man Zeus loved most, escaped death; fate and the bitter anger of Hera brought him down. So I too will lie still, when I die, if the same doom is set for me. But until then, let me win glory — let me make some Trojan woman, some daughter of Dardanus, wipe the tears from her soft cheeks with both hands and sob out loud, so they all know I have stayed out of the war long enough. Don't try to hold me back, mother, much as you love me. You will not move me.”

Silver-footed Thetis answered: “What you say is true, my child. It is a fine thing to keep your comrades from ruin. But your beautiful armor is in Trojan hands; Hector wears it himself and struts in it — though not for long, I tell you, for his own death is close. Only do not go into the press of battle until you see me come back. At dawn, with the rising sun, I will be here, and I will bring you fine new armor from Hephaestus the lord.”

With that she turned from her son and said to her sea-sisters: “Dive now into the wide lap of the sea and go to the house of our father, the old sea-god. Tell him everything. I am going up to high Olympus, to Hephaestus the master craftsman, to ask him for a suit of glorious armor for my son.” At once they slipped beneath the waves, and silver-footed Thetis went on her way to fetch the armor for her son.

While her feet carried her up to Olympus, the Greeks were running with great cries before man-killing Hector, all the way back to the ships and the Hellespont. They could not pull the body of Patroclus out of range of the weapons raining down on it, for Hector, son of Priam, had caught up with it again, men and horsemen both, like a sheet of roaring fire. Three times glorious Hector seized the body by the feet, straining to drag it off, shouting to the Trojans; and three times the two Ajaxes, clothed in fighting fury, beat him back from it. But he held his ground, sure of himself, now charging into the thick of the fight, now planting his feet and shouting — and never giving an inch. As shepherds in the hills cannot drive a starving lion off a carcass, so the two Ajaxes could not frighten Hector, son of Priam, away from the body.

And now he would have dragged it off and won undying glory, if Iris, swift as the wind, had not come racing from Olympus to the son of Peleus, telling him to arm. Hera had sent her, in secret, without the knowledge of Zeus or the other gods. She came close and said: “Up, son of Peleus, most terrifying of men. Save Patroclus — it is for him this savage fight rages now by the ships. They are killing one another, the Greeks defending the dead body, the Trojans straining to drag it off to windy Troy. Hector is wildest of them all, mad to hack the head from the shoulders and fix it on a stake of the wall. Up, and lie here no longer. The shame of it, if Patroclus should become a plaything for the dogs of Troy. The disgrace is yours, if his body is defiled.”

Swift-footed Achilles said: “Iris — which of the gods sent you to me?” And Iris answered: “It was Hera, the honored wife of Zeus. The son of Cronus does not know I came, nor do any of the immortals who live on snow-capped Olympus.”

Swift-footed Achilles said: “But how can I go into the fighting? They have my armor. And my mother told me not to arm until I saw her come back; she promised to bring me fine armor from Hephaestus. I know of no one whose gear I could put on — except the shield of Ajax, son of Telamon, and surely he is up in the front rank, working his spear over the body of dead Patroclus.”

Iris said: “We know well your armor was taken. But go as you are — just show yourself at the trench, so the Trojans see you and shrink back, and break off the fighting. That will give the worn-out Greeks a moment to breathe, brief as it may be in the heat of battle.”

Iris said this and was gone. Then Achilles, dear to Zeus, rose up, and Athena flung her tasseled storm-shield, the aegis, around his strong shoulders. The bright goddess wrapped his head in a golden cloud and kindled a blaze of fire from it. As when smoke rises into the high sky from a city far off on an island, ringed by enemies — all day long its men fight it out from the walls, and at sundown the beacon-fires flare up in a line, the glow shooting high for the neighbors to see, in hope that they will come by ship to fight off the ruin — so the light blazed from Achilles' head into the sky. He went from the wall and stood at the trench, but he did not mix with the Greeks, for he obeyed his mother's word.

There he stood, and shouted, and from far off Athena raised her voice with his, and panic past all telling broke over the Trojans. Sharp as a trumpet's blast when a city is ringed by murderous foes, so sharp and brazen was the voice of the son of Aeacus. And when the Trojans heard that brazen cry, the heart went out of them; their long-maned horses wheeled the chariots around, sensing the ruin to come, and their drivers stood aghast at the steady fire blazing over the head of great-hearted Achilles — the fire the gray-eyed goddess had kindled.

Three times brilliant Achilles shouted across the trench, and three times the Trojans and their famous allies were thrown into confusion. There and then twelve of their best men died under their own chariots and on their own spears. And the Greeks, overjoyed, drew Patroclus out of range of the weapons and laid him on a litter. His comrades stood around him, mourning, and among them was swift-footed Achilles, weeping hot tears at the sight of his loyal friend lying torn on the bier. He had sent him out with horses and chariot into the fighting — and would never welcome him back.
Then Hera sent the tireless sun, unwilling, down into the streams of Ocean. So the sun set, and the Greeks had a rest from the grinding work of war.

On the Trojan side, when they had broken off the fight, they unyoked their horses and gathered in assembly before thinking of supper. They stayed on their feet — not a man dared sit down, for fear had hold of all of them, now that Achilles had shown himself after staying so long out of the bitter fighting. Polydamas, son of Panthous, was the first to speak. He alone of them could see ahead and behind, weigh past against future. He was Hector's friend, born on the same night, but better with words than with the spear. With clear good will he spoke:

“Think it over carefully, my friends. My counsel is this: let us go back to the city now, and not wait here by the ships for dawn out on the open plain, far from our walls. As long as this man was at odds with Agamemnon, the Greeks were easier to face, and I was glad enough to camp by their ships, hoping to take them. But now I am badly afraid of the swift son of Peleus. The way his spirit drives him, he will not be content to stay on the plain, where Trojans and Greeks share the fighting between them; he will fight for the city itself, for our wives. Let us pull back. Hear me, for this is how it will go: night, for now, holds off the son of Peleus. But if he finds us still here in the morning, when he comes out in his armor, then we will know him for what he is — and the man who gets back to Troy alive will count himself lucky, for the dogs and vultures will feed on many a Trojan. May that word never reach my ears. If we do as I say, hard as it is, we will keep our strength through the night in counsel, and the great gates and their tall doors will guard the city. At dawn we will arm and man the walls — and it will go badly for him if he comes up from the ships to fight us there. He will go back when he has worn his horses out, driving them every which way under our walls. He will never have the heart to force his way inside, and he will never sack it. The dogs will eat him first.”

But Hector glared at him and said: “Polydamas, I don't like what you're saying — telling us to fall back and shut ourselves in the city. Haven't you had enough of being penned behind walls? There was a time when the whole world spoke of Priam's city for its gold and its bronze — but our treasures are gone from our houses now, sold off to Phrygia and lovely Maeonia, since Zeus turned against us. And now, when the son of crooked Cronus has granted me glory here, to pin the Greeks against the sea by their ships — now is no time to peddle that kind of talk to the people. Not one Trojan will follow you; I won't allow it. Do as I say, all of you. Take your supper through the ranks, keep the watch, every man of you stay awake. Any Trojan who frets over his wealth — let him gather it and hand it out to the army; better our own men have the good of it than the Greeks. At first light we arm and take the fight to the ships. And if it's true that brilliant Achilles has risen up to defend them, so much the worse for him. I will not run from him. I will stand and face him, to win or to fall. Ares fights for both sides alike — and the killer is often killed.”

So Hector spoke, and the Trojans — the fools — roared their approval, for Pallas Athena had stripped them of their wits. They cheered Hector and his ruinous plan, and not a man had a word for the wise counsel of Polydamas. They took their supper through the camp. And all night long the Greeks mourned Patroclus, with the son of Peleus leading the lament. He laid his man-killing hands on his friend's breast and groaned over him again and again, like a bearded lion whose cubs a hunter has stolen from some thick wood; the lion comes back to find them gone and ranges through the glens, hunting the man's track, mad with fury — so Achilles groaned, and spoke among his Myrmidons: “What an empty promise I made, that day I tried to comfort the old hero Menoetius in his own house. I told him I would bring his brave son back to Opoeis covered in glory, with his share of the spoils, once we had sacked Troy. But Zeus does not grant men everything they hope for. The same earth here at Troy is fated to drink the blood of us both — for I will never come home either, never be welcomed by the old horseman Peleus, or by my mother Thetis; this ground will cover me too. But now, Patroclus, since I go down into the earth after you, I will not bury you until I have brought back the armor and the head of Hector, who killed you. And I will cut the throats of twelve noble sons of Troy before your pyre, in my fury at your death. Until then you will lie here by my curved ships just as you are, and the women of Troy and Dardania, the ones we took with the spear when we sacked rich cities, will weep over you night and day.”

Then Achilles told his men to set a great cauldron on the fire and wash the clotted blood from Patroclus' body. They set a tripod of bath-water over the blaze and heaped wood under it, and the flames licked the cauldron's belly until the water was hot. When it boiled, they washed the body, anointed it with oil, and filled its wounds with a salve nine years old. Then they laid him on a bier, wrapped him in soft linen from head to foot, and spread a clean white cloth on top. So all night long the Myrmidons gathered around Achilles, mourning Patroclus.

Then Zeus said to Hera, his wife and his sister: “So you've had your way after all, ox-eyed lady Hera — you've roused swift-footed Achilles. Anyone would think the long-haired Greeks were your own children.” And Hera answered: “Dread son of Cronus, what a thing to say. Even a mortal, who knows so much less than we do, will do all he can for another man. Was I, then — the highest of the goddesses, both by my birth and as your wife, you who rule all the gods — not to plot ruin for the Trojans in my anger?”

So the two of them talked. Meanwhile silver-footed Thetis came to the house of Hephaestus — a house that never dies, set with stars, the finest of all the immortal halls, built of bronze by the lame god's own hands. She found him sweating over his bellows, hard at work, finishing twenty tripods to stand around the wall of his hall. He had set golden wheels under each one, so they could roll off to the gatherings of the gods on their own and roll home again — a marvel to see. They were nearly done; only the finely worked handles were left to fit, and he was hammering out the rivets. As he worked at this, silver-footed Thetis came to him. Charis of the bright headdress, the lovely wife of the famous lame god, saw her and came forward, took her by the hand, and said: “Thetis, honored and always welcome — what brings you to our house? You come so seldom. Come inside, and let me set something before you.”

She led the way in and seated Thetis on a beautiful silver-studded chair, with a footstool beneath her feet, and called out: “Hephaestus, come here — Thetis needs you.” And the famous lame god answered: “Then it is a goddess I honor and revere who has come to my house — the one who saved me when I was in pain after my great fall, when my own shameless mother wanted me out of sight because I was lame. I would have suffered badly then, if Eurynome and Thetis had not taken me to their breasts — Eurynome, daughter of Ocean that flows in a ring around the world. Nine years I stayed with them in their cave, working all kinds of fine bronze — brooches, curved armlets, cups, and chains — with the great stream of Ocean roaring and foaming past us, and no one knew, god or man, except Thetis and Eurynome who saved me. Now Thetis has come to my house, and I must pay back everything I owe her for my life. Set out a fine welcome for her, while I put away my bellows and my tools.”

With that the huge, sooty creature heaved himself up from the anvil, his thin legs working busily under him. He set the bellows back from the fire and gathered his tools into a silver chest, then sponged the sweat from his face and hands, his thick neck and hairy chest. He pulled on his tunic, took up a stout staff, and limped to the door. Golden serving-women bustled around to support their master — they looked like living girls, with minds and voices and strength, and all the skills the gods had taught them. They moved to hold him up as he came near Thetis, sat her on a fine chair, took her hand, and said: “Thetis, honored and always welcome — what brings you to our house? You come so seldom. Tell me what you want; my heart says do it, if it can be done, if it is the kind of thing that can be done at all.”

Thetis answered him through her tears: “Hephaestus, is there another goddess on Olympus who has had to carry such grief in her heart as Zeus has loaded on me? Of all the sea-goddesses, he forced me alone to submit to a mortal man, Peleus, son of Aeacus — and I endured a mortal's bed, sorely against my will, and now he lies at home, worn out with age. And that is not the end of it. He gave me a son to bear and raise, a hero among heroes, and he shot up like a young tree. I tended him like a plant in a rich garden and sent him out in his ships to Troy to fight the Trojans — and I will never welcome him home to the house of Peleus. As long as he lives and sees the light of the sun, he lives in pain, and I cannot help him, though I go to him. The girl the Greeks chose out for him as his prize, King Agamemnon tore from his hands — and he was wasting his heart out with grief for her, when the Trojans penned the Greeks against the sterns of their ships and would not let them out. The elders of the Greeks pleaded with him and named him splendid gifts. He would not go to their rescue himself — but he put his own armor on Patroclus and sent him into battle with a great force behind him. All day they fought at the Scaean gates, and would have sacked the city that very day, if Apollo had not given Hector the glory of killing the brave son of Menoetius, who had done the Trojans so much harm in the front line. That is why I have come to your knees — to beg you, if you will, to give my son, whose death is near, a helmet and a shield, fine greaves with ankle-clasps, and a breastplate. For he lost his own when his loyal friend went down to the Trojans — and now he lies in the dirt, his heart broken.”

And Hephaestus answered: “Take heart, and let none of this trouble you. I wish I could hide him from cruel death when his hour comes, as surely as I can give him armor so splendid that everyone who sees it will be amazed.”

So he said, and left her there and went back to his bellows, turning them to the fire and ordering them to work. Twenty bellows blew on the crucibles, breathing every kind of blast — fierce gusts to drive the work when he needed them, gentler ones as he willed it, whatever served the labor in hand. He threw tough bronze into the fire, and tin, and precious gold and silver. He set his great anvil on its block, took the heavy hammer in one hand and the tongs in the other.

First he made the shield — huge and strong, worked all over, and bound around the rim with a bright triple band; and the strap was silver. The shield itself was five layers thick, and across its face he worked his cunning into one wonder after another.

On it he made the earth, and the sky, and the sea; the tireless sun and the moon at the full; and all the stars that crown the heavens — the Pleiades, the Hyades, the great strength of Orion, and the Bear, which men also call the Wagon: it wheels in one place, watching Orion, and alone has no share in the baths of Ocean.

On it he made two cities of mortal men, both beautiful to see. In one there were weddings and feasts: by the light of torches they were leading the brides from their chambers through the city, and the wedding-song rose loud, and young men whirled in the dance to the cry of flutes and lyres, while the women stood in their doorways, each marveling at the sight. But the people had crowded into the marketplace, where a quarrel had broken out: two men were contending over the blood-price for a man who had been killed. One swore before the people that he had paid it in full; the other denied he had taken anything. Both were pressing to have the matter settled by a judge. The crowd shouted for both sides, taking their parts, and the heralds held them back. The elders sat on polished stones in a sacred circle, holding in their hands the staves of the clear-voiced heralds; with these they rose, each in turn, and gave their judgment. And in the middle lay two talents of gold, to be given to the one among them who spoke the judgment most justly of all.

Around the other city sat two armies, their armor flashing. They were divided between two plans — to storm the place and sack it, or to take half of all the wealth it held. But the townsmen would not give in, and were arming for an ambush. Their wives and little children stood guard on the walls, and with them the old men, past fighting; the rest went out, with Ares and Pallas Athena at their head — both worked in gold, golden in their robes, great and beautiful in their armor as gods should be, and standing out above the smaller mortals who followed them. When they reached the place chosen for the ambush, a riverbed where the herds came down to drink, they settled there, hidden, sheathed in bright bronze. Two scouts kept watch some way off for the coming of sheep and cattle. Soon the animals came, with two herdsmen behind them playing their pipes, never dreaming of the trap. The men in ambush saw them, rushed out, and quickly cut off the herds of cattle and the fine flocks of white sheep, and killed the herdsmen too. When the besiegers, sitting in council before their walls, heard the great uproar among the cattle, they sprang up behind their horses and came at a gallop, and soon reached the place. They drew up for battle along the banks of the river and hurled their bronze-tipped spears at one another. And among them moved Strife and Uproar, and deadly Fate — she had one man freshly wounded in her grip, and another not yet hit, and a third already dead, and she was dragging him by the feet through the press; the cloak across her shoulders was soaked red with the blood of men. They closed and fought like living men, and hauled away each other's dead.

On it he set a soft fallow field, broad and rich, three times plowed; and many plowmen were driving their teams up and down across it, turning at each end. Every time they came back to the headland, a man would meet them and put a cup of honey-sweet wine in their hands, and they would turn down the furrows again, working toward the far edge of the deep field. The ground turned black behind them, the look of plowed earth — though it was made of gold. That was the wonder of his craft.

On it he set a king's estate, where reapers were cutting the harvest with sharp sickles in their hands. Armful after armful of grain fell along the swath; others bound it with twisted straw. There were three binders standing ready, and behind them boys gathered up the cut grain in their arms and kept bringing it to be bound. And among them the king stood in silence by the swath, leaning on his staff, glad at heart. Off to one side, under an oak, heralds were making a feast: they had killed a great ox and were dressing it, while the women sprinkled white barley in handfuls for the workers' meal.

On it he set a vineyard heavy with grapes, beautiful, all of gold, with the clusters hanging dark and the vines staked up on poles of silver. He ran a ditch of dark enamel around it and a fence of tin, and left one path leading in, the one the pickers took at the vintage. Young men and girls, light-hearted, were carrying off the sweet fruit in woven baskets, and in their midst a boy played a clear-toned lyre and sang the lovely Linus-song in his thin sweet voice; and they followed, beating the ground in time, singing and shouting as they skipped along.

On it he set a herd of straight-horned cattle. The cows were worked in gold and tin, and they came lowing from the farmyard to pasture along a murmuring river, by the swaying reeds. Four golden herdsmen walked beside the cattle, and nine quick dogs ran with them. But two terrible lions had brought down a bellowing bull among the lead cows, and were dragging him off as he roared, while the dogs and the young men gave chase. The lions had torn through the bull's tough hide and were gulping his blood and his inner parts, and the herdsmen kept urging the fast dogs on, in vain; the dogs would not close their jaws on the lions but stood near, barking, then shrank away.
On it the famous lame god set a meadow, broad and lovely, in a beautiful mountain glen, where a great flock of white sheep grazed, with their pens and roofed huts and folds.

And on it the famous lame god worked a dancing-floor, like the one Daedalus once made for lovely-haired Ariadne in broad Cnossus. There young men and girls worth many cattle were dancing, holding one another by the wrist. The girls wore fine linen, and the young men wore well-woven tunics with a soft sheen of oil; the girls had lovely garlands, and the young men carried golden daggers on silver belts. Now they would run in a ring on knowing feet, light and easy, the way a potter sits and tries his wheel to see if it will spin; and now they would run in lines toward one another. A great crowd stood around the lovely dance, enjoying it, and among them a singer sang to his lyre, while two tumblers spun and led the dance through the middle of them.
And around the very rim of the strong shield he set the great River Ocean.

When he had finished the shield, huge and strong, he made a breastplate brighter than the blaze of fire, and a heavy helmet, fitted close to the temples, beautifully worked, with a golden crest on top; and he made greaves of beaten tin. And when the famous lame god had finished all the armor, he gathered it up and laid it before the mother of Achilles. And she swooped down like a hawk from snowy Olympus, carrying the gleaming armor from the house of Hephaestus.
books.title: The Shield of Achilles

books.label: Book XIX
paragraphs: Dawn rose in her saffron robe out of the streams of Ocean, bringing light to gods and to mortal men, and Thetis came to the ships with the gift of the god. She found her son fallen across the body of Patroclus, weeping without restraint, and around him many of his men were weeping too. The goddess stepped into their midst and took her son's hand in hers and said: “My child, for all our grief we must let this man lie. He has fallen by the will of heaven. Take now from Hephaestus this armor, splendid beyond anything a man has ever carried on his shoulders.”

She set the armor down before Achilles, and all its worked metal rang. A tremor ran through the Myrmidons; not one of them could look straight at it, and they shrank back in fear. But Achilles, when he saw it, blazed up the harder — his eyes flashed out from under his brows like flame, and his heart filled with joy to hold in his hands the glory the god had made. When he had fed his eyes on it, he said to his mother: “Mother, the god has given me armor such as only the immortals make, that no living man could have forged. I'll arm now. But it cuts at me — I'm afraid that flies will get into the wounds of the brave son of Menoetius and breed worms in them, and foul the body now the life is gone out of it, and rot the flesh.”

Silver-footed Thetis answered: “My child, don't let that trouble your heart. I will keep the cruel swarms off him, the flies that feed on men killed in war. He could lie a full year and his flesh stay as sound as now, or sounder. Only call the Greek fighters to assembly, give up your rage against Agamemnon, arm yourself at once, and put on your strength for the fight.” With that she breathed force and daring into him; and she dripped ambrosia and red nectar into Patroclus through the nostrils, so the body would not change.

Then Achilles went out along the shore and gave a great shout to call the Greek fighters together. And now even those who had always stayed back among the ships — the steersmen who hold the helms, the stewards who served out the rations — even they came to the assembly, because Achilles had shown himself at last, after holding so long out of the fighting. Two men came limping, Odysseus and the son of Tydeus, both still in pain from their wounds, leaning on their spears; and they took their seats in the front. Last of all came Agamemnon, lord of men, wounded too — Coon, son of Antenor, had run him through with a spear in the battle.

When the Greeks were all gathered, Achilles stood and spoke among them: “Son of Atreus — was this better, for you or for me, that the two of us, sick at heart over a girl, tore into each other in a quarrel that ate our hearts out? I wish Artemis had shot Briseis dead at the ships the day I took her, when I sacked Lyrnessus. Then so many Greeks would not have bitten the dust under enemy hands while I nursed my anger. It was Hector and the Trojans who gained by it; the Greeks, I think, will remember our quarrel a long time. But let it go. It is finished. Hard as it is, I beat down the heart in me, because I must. Here, now, I put an end to my rage. It is not right to go on burning forever. So — call the army to arms, and let me go out against the Trojans and find out whether they still have any wish to spend the night by our ships. There's many a man, I think, who'll be glad to rest his knees, if he gets clear of my spear when I'm in the fight.”
So he spoke, and the Greeks were glad that the great-hearted son of Peleus had set his rage aside.

Then Agamemnon, lord of men, spoke to them — rising in his place, not coming out into the middle: “Fighters of the Greeks, servants of Ares: when a man stands up to speak, it is right to hear him out and wrong to break in; that is hard even on a skilled speaker. Who can hear, who can say a word, in an uproar? The clearest voice is drowned. To the son of Peleus I will explain myself; the rest of you, listen, and mark what I say. The Greeks have thrown this in my face before, again and again. But it was not I who did it. Zeus did it, and Fate, and the Fury who walks in the dark — they cast a wild blindness on my mind, that day in the assembly when I tore from Achilles the prize that was his. What could I do? A god brings everything to its end. Ate, eldest daughter of Zeus, is the one who blinds us all — ruin herself. Her feet are soft; she never touches the ground, but moves across the heads of men and trips them, and snares first one and then another.

“Once she even blinded Zeus, who they say is greatest of gods and men. Even him Hera fooled, woman though she was, on the day Alcmene was about to bring forth mighty Heracles in the strong-walled city of Thebes. Zeus, exulting, made his boast to all the gods: 'Hear me, every god and goddess, while I say what the heart in me moves me to say. This day Eileithyia, who brings women to their pangs, will bring into the light a man-child who will be lord over all the people around him — one of the line of men sprung from my own blood.' But Hera, with all her cunning, set a trap: 'You'll break your word — you won't hold to this. Come, Olympian, swear me a great oath that the child who falls this day between a woman's feet, born of your blood and line, shall be lord over all the people around him.'

“So she spoke, and Zeus saw nothing of the guile in it, but swore the great oath — and bitterly he paid for it after. Down she darted from the high peak of Olympus and came in haste to Achaean Argos, where she knew the noble wife of Sthenelus, son of Perseus, was carrying a child. The woman was in her seventh month, but Hera brought the boy to birth before his time, while she held back Alcmene's labor and kept the birth-goddesses away. Then she went to Zeus herself with the news: 'Father Zeus, lord of the bright bolt, I have a word for your ear. A fine boy is born this day, Eurystheus, son of Sthenelus, son of Perseus — of your own line. It is fitting that he should rule the Argives.' At that a sharp grief struck Zeus to the very heart. In his rage he caught Ate by the bright hair of her head and swore a great oath that never again should she come back to Olympus and the starry sky — she, the ruin of all. He swung her round and hurled her out of the starry heaven, and down she fell among the works of men. And he groaned over her ever after, whenever he watched his own son crushed under the shameful labors Eurystheus laid on him.

“It was the same with me. While great Hector kept killing Greeks at the ships, I could not put Ate out of my mind — the blindness she first cast on me. I was blind; Zeus took my wits away. But now I want to make it right, and to give freely besides, to make amends. So go out to the fight, you and your men with you, and I'll bring you everything Odysseus offered yesterday in your hut. Or wait, if you'd rather, hot as you are for battle, and my men will fetch the gifts from my ship, so you can see for yourself that what I give you is enough.”

Swift-footed Achilles answered: “Son of Atreus, most honored Agamemnon, lord of men — give the gifts, as is right, or keep them: that's yours to decide. But now let us think about the fight. There's no time to stand here trading words; there's work still to be done. Let every man see Achilles again among the front ranks, breaking the lines of the Trojans with the bronze — and let each of you keep that in mind, and fight.”

But Odysseus, the man of many counsels, said: “Not so fast, brave as you are, godlike Achilles. Don't send the Greeks against Troy to fight on empty stomachs. The battle, once it's joined, will be no short one, when a god breathes fury into both sides. No, tell the men to take food and wine first by the ships — there's strength in that, and staying power.
